\chapter{Statistical Physics \sphinxhyphen{} Statistics Miscellanea}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/statistics:statistical-physics-statistics-miscellanea}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/statistics:statistical-mechanics-statistics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/statistics::doc}}\subsubsection*{Information content and Entropy}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given a discrete random variable \(X\) with probability mass function \(p_X(x)\), the self\sphinxhyphen{}information (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{what about mutual information of random variables?}) is defined as the opposite of the logaritm of the mass function \(p_X(x)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}I_X(x) := - \ln \left( p_X(x) \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Information content of indenpendent random variables is additive. Since \(p_{X,Y}(x,y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}I_{X,Y}(x,y) = - \ln \left( p_{X,Y}(x,y) \right) = -\ln \left( p_X(x) p_Y(y) \right) = - \ln p_X(x) - \ln p_Y(y) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Shannon entropy.} Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) is defined as the expected value of the information content,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(X) := \mathbb{E}[ I_X(X)] = \sum p_X(x) I_X(x) = - \sum p_X \ln p_X(x) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Gibbs entropy.} Gibbs entropy was defined by J.W.Gibbs in 1878,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S = - k_B \sum_i p_i \ln p_i \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Additivity holds for independent random variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Boltzmann entropy.} Boltmann entropy holds for uniform distributions over \(\Omega\) possible states, \(p_i = \frac{1}{\Omega}\). Gibbs’ entropy of this uniform distribution becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S = - k_B \Omega \frac{1}{\Omega} \ln \frac{1}{\Omega} = k_B \ln \Omega \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy in Quantum Mechanics.} \sphinxstylestrong{todo}
\subsubsection*{Boltzmann distribution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given a set of discrete states with probability \(p_i\), and the average measure as “macroscopic quantity” \(E = \sum_i p_i E_i\), Boltzann distribution maximizes the entropy (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Link to min info, max uncertainty})
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S = - k_B \sum_i p_i \ln p_i \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The distribution follows from the constrained optimization
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\widetilde{S} = S - \alpha \left( \sum_i p_i -1  \right) - \beta \left( \sum_i p_i E_i - E \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = \partial_{\alpha} \widetilde{S} = - \sum_i p_i - 1 \\
  0 & = \partial_{\beta}  \widetilde{S} = - \sum_i p_i E_i - E \\
  0 & = \partial_{p_k}    \widetilde{S} = -k_B \left( \ln p_k + 1 \right) - \alpha - \beta E_k \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_k = e^{- 1 - \frac{\alpha}{k_B} - \frac{\beta}{k_B} E_k} = e^{-\left( 1 + \frac{\alpha}{k_B} \right)} e^{- \frac{\beta}{k_B} E_k} = C e^{-\frac{\beta}{k_B} E_k} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the normalization constant \(C\) is determined by normalization condition
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 = \sum_k p_k = C \sum_{k} e^{-\frac{\beta E_k}{k_B}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The inverse \(Z = C^{-1}\) is defined as the \sphinxstylestrong{partition function},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} Z = C^{-1} = \sum_k e^{-\frac{\beta E_k}{k_B}}\ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the probability distribution becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_k = \frac{e^{-\frac{\beta E_k}{k_B}}}{Z} =  \frac{e^{-\frac{\beta E_k}{k_B}}}{ \sum_{i} e^{-\frac{\beta E_i}{k_B}}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Properties.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{p_k}{p_i} = e^{-\frac{\beta}{k_B}(E_k - E_i)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Thermodynamics. Comparison of statistics and classical thermodynamics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
First principle of classical thermodynamics (for a monocomponent gas with no electric charge,…) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T \, dS = d E + P \, dV\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy for Boltzmann distribution} reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  S 
  & = - k_B \sum_i p_i \ln p_i = \\
  & = - k_B \sum_i \left[ p_i \left( - \frac{\beta E_i}{k_B} - \ln Z \right) \right] = \\
  & = \beta \langle E \rangle + k_B \ln Z
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From classical thermodyamics, temperature \(T\) can be defined as the partial derivative of the entropy of a system w.r.t. its internal energy keeping constant all the other independent variables,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{1}{T}
  & = \left.\left( \dfrac{\partial S}{\partial E} \right)\right|_X = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta + k_B \frac{\partial \ln Z}{\partial E} = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta + k_B \frac{1}{Z} \frac{\partial Z}{\partial E} = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta + k_B \frac{1}{Z} \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \beta} \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta + k_B \frac{1}{Z} \left( - \sum_i \frac{E_i}{k_B} e^{-\frac{\beta E_i}{k_B}} \right) \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta - \left( \sum_i E_i p_i \right) \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} = \\
  & = \dfrac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} E + \beta - E \frac{\partial \beta}{\partial E} = \beta \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Metropolis\sphinxhyphen{}Hastings}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:metropolis-hastings}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Metropolis\sphinxhyphen{}Hastings algorithm is designed to generate a collection of states according to a desired distribution \(p(s)\), using a \sphinxstylestrong{Markov process} with a unique \sphinxstylestrong{stationary distribution} \(\pi(s) = p(s)\).
\subsubsection*{Algorithm}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initialize state \(s_0\) with energy \(E_0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
while \sphinxstylestrong{not} terminal condition:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flip the spin of a randomly chosen site, to get the possible state \(s_{\widetilde{n}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
calculate the change in energy of the state \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n := \widetilde{E}_n - E_{n-1}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
update state:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n < 0\) accept the change, \(s_n = s_{\widetilde{n}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n > 0\) accept the change with probability \(\exp\left( - \frac{\Delta \widetilde{E}_n}{T} \right)\)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting from the \sphinxstylestrong{detailed balance} (sufficient but not necessary condition for the existence of a (unique?) stationary state), \(P(s'|s) p(s) = P(s|s') p(s')\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{P(s'|s)}{P(s|s')} = \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
each transition is splitted in \sphinxstylestrong{two sub\sphinxhyphen{}steps}: proposal and acceptance\sphinxhyphen{}rejection steps. Transition is written as \(P(s'|s) = g(s'|s) A(s',s)\) being \(g(s'|s)\) the proposal conditional probability, and \(A(s',s)\) the acceptance probability. Acceptance probability is choosen in a way to satisfy the conditions of time\sphinxhyphen{}reversal and ergodicity. Metropolis choice reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A(s', s) = \min \left( 1, \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \frac{g(s|s')}{g(s'|s)} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{check if Metropolis choice fulfills the necessary conditions.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example: Boltmann distribution with uniform proposal.} Let a system have Boltzmann stationary distribution, \(p(s) \propto \exp\left( - \beta E(s) \right)\), and uniform proposal conditional probability \(g(s'|s) = \frac{1}{N}\), with \(N\) the number of accessible states from the state \(s\).
\label{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 11.1.1 (Ising model on a 2D lattice with 1 flip per update)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, for an Ising model on a 2D lattice with dimension \(m \times n\) with proposal update with \(1\) flip \(N = mn\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:example-1}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 11.1.2 (Ising model on a 2D lattice with \protect\(k\protect\) flips per update)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Is a probability built with independent successive flips ok? Target states at each flip have the same probability, s.t. the probability of reaching steps \(s_k\) after \(k\) flips starting from \(s_0\) is not uniform.}


\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(g(s|s') = g(s'|s)\). The acceptance probability of the transition between different states \(s' \ne s\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A(s',s) = \min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the corresponding element of transition matrix is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(s'|s) = \frac{1}{N} \min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{diagonal elements} of the probability transition matrix \sphinxhyphen{} representing no state transition \sphinxhyphen{} are evaluated as the probability that makes \(\sum_{s'} P(s'|s) = P(s|s) + \sum_{s' \in T(s)} P(s'|s) = 1\), i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(s|s) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\begin{aligned} s' & \in T(s) \\ E(s') & > E(s) \end{aligned}} \left( 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right)  \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(P(s|s)\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  P(s|s) 
  & = 1 - \sum_{s' \in T(s)} P(s'|s) = \\
  & = 1 - \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \frac{1}{N} \min \left( 1, e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \left[ 1 - \min \left( 1, e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) \right] = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \max \left( 0, 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\begin{aligned} s' & \in T(s) \\ E(s') & > E(s) \end{aligned}} \left( 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right)  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It’s easy to prove that this probability functions are related by the detailed balance equations,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{P(s'|s)}{P(s|s')} = \frac{\min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) }{\min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s) - E(s') )  } \right) } = e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } = \frac{e^{-\beta E(s')}}{e^{-\beta E(s)}} = \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Markov processes}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:markov-processes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/rl/mdp.html}{\sphinxstylestrong{Markov Process.}} Let \(S\) a finite set of state \(s\) that can be indexed with integer indices \(i\), \(P\) the transition probability between two states at consecutive time\sphinxhyphen{}steps, \(P_{ss'} = P(s'|s)\), and \(p_0\) the initial probability. A Markox process is uniquely defined by the triple
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle S, P, p_0 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the Markov process is \sphinxstylestrong{time\sphinxhyphen{}homogeneous}, state transition matrix \(P\) is independent from the time\sphinxhyphen{}step.


\subsection{State transition matrix}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:state-transition-matrix}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-transition-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the finite set of states with integer indices, their probabilities at time \(n\) can be collected in the \(|S|\)\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional vector \(\mathbf{p}_n\). Transition from time \(n-1\) to \(n\) can be represented as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n(s') = \sum_s P (s'|s) p_{n-1}(s) = \sum_s P_{ss'} p_{n-1}(s)  \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or using matrix formalism
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}^T_{n} = \mathbf{p}^T_{n-1} \mathbf{P} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\mathbf{p}_n\) and \(\mathbf{P}\) represents probability, their elements are non\sphinxhyphen{}negative. As the \(i^{th}\) element of \(\mathbf{p}_n\) represents the probability of the system of being in state \(i\) at time \(n\), it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_i \left\{ \mathbf{p}_n \right\}_i = \sum_i p_n(i) = 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the element \(P_{ij} = P(i|j)\) represents the conditional probability of reaching \(j\) from state \(i\) in one step, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{j} \left\{ \mathbf{P} \right\}_{ij} = \sum_j P(j|i) = 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Properties}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:properties}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-properties}}

\subsubsection{Eigenvalue \protect\(s = 1\protect\), and stationary state \protect\(\ \boldsymbol\pi\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:eigenvalue-s-1-and-stationary-state-boldsymbol-pi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum of the elements of each row of \(\mathbf{P}\) is equal to \(1\), as \(\sum_{s'} P_{ss'} = \sum_{s'} P(s' | s) = 1\). Equivalently, state transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\), with the uniform right eigenvector \(\mathbf{1}\), i.e. \(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The corresponding left eigenvector is a stationary state \(\boldsymbol\pi\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boldsymbol\pi^T \mathbf{P} = \boldsymbol\pi^T \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Spectrum of the transition matrix and asymptotic behavior of the system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:spectrum-of-the-transition-matrix-and-asymptotic-behavior-of-the-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Are all the transition matrices diagonalizable?}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming the transition matrix can be diagonalized, the evolution of the system from the initial probability \(\mathbf{p}_0\) can be easily represented. The initial probabbility is written as \(\mathbf{p}_0 = c_k \mathbf{w}_k\), being \(\mathbf{w}_k\) the left eigenvectors of the transition matrix, and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{p}^T_n
  =\mathbf{p}^T_{n-1} \mathbf{P}
  =\mathbf{p}^T_{0} \underbrace{\mathbf{P} \dots \mathbf{P}}_{ n \text{ times} }
  =a_k \underbrace{\mathbf{w}^T_k \mathbf{P}}_{= \lambda_k \mathbf{w}_k^T} \dots \mathbf{P}
  =a_k \lambda_k^n \mathbf{w}_k^T \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(n \rightarrow +\infty\) only the contributions of the eigenvectors with \(|\lambda_k| = 1\) survive. If there’s only one of these eigenvalues, \(\lambda_1 = 1\), the system converges to \(\mathbf{1}\). If there are many eigenvalues with \(\lambda_i = 1\), there system converges with probability \(a_i\) to those stationary states, being \(a_i\) the component of the initial state of the system along the \(i^{th}\) eigenvector,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}_n \sim a_k \mathbf{w}_k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Components \(a_i\) can be evaluated as the dot product between the \sphinxstylestrong{dual basis} \(\{ \mathbf{v}_i \}_i\) w.r.t. the left eigenvectors and the initial state \(\mathbf{p}_0\), as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \mathbf{p}_0^T \mathbf{v}_i = a_k \underbrace{\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{v}_i}_{ = \delta_{ik} \text{, def. of dual basis} } = a_i \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}


\sphinxAtStartPar
Existence of eigenvalues \(|s_j| = 1\), \(s_j = e^{i \theta_j}\) makes limit cycles possible as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}_n \sim \mathbf{w}_j e^{i n \theta_j} \text{ + c.c.} = 2 \left( \text{re}\{ \mathbf{w}_j \} \cos \theta_j - \text{im}\{ \mathbf{w}_j \} \cos \theta_j \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss the possibility (?) of negative components. What’s a negative probability?}


\subsubsection{Detailed balance}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:detailed-balance}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-properties-detailed-balance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By definition, a \sphinxstylestrong{reversible Markov chain} has a positive stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi\) that satisfies the detailed balance equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the flow between each pair of states \(i\), \(j\) is individaully balanced. Reversibility is a sufficient \sphinxhyphen{} even not necessary \sphinxhyphen{} condition for the existence of a stationary state.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\pi_i \ne 0\) for \(\forall i\), it’s possible to define a symmetric matrix via a similarity transformation, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \sqrt{\pi_i}\sqrt{\pi_i} P_{ij} & = \sqrt{\pi_j}\sqrt{\pi_j} P_{ji} \\
  \sqrt{\pi_i} P_{ij} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi_j}} & = \sqrt{\pi_j} P_{ji} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi_i}} \\
  S_{ij} & = S_{ji} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{D} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{D}^{-1}\), with \(\mathbf{D} = \text{diag}\{ \sqrt{\pi_i} \}\). As the matrices \(\mathbf{P}\) and \(\mathbf{S}\) are related via a similarity transformation, they have the same eigenvalues

The relation between state probability \(P(E)\) \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. probability of getting a microstate with energy \(E\) \sphinxhyphen{}, degeneracy number \(g(E)\) \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the number of microstates with energy \(E\) \sphinxhyphen{} and the Boltzmann distribution \(\propto e^{-\beta E}\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(E) = \frac{g(E) e^{-\beta E}}{Z} = \frac{g(E) e^{-\beta E}}{\sum_{E'} g(E') e^{-\beta E'}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the value \(E\) of energy levels is known, the exponential is known. Probability \(P(E)\) is sampled from experiments. Thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{g(E)}{Z} = P(E) e^{\beta E} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the total number of microstate is not known, \(g(E)\) can be evaluated up to a multiplicative constant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the total number of microstates is known, \(\sum_E g(E) = N\), it’s possible to compute all the values of \(g(E)\) and \(Z\). In this case, a linear system reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases} 
  g(E) = Z P(E) e^{\beta E} \\ \\
  \displaystyle\sum_{E'} g(E') = N \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  Z = \frac{N}{\sum_{E'} P(E') e^{\beta E'}} \quad , \quad
  g(E) = \frac{N P(E) e^{\beta E}}{\sum_{E'} P(E') e^{\beta E'}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Log to avoid numerical exceptions.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ln g(E) = \ln Z + \ln P(E) + \beta E\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to evaluate \(Z\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_{E} g(E) e^{-\beta E} = \sum_{E} e^{\ln g(E) - \beta E} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and avoid overflow, the largest contribution is factored using the relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ln \sum_i e^{x_i} = \ln \left( e^{x_{max}} \sum_i  e^{-(x_{max}-x_i)} \right) = \ln e^{x_{max}} + \ln \sum_i e^{-(x_{max} - x_i )} = x_{max} +  \ln \sum_i e^{-(x_{max} - x_i )} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The largest exponential corresponds to energy value \(E_0\) at the maximum of \(P(E)\) as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E_0
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \left( \ln g(E) - \beta E \right) =  \\
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \left( \ln Z + \ln P(E) \right) =  \\
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \ln P(E) = \\
  & = \text{argmax}_E P(E) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Then the value of the partition function becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_E e^{\ln g(E) - \beta E} = \ln g(E_0) - \beta E_0 + \sum_E e^{- \Delta \left( \ln g(E) - \beta E \right)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
begin \(\Delta f = f(E) - f(E_0)\), and \(E_0\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(N\) is known, \(N = \sum_E g(E)\)

\chapter{Entropy and arrow of time}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:entropy-and-arrow-of-time}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:statistical-mechanics-entropy}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Microscopic view vs. macroscopic view.} Usually we don’t know it accurately/we don’t care to know it, and summarize it with a macroscopic view: in this description some information is lost

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Microscopic symmetry, with uniform transition matrix

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many microstates correspond to the same macrostate

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the system evolves, its macrostate may evolve towards a stationary state, corrsponding with the macrostate with the most microstates. This evolution has a preferred direction \sphinxhyphen{} defining an \sphinxstylestrong{arrow of time} \sphinxhyphen{}, the one with \sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}decreasing} expected \sphinxstylestrong{entropy}. This evolution can also be described in terms of \sphinxstylestrong{increasing ignorance}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A macroscopic equilibrium corresponds to a stationary distribution of the macrostates with quite sharp maximum. While the macroscopic view looks stationary, the system is still evolving at the microscopic level. The amplitude of oscillations around an equilibrium decreases as \(\sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\)

\end{itemize}


\section{Box occupation example}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:box-occupation-example}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:statistical-mechanics-entropy-box-occupation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} In this example, the microscopic dynamics of the system is not deterministic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A box with two rooms contains \(N\) chambers. This balls are numbered so that they are distingushable if you can see their labels.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Macrostate definition.} A macrostate of the system is defined here by the number of balls in each room, \((N_L, N_R)\). As the total number of balls is given and constant, the number of balls in one chamber, e.g. \(N_L\) in the left chamber, is enough to determine the macrostate being \(N_R = N - N_L\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Microstate counting.} The number of microstates producing the macrostate \(N_L\) is the number of combinations, \(C_{N, N_L}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Omega(N_L) = C_{N, N_L} = \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ N_L \end{matrix} \right) = \frac{N!}{(N-N_L)! N_L!} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy of a macrostate.} …
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S(n) = \ln \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Probability transition between macrostates.} Being the probability uniform for any transition of microstates, the probability of transition between macrostates reads
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:eq:entropy:box:trans-prob}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  P_{-}(n) := P(n \rightarrow n-1) & = \frac{n}{N} \\
  P_{+}(n) := P(n \rightarrow n+1) & = \frac{N-n}{N} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Expected change of entropy.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] 
  & = \sum_{i} P_i(n) \Delta S_i(n) = \\
  & = P_{-}(n) \left( S(n-1) - S(n) \right) + P_{+}(n) \left( S(n+1) - S(n) \right) = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n-1 \end{matrix} \right) }{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) } + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n+1 \end{matrix} \right) }{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) } = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} \frac{(N-n)!n!}{N!} + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} \frac{(N-n)!n!}{N!} = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n)!n!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n)! n!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} = \\
  & = \ln \frac{(N-n)! n!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} = \\
  & = \ln \frac{(N-n)}{n+1} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{n (n+1)}{(N-n)(N-n+1)} = \\
  & = \dots
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{keep going with the algebra without the limit of large number of particles…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{In the limit} \(N \gg 1\), \(n \gg 1\), \(N-n \gg 1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] 
  & \simeq \ln \frac{N-n}{n} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{n^2}{(N-n)^2} = \\
  & =      \ln \frac{N-n}{n} - \frac{2n}{N} \ln \frac{N-n}{n} = \\
  & =      \left( 1 - 2 \frac{n}{N} \right) \ln \frac{1 - \frac{n}{N}}{\frac{n}{N}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both factors change sign when \(\frac{n}{N} = \frac{1}{2}\). For \(\frac{n}{N} < \frac{1}{2}\) both factors are positive, for \(\frac{n}{N} > \frac{1}{2}\) both factors are negative. Thus, the expected variation of entropy of this process is non\sphinxhyphen{}negative for every value of \(n \in [0,N]\) and thus for every transition,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] \ge 0 \ , \quad \forall n \in [0,N] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Markov process of macrostates.} The macrostates and the transition between them can be model as a stationary \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/rl/mdp.html}{Markov process}. The probability of the system of being in (macro)state \(n\) at time \(t\) is \(p_n(t)\), and using the transition probability \(P(n|m)\) from state \(m\) at \(t-1\) to state \(n\) at \(t\), the following holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n(t) = \sum_{m} P(n|m) p_m(t-1) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or using matrix formalism, introducing transition probability matrix \(\left\{\mathbf{P}\right\}_{mn} := P(n|m)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{p}(t-1) \mathbf{P} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The transition probabilities \eqref{equation:ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:eq:entropy:box:trans-prob} define the elements of the transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{P} = \begin{bmatrix}
\cdot       & 1           &               &               &               &             &             \\ 
\frac{1}{N} & \cdot       & 1-\frac{1}{N} &               &               &             &             \\ 
            & \frac{2}{N} & \cdot         & 1-\frac{2}{N} &               &             &             \\ 
            &             & \dots         & \cdot         &         \dots &             &             \\ 
            &             &               & 1-\frac{2}{N} &         \cdot & \frac{2}{N} &             \\ 
            &             &               &               & 1-\frac{1}{N} & \cdot       & \frac{1}{N} \\ 
            &             &               &               &               & 1           & \cdot       \\ 
\end{bmatrix} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Stationary distribution.} The stationary distribution \(\mathbf{p}^*\) is invariant under a transition, i.e. it satisfies \(\mathbf{p}^* = \mathbf{p}^* \mathbf{P}\). The stationary distribution of the process is the Binomial distribution
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p^*_n = \frac{1}{2^N} \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be proved by direct computation. The first element reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_0^* = \frac{1}{N} p_1^* \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{2^N} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{N} \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{1}{N} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(n^{th}\) element (\(n \in (1,N-1)\)) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n^* = \left( 1-\frac{n-1}{N} \right) p_{n-1}^* + \frac{n+1}{N} p_{n+1}^* \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!}
 & = \left( 1 - \frac{n-1}{N} \right) \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)! (n-1)!} + \frac{n+1}{N} \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)! (n+1)!} = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \left[ \frac{N-n+1}{N} \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} + \frac{n+1}{N} \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!} \left[ \frac{n}{N} + \frac{N-n}{N} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Statistics of the stochastic process.} …

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Statistics of the stationary distribution.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average \(\mu = \frac{N}{2}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Variance \(\sigma^2 = \frac{N}{4}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Standard deviation  \(\sigma = \frac{\sqrt{N}}{2}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the relative fluctuation around the average can be estimated with the ratio of the standard deviation and the average value,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\sigma}{\mu} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so, the relative fluctuation decreases as \(N\) increases.

\subsubsection*{Average of a binomial distribution}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[n]
  & = \sum_{n=0}^{N} n \, p_n^* = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} \sum_{n=0}^{N} n \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} N \left( \begin{matrix} N-1 \\ n-1 \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \left( \begin{matrix} N-1 \\ n \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} N 2^{N-1} = \frac{N}{2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Variance of a binomial distribution}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma^2_n = \mathbb{E}[n^2] - \left( \mathbb{E}[n] \right)^2 \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}[n^2] = \mathbb{E}[n(n-1)] + \mathbb{E}[n] \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the first term follows from a similar procedure as the one used for the average, using the identity \(n(n-1)\left(\begin{matrix} N \\n \end{matrix}\right) = N(N-1) \left( \begin{matrix} N-2 \\ n-2 \end{matrix} \right)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}[n(n-1)] = \frac{N(N-1)}{4} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the variance reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma^2_n = \frac{N(N-1)}{4} + \frac{N}{2} - \frac{N^2}{4} = \frac{N}{4} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Markov process of microstates.} A microstate is defined by the id of the box of each of the \(N\) balls. One\sphinxhyphen{}step transition switch the index of one ball. If the transition probability between these microstates is uniform it has probability \(\frac{1}{N}\). Not, let’s consider two states \(i\), \(j\). If these states are adjacent, the probabilities \(P^{micro}(i \rightarrow j) = P^{micro}(j \rightarrow i) = \frac{1}{N}\), and zero otherwise. Thus, the transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}^{micro}\) between microstates is symmetric. Since the \sphinxstylestrong{transition matrix is symmetric}, the \sphinxstylestrong{stationary distribution is uniform}. This is immediately proved using the normalization condition \(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\), and the definition of a stationary distribution, \(\mathbf{p}^{* T} = \mathbf{p}^{* T} \mathbf{P}\), and the definition of symmetric transition matrix \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}^T\). The transpose of the definition of the stationary distribution, \(\mathbf{p}^* = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{p}^*\), compared with the normalization condition, provides the relation \(\mathbf{p}^* = \alpha \mathbf{1}\), and normalization condition \(1 = |\mathbf{p}^*|_1 = \alpha N\), and \(\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\). The stationary distribution for the symmetric Markov process is \(\mathbf{p}^* = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{1}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea-hs/ch/statistics/combinatorics.html}{Combinatorics} naturally links the distribution of microstates and the distribution of the macrostates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{H\sphinxhyphen{}Theorem for symmetric Markov chains.} A discrete version of the Boltzmann’s H\sphinxhyphen{}Theorem exists for symmetric Markov process, assessing that the entropy \(H(\mathbf{p}(t)) := - \sum_k p_k(t) \ln p_k(t)\) is non\sphinxhyphen{}decreasing, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(\mathbf{p}(t+1)) \ge H(\mathbf{p}(t)) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} A generic transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) satisfies the normalization condition \(\sum_j P_{ij} = 1\), for every \(i\) (row sum). For a symmetric probability matrix \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}^T\), also the column sum holds \(\sum_i P_{ij} = 1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The function \(f(x) = x \ln x\) is convex, i.e. \(f''(x) > 0\), for \(x > 0\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  f' (x) & = \ln x + 1 \\
  f''(x) & = \frac{1}{x} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  H(t+1) 
  & = - \sum_k p_k(t+1) \ln p_k(t+1) = \\
  & = - \sum_k f( p_k(t+1) ) = \\
  & = - \sum_k f \left( \sum_i p_i(t) P_{ik} \right) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jensen’s Inequality.} As \(f\) is convex, and \(\sum_{i} P_{ik} = 1\), with \(P_{ik} \in (0,1)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f \left( \sum_i p_i P_{ik}  \right) \le \sum_i P_{ik} f( p_i ) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Jensen’s inequality in the expression of \(H(t+1)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
H(t+1)
 & \ge - \sum_k \sum_i P_{ik} f(p_i) = \\
 & = - \sum_i f(p_i) \underbrace{\sum_k P_{ik}}_{=1} 
   = H(t) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. \(H(t+1) \ge H(t)\).

\section{Mathematical tools for quantum mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:mathematical-tools-for-quantum-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-math}}\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.1 (Operator)}


\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Adjoint Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.2 (Adjoint operator)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Given an operator \(\hat{A}: U \rightarrow V\), its adjoint operator \(\hat{A}^*: V \rightarrow U\) is the operator s.t.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(\mathbf{v}, \ \hat{A} \mathbf{u})_{V} = (\mathbf{u}, \hat{A}^* \mathbf{v} )_{U}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
holds for \(\forall \mathbf{u} \in U, \ \mathbf{v} \in V\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Self-Adjoint Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.3 (Hermitian (self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint) operator)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
The operator \(\hat{A}: U \rightarrow U\) is a self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint operator if
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}^* = \hat{A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint operators have real eigenvalues, and orthogonal eigenvectors (at least those associated to different eigenvalues; those associated with the same eigenvalues can be used to build an orthogonal set of vectors with orthogonalization process).

\subsection{Operators and Observables}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:operators-and-observables}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-observables-operators}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given \(\hat{A}\) and the set of its eigenvectors \(\{ |A_i \rangle \}_i\) (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{continuous or discrete spectrum…, need to treat this difference quite in details}), with associated eigenvalues \(\{ a_i \}_i\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A} |A_i \rangle = a_i |A_i\rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle = | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \Psi \rangle =  | A_i \rangle \Psi_i^A \end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle A_j | \Psi \rangle = \langle A_j | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \Psi \rangle = \Psi_j^A \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \Psi_j^A    & = \langle A_j  | \Psi \rangle \\

\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
identity operator \(\sum_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | = \mathbb{I}\), since
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \Psi \rangle = \sum_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \Psi_j^A A_j \rangle =
  \sum_i | A_i \rangle \delta_{ij} \Psi_j^A = \sum_i | A_i \rangle  \Psi_i^A  = | \Psi \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normalization:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 =\langle \Psi | \Psi \rangle = \Psi_j^{A*} \underbrace{\langle A_j | A_i \rangle}_{\delta_{ij}} \Psi_i^{A} = \sum_i \left| \Psi_i^A \right|^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(|\Psi_i^A|^2\) that can be interpreted as the probability of finding the system in state \(|\Psi_i^a\rangle\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected value of the physical quantity in the a state \(|\Psi\rangle\), with possible values \(a_i\) with probability \(|\Psi_i^A|^2\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
    \bar{A}_{\Psi} & = \sum_i a_i |\Psi_i^A|^2 = \\
            & = \sum_i a_i \Psi_i^{A*} \Psi_i^A =  \\ 
            & = \sum_i a_i \langle \Psi | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \Psi \rangle = \\
            & = \langle \Psi | \left( \sum_i a_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \right) | \Psi \rangle = \\
            & = \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle = \\
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since an operator \(\hat{A}\) can be written as a function of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
   \left( \sum_i a_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \right) \Psi \rangle 
   & = \left( \sum_i a_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \right) c_k | A_k \rangle = \\
   & =  \sum_i a_i | A_i \rangle c_i = \\
   & =  \sum_i \hat{A} | A_i \rangle c_i = \\
   & = \hat{A} \sum_i | A_i \rangle c_i = \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle \ . 
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}




\subsection{Space and Momentum Representation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:space-and-momentum-representation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-basis}}

\subsubsection{Space Representation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:space-representation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-basis-space}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Position operator} \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\) has eigenvalues \(\mathbf{r}\) identifying the possible measurements of the position
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle = \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\mathbf{r}\) the result of the measurement (position in space, mathematically it could be a vector), and \(| \mathbf{r} \rangle\) the state function corresponding to the measurement \(\mathbf{r}\) of the position.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Result of measurement, \(\mathbf{r}\), is a position in space. As an example, it could be a point in an Euclidean space \(P \in E^n\). It could be written using properties of Dirac’s delta “function”
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
    \mathbf{r} = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \delta (\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r}) \, \mathbf{r}' d \mathbf{r}'
  \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Projection of wave function over eigenstates of position operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle(t) = \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}') \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle (t) d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \underbrace{\left( \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | d \mathbf{r}' \right)}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}}} | \Psi \rangle (t) \ .
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used orthogonality (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{why? provide definition and examples of operators with continuous spectrum})
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r}' | \mathbf{r} \rangle = \delta(\mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Expansion of a state function \(|\Psi\rangle (t)\) over the basis of the position operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  | \Psi \rangle (t) = \hat{\mathbf{1}} | \Psi \rangle(t) 
    = \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' d \mathbf{r}' \right) | \Psi \rangle(t) 
    = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle(t) \, d \mathbf{r}' \ .
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unitariety and probability density
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  1 = \langle \Psi | \Psi \rangle (t) 
    & = \langle \Psi | \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' d \mathbf{r}' \right) | \Psi \rangle \\
    & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \Psi | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle \, d \mathbf{r}' \\
    & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi^*(\mathbf{r}',t) \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) \, d \mathbf{r}' \\
    & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \left| \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) \right|^2 \, d \mathbf{r}' \\
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(\left|\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)\right|^2\) can be interpreted as the \sphinxstylestrong{probability density function} of measuring position of the system equal to \(\mathbf{r}'\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average value of the operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \int_{\mathbf{r}''} \langle \Psi | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \hat{\mathbf{r}} |  \mathbf{r}'' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}'' | \Psi \rangle \, d \mathbf{r}'  d \mathbf{r}'' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \int_{\mathbf{r}''} \langle \Psi | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \underbrace{\langle \mathbf{r}' |  \mathbf{r}'' \rangle}_{=\delta(\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r}'')} \mathbf{r}'' \langle \mathbf{r}'' | \Psi \rangle \, d \mathbf{r}'  d \mathbf{r}'' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \Psi | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \mathbf{r}' \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle \, d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi^*(\mathbf{r}',t) \ \mathbf{r}' \ \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) \, d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}'}  \left| \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) \right|^2 \, \mathbf{r}' \, d \mathbf{r}' \ .
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{From position to momentum representation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:from-position-to-momentum-representation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-basis-space-momentum}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Momentum and wave vector, \(\mathbf{p} = \hbar \mathbf{k}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{p} | \Psi \rangle
  & = \langle \mathbf{p} | \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \mathbf{p} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \exp \left[ i \frac{\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{r}}{\hbar} \right] \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Relation between position and wave\sphinxhyphen{}number representation can be represented with a Fourier transform
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{k} | \Psi \rangle
  & = \langle \mathbf{k} | \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \langle \mathbf{k} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \exp \left[ i \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}' \right] \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi\rangle d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \exp \left[ i \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}' \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r}') d \mathbf{r}' = \\
  & = \mathscr{F}\{ \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \} (\mathbf{k})
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Schrodinger Equation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:schrodinger-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-schrodinger-equation}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi \rangle = \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\hat{H}\) the Hamiltonian operator and \(|\Psi\rangle\) the wave function, as a function of time \(t\) as an independent variable.


\subsubsection{Stationary States}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:stationary-states}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-schrodinger-equation-hamiltonian}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Eigenspace of the Hamiltonian operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} |\Psi_k \rangle = E_k |\Psi_k \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(E_k\) possible values of energy measurements. \sphinxstyleemphasis{If no eigenstates with the same eigenvalue exists, then…otherwise…}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Without external influence} \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{be more detailed!}, energy values and eigenstates of the systems are constant in time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, exapnding the state of the system \(|\Psi\rangle\) over the stationary states gives \(|\Psi_k\rangle\), \(|\Psi\rangle = |\Psi_k\rangle c_k(t)\), and inserting in Schrodinger equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{c}_k |\Psi_k\rangle = c_k  E_k |\Psi_k\rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and exploiting orthogonality of eigenstates, a diagonal system for the amplitudes of stationary states ariese,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{c}_k = c_k E_k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_k(t) = c_{k,0} \exp \left[- i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the state of the system evolves like a superposition of monochromatic waves with frequencies \(\omega_k = \frac{E_k}{\hbar}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle = | \Psi_k \rangle c_k(t) = | \Psi_k \rangle c_{k,0}\exp\left[-i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{d}{dt} \bar{A}
 & = \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle \right) = \\
 & = \dfrac{d}{dt} \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle + \langle \Psi | \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} | \Psi \rangle + \langle \Psi | \hat{A} \frac{d}{dt} | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \langle \Psi | \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} | \Psi \rangle + \frac{i}{\hbar} \langle \Psi | \hat{H} \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle - \frac{i}{\hbar} \langle \Psi | \hat{A} \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \langle \Psi | \left( \frac{i}{\hbar} [ \hat{H}, \hat{A} ] + \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} \right) | \Psi \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

While Schrodinger picture works with (usually) time\sphinxhyphen{}independent operators and time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent wave functions, Heisenberg picture works with time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent operators and time\sphinxhyphen{}independent wave functions. The state of a quantum system at two different times is connected by a unitary operator \(U_{t,t_0}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_t \rangle = U_{t,t_0} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Expected value.} The expected value of the physical quantity represented by the Hermitian operator \(\hat{A}\) reads

 & = \langle \Psi_{t_0} | U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0} \hat{A} U_{t,t_0} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle = \\

\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

having defined the counterpart in Heisenberg picture, \(\hat{A}_H(t) = U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0} \hat{A} U_{t,t_0}\) of the operator \(\hat{A}\) in Schrodinger picture.

\paragraph{Interaction}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:interaction}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-intro-non-relativistic-schrodinger-equation-pictures-interaction}}

\subsection{Operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:operators}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Commuting operators, \(0 = [ \hat{A}, \hat{B} ] = \hat{A} \hat{B} - \hat{B} \hat{A}\). Their eigenvalue problems read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{A} | a \rangle & = a | a \rangle \\
  \hat{B} | b \rangle & = b | b \rangle \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  a \hat{B} | a \rangle = \hat{B} \hat{A} | a \rangle = \hat{A} \left( \hat{B} | a \rangle \right) \\
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the state \(\hat{B} | a \rangle\) is an eigenstate of \(\hat{A}\), with the same eigenvalue \(a\). If the eigenvalue is non\sphinxhyphen{}degenerate, this eigenstate must be proportional to the original eigenstate, and thus \(\hat{B} | a \rangle = b | a \rangle\). If the eigenvalue is degenerate, the state \(\hat{B} | a \rangle\) can be a linear combination of all the eigenstates \(| a_i \rangle\) with eigenvalue \(a_i = a\).

\begin{split}\sigma_{r_a} \sigma_{p_b} \ge \frac{1}{2} \left|\overline{[\hat{r}_a, \hat{p}_b]}\right| = \frac{\hbar}{2}  \delta_{ab} \ .\end{split}

\section{Schrodinger}

\subsection{Derivation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:derivation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From the probability interpretation of the wave function \(| \Psi_t \rangle\), and the unitary condition \(\langle \Psi_t | \Psi_t \rangle = 1\), for every \(t\), the evolution of the system must be governed by a unitary operator \(U_{t,t_0}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} | \Psi_t \rangle = U_{t,t_0} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
for the unitary condition to hold at every \(t\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 =  \langle \Psi_{t} | \Psi_{t} \rangle = \langle U_{t,t_0} \Psi_{t_0} |  U_{t,t_0} \Psi_{t_0} \rangle = \langle \Psi_{t_0} | \underbrace{U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0}  U_{t,t_0}}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}}} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle =  \langle \Psi_{t_0} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{t,t_0}^{-1} = U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Taking the time derivative w.r.t. \(t\) of the evolution relation, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \dot{\Psi}_t \rangle = \partial_t U_{t,t_0} | \Psi_{t_0} \rangle = \underbrace{ \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0}}_{ \hat{A}(t,t_0)} | \Psi_{t} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Composition.} As \(| \Psi_{t} \rangle = U_{t,t_1} | \Psi_{t_1} \rangle =  U_{t,t_1} U_{t_1,t_0}| \Psi_{t_0} \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{t,t_0} = U_{t,t_1} U_{t_1,t_0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Indpendence of \(\hat{A}(t,t_0) = \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U_{t,t_0}\) from \(t_0\).} The operator \(\hat{A}(t,t_0) = \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U_{t,t_0}\) can thus be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}(t,t_0) = \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U_{t,t_0}^{\dagger} = \partial_t U_{t,t_1} \underbrace{U_{t_1,t_0} U_{t_1, t_0}^{\dagger}}_{ = \hat{\mathbf{1}} } U_{t,t_1}^{\dagger} = \partial_t U_{t,t_1} U_{t,t_1}^{\dagger} = \hat{A}(t,t_1) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
showing that it’s independent from the initial time, \(\hat{A}(t,t_0) = \hat{A}(t)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\(\hat{A}(t)\) is anti\sphinxhyphen{}Hermitian.} As
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \partial_t \underbrace{\left( U_{t,t_0} U_{t,t_0}^{\dagger} \right)}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}} } = \underbrace{ \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U_{t,t_0}^\dagger}_{ = \hat{A}(t)} + \underbrace{ U_{t,t_0} \, \partial_t U_{t,t_0}^\dagger}_{= \hat{A}^\dagger(t)} = \hat{A}(t) + \hat{A}^\dagger(t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(\hat{A} = - \hat{A}^\dagger\). Thus the operator \(\hat{A}\) can be written as \(\hat{A} = i \hat{\tilde{H}}\), being \(\hat{\tilde{H}}\) and Hermitian operator. For the correspondence principle (classical limit for \(\hbar \rightarrow 0\)) the Hermitian operator is found to be \(\hat{\tilde{H}} = -\frac{1}{\hbar} \hat{H}\), being \(\hat{H}\) the Hamiltonian operator. \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add a link to “correspondence principle”, either Ehrenfest theorem and/ or equations in Heisenberg picture}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the wave equation becomes
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:eq:schrodinger}
\begin{split}| \dot{\Psi} \rangle = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle \qquad \text{or} \qquad i \hbar | \dot{\Psi} \rangle = \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian can be written as a function of the unitary operator \(U_{t,t_0}\) and its time derivative as
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:eq:h-u-dtu}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = i \hbar \, \partial_t U_{t,t_0} U^{\dagger}_{t,t_0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Energy eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:energy-eigen-states}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} | \Psi_k \rangle = E_k | \Psi_k \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the Hamiltonian be independent from time, thus also the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are independent from time. Let a state be a superposition (linear combination) of eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_t \rangle = c_{k}(t) | \Psi_k \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the time evolution immedately follows as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \dot{c}_k | \Psi_k \rangle = c_k \hat{H} | \Psi_k \rangle = c_k E_k | \Psi_k \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
from orthogonality condition \(\langle \Psi_j | \Psi_k \rangle = \delta_{jk}\), that gives the dynamical equation for the coefficients \(c_i\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{c}_k = - i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} c_k \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution is \(c_k(t) = c_{k,0} \exp \left( - i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right)\). The evolution of the state is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_t \rangle = | \Psi_k \rangle c_{k,0} \exp\left( - i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right) = | \Psi_k \rangle \langle \Psi_k | \Psi_0 \rangle \exp\left( - i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Properties.} If an \sphinxstylestrong{isolated system} starts in an eigen\sphinxhyphen{}state of the Hamiltonian operator, i.e. \(| \Psi_0 \rangle = | \Psi_a \rangle\), \(|c_{k,0}|^2 = \delta_{ka}\), then the evolution of the system reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_t \rangle = | \Psi_a \rangle \exp\left( - i \frac{E_a}{\hbar} t \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the probability of measuring the \(k^{th}\) energy is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(E = E_k) = | \langle \Psi_k | \Psi_t \rangle |^2 = \left| \underbrace{\langle \Psi_k | \Psi_a \rangle}_{\delta_{ka}} \exp\left(-i \frac{E_a}{\hbar} t\right) \right|^2 = \delta_{ka} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. there’s probability of finding it in the same state as the initial state \(a\) is \(p(E = E_a) = 1\), while the probability of finding in any other state is zero, \(p(E = E_k) = 0\), \(k \ne a\).


\subsection{Space and momentum operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:space-and-momentum-operators}}\subsubsection*{Position operator}
\subsubsection*{Definition}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle = \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Wave function in space basis}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) := \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi_t \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Orthonality, and identity operator}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  1
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in \Omega} \Psi^*(\mathbf{r},t) \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) d \mathbf{r} = \\
  & = \langle \Psi_t | \, \underbrace{\int_{\mathbf{r} \in \Omega} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r}}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}} } \, | \Psi_t \rangle  = \\
  & = \langle \Psi_t | \Psi_t \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
So that the identity operator in space basis reads \(\hat{\mathbf{1}} = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in \Omega} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r}\). A wave function can be thus written as
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:eq:quantum:space-representation}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle = \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in \Omega} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \, d \mathbf{r}' \, | \Psi \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Expansion in space basis}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle = \Psi(\mathbf{r},t)
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in \Omega} \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}') \Psi(\mathbf{r}',t) \, d \mathbf{r}'
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparing the last expression, with the projection of the expression \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/wave-mechanics:eq:quantum:space-representation} over \(\langle \mathbf{r} |\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle = \langle \mathbf{r} |  \ , \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in \Omega} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \, d \mathbf{r}' \, | \Psi \rangle = \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in \Omega} \langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle \,  d \mathbf{r}' = \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in \Omega} \langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \Psi(\mathbf{r'},t ) \,  d \mathbf{r}' \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if follows the orthogonality condition \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle = \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}')\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The classical Hamiltonian of  the system reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{p}) = \frac{| \mathbf{p} |^2 }{2m} - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon | \mathbf{r} |} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the promotion to the Hamiltonian operator is thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \frac{| \hat{\mathbf{p}} |^2}{2 m } - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \hat{|\mathbf{r}|}^{-1} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Power of an operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Positive integer power
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}^n = \underbrace{\hat{A} \dots \hat{A}}_{\text{$n$ times}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the eigenproblem of the operator be \(\hat{A} | a \rangle = a | a \rangle\), with \(a \in \mathbb{R}\). Then, the eigenproblem for the operator \(\hat{A}^n\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}^n | a \rangle = a^n | a \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The inverse of an operator has the eigenproblem
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}^{-1} | a \rangle = \frac{1}{a} | a \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as \(| a \rangle = \hat{A} \left( \hat{A}^{-1} | a \rangle \right) = \frac{1}{a} \hat{A} | a \rangle = \frac{1}{a} \, a | a \rangle = | a \rangle\).
\subsubsection*{Vector operators}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Momentum operator, \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}\), in space base \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} = -i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} |\).
Using Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \, \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_a = - \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \, i \hbar \partial_a \langle \mathbf{r} |\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The operator of the square magnitude reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\left( | \mathbf{p}|^2 \right)} = \hat{\left( p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2 \right)} = \hat{p_x^2} +  \hat{p_y^2} + \hat{p_z^2} \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and in space coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\left( |\mathbf{p} |^2 \right)} = - \hbar^2 \partial_{aa} \langle \mathbf{r} | = - \hbar^2 \nabla^2 \langle \mathbf{r} | \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Angular Momentum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum:angular-momentum}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before going into details, an introduction is likely to be required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spatial}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Spatial (orbital) angular momentum, \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\)}}}}.} Spatial angular motion is the quantum mechanical counterpart of the angular momentum in classical mechanics, \(\hat{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}\), due to the spatial motion of the system w.r.t. a point. The angular momentum operator in quantum mechanics can be defined promoting the classical space and momentum variables to the corresponding operators,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} \qquad \rightarrow \qquad \hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \hat{\mathbf{p}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose representation using spatial basis reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{L}} = -i \hbar \mathbf{r} \times \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} | \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This operator has several properties that will be investigated in details in the dedicated section. This operator applies to a wave function representing the position, momentum, and physical quantities with classical analogous, here called \(| \psi \rangle\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spin}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Spin (intrinsic) angular momentum, \(\hat{\mathbf{S}}\)}}}}.} Quantum systems may have intrinsic properties, with no classical counterpart. Spin momentum is one of these variables. Spin angular momentum \(\hat{\mathbf{S}}\) is defined in analogy with the spatial orbital momentum, with the same properties and acts on a spin state vector \(| s \rangle\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the full state of the system belongs to a space state that is a tensor product of a space and a spin state space,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_{space} \otimes \mathcal{H}_{spin} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
defined as the tensor product of a spatial state vector and a spin state vector,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle = | \psi \rangle \otimes | s \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-total:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-total}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Total angular momentum \(\hat{\mathbf{J}}\)}}}}.} Total angular momentum can be defined as the sum of the spatial and the spin angular momentum,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{J}} = \left( \hat{\mathbf{L}} \otimes \hat{\mathbf{1}} \right) + \left( \hat{\mathbf{1}} \otimes \hat{\mathbf{S}} \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, remembering that \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) only acts on \(| \psi \rangle\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{S}}\) onlt acts on \(| s \rangle\), it’s usually written as \(\hat{\mathbf{J}} = \hat{\mathbf{L}} + \hat{\mathbf{S}}\).

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Spatial Angular Momentum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:spatial-angular-momentum}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spatial}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Promoting the classical definition of angular momentum \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}\), the angular momentum operator in quantum mechanics reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \hat{r} \hat{p}_c \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and using space basis
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \underbrace{\left( - i \, \hbar \, \varepsilon_{abc}\, r_b \, \partial_c \langle \mathbf{r} | \right) }_{= \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{L}_a }\ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Properties}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Composition of 2 components of the angular momentum operator.} Using Cartesian coordinates

\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}

  & = - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{acd} \varepsilon_{bef} r_c \left( \delta_{de} \partial_f + r_e \partial_{df} \right) = \\
  & = - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{acd} \varepsilon_{bdf} r_c \partial_f - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{acd} \varepsilon_{bdf} r_c r_e \partial_{df} = \\
  & = - \hbar^2 \left( \delta_{af} \delta_{cb} - \delta_{ab} \delta_{cf} \right) r_c \partial_f - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{acd} \varepsilon_{bef} r_c r_e \partial_{df} = \\
  & = - \hbar^2 r_b \partial_a + \hbar^2 \delta_{ab} r_c \partial_c - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{acd} \varepsilon_{bef} r_c r_e \partial_{df} = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The last term is symmetric w.r.t. \(a\), \(b\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutators.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{L}_a, \hat{L}_b ] = \hat{L}_a \hat{L}_b -  \hat{L}_b \hat{L}_a = - \hbar^2 ( r_b\partial_a - r_a \partial_b) \end{split}

If \(a = b\), the obvious result follows, as an operator commutes with itself. If \(a \ne b\),

or with a compact “vector notation”, \(\hat{\mathbf{L}} \times \hat{\mathbf{L}} = i \hbar \hat{\mathbf{L}}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Magnitude of the angular momentum, \(|\hat{L}|^2\).} Using Cartesian coordinates,

\subsection{Eigenproblem of angular momentum operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:eigenproblem-of-angular-momentum-operators}}

In this section, the eigenproblems of \(\hat{L}^2\) and \(\hat{L}_z\) are discussed. Here, all the operators and state functions are written in components using space basis, without explicitly writing the projection \(\langle \mathbf{r} |\).
\begin{itemize}

\subsection{Properties of spin angular momentum operators \protect\(\hat{S}^2\protect\), \protect\(\hat{S}_z\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:properties-of-spin-angular-momentum-operators-hat-s-2-hat-s-z}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spin-operator}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In analogy with the spatial angular momentum, and using Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left[ S_a, S_b \right] & = i \hbar \, \varepsilon_{abc} S_c \\
  \left[ S_a, S^2 \right] & = 0 \ . \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the operators \(S_z\) and \(S^2\) commute, they share the same eigenvectors \(| s, m_s \rangle\) (all the eigvecs?) and their eigenproblems read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  S_z | s, m_s \rangle & = \hbar m_s | s, m_s \rangle \\
  S^2 | s, m_s \rangle & = \hbar^2 s ( s + 1 ) | s, m_s \rangle \ , 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of \(s\) depends on the system of interest: for an electron \(s = \frac{1}{2}\). The value of the spin projection quantum number \(m_s\) belongs to \(m_s \in \{ -s, -s+1, \dots, s-1, s \}\). For an electron, \(m_s \in \left\{ - \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right\}\).


\subsection{Pauli matrices}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:pauli-matrices}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spin-pauli-matrices}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \sigma_x & = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &  1 \\ 1 &  0 \end{bmatrix} \\
 \sigma_y & = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i &  0 \end{bmatrix} \\
 \sigma_z & = \begin{bmatrix} 1 &  0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Properties}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:properties}}

\subsubsection{Pauli vectors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:pauli-vectors}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a Cartesian basis, a Pauli vector is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boldsymbol\sigma := \sum_k \sigma_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the dot product with a vector \(\mathbf{a} = \sum_k a_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \mathbf{a} \cdot \boldsymbol\sigma 
 & = \sum_{l,k} a_l \underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_l \cdot \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k}_{\delta_{kl}} \sigma_k = \sum_k a_k \, \sigma_k
   = \begin{bmatrix} a_3 & a_1 - i a_2 \\ a_1 + i a_2 & - a_3 \end{bmatrix} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Eigenvalue problem of the total angular momentum for an electron}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-total:eigenvalue-problem-of-the-total-angular-momentum-for-an-electron}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutation of operators.} The operators \(\hat{J}^2\), \(\hat{J}_z\), \(\hat{L}^2\), \(\hat{S}^2\) commute, and thus they share common eigenvectors

\sphinxAtStartPar
The operator \(\hat{J}_z\) commutes with \(\hat{L}^2\) and \(\hat{S}^2\), \(\left[ \hat{J}_z, \hat{L}^2 \right] = 0\), \(\left[ \hat{J}_z, \hat{S}^2 \right] = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Proof}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left[ \hat{J}_z, \hat{L}^2 \right]
  & = \hat{J}_z \hat{L}^2 - \hat{L}^2 \hat{J}_z = \\
  & = \hat{L}_z \hat{L}^2 + \hat{S}_z \hat{L}^2 - \hat{L}^2 \hat{L}_z - \hat{L}^2 \hat{S}_z = \\
  & = \underbrace{\left[ \hat{L}_z,  \hat{L}^2 \right]}_{ = 0 } + \underbrace{\left[ \hat{S}_z, \hat{L}^2 \right]}_{ = 0} = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The last term holds because \(\hat{S}_z\) and \(\hat{L}^2\) acts on two different sub\sphinxhyphen{}spaces, or explicitly for any \(| \Psi \rangle = | \psi \rangle \otimes | \sigma \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{S}_z \hat{L}^2 | \Psi \rangle
  & = ( \hat{\mathbf{1}} \otimes \hat{S}_z ) ( \hat{L}^2 \otimes \hat{\mathbf{1}} ) | \psi \rangle \otimes | \sigma \rangle = \\ 
  & = ( \hat{\mathbf{1}} \otimes \hat{S}_z ) ( \hat{L}^2 | \psi \rangle \otimes | \sigma \rangle ) = \\ 
  & = \hat{L}^2 | \psi \rangle \otimes \hat{S}_z | \sigma \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and \(\hat{L}^2 \hat{S}_z | \Psi \rangle\) provides the same result for any \(| \Psi \rangle = | \psi \rangle \otimes | \sigma \rangle\).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\chapter{Density Operator}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/density-operator:density-operator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/density-operator:quantum-mechanics-density-operator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/density-operator::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s start from an example of the preparation of a system of subsystems in pure states \(| \psi_i \rangle\), with probability \(p_i\), \(\sum_i p_i = 1\). Let \(M\) an observable, with the corresponding Hermitian operator \(\hat{M}\) with discrete values \(m_\mu\) and corresponding states \(| m_{\mu} \rangle\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, the probability of measuring the value \(m_{\mu}\) for a system in state \(| \psi_i \rangle\), i.e. the conditional probability \(p(m=m_{\mu} | | \psi \rangle = | \psi_i \rangle)\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(m=m_{\mu} |  | \psi \rangle = | \psi_i \rangle ) = | \langle m_{\mu} | \psi_i \rangle |^2 =  \langle  \psi_i | m_{\mu} \rangle  \langle m_{\mu} | \psi_i \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The probability of measuring \(m\) from the ensemble is the marginal probability,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & = \sum_i p(m = m_{\mu} | | \psi \rangle = | \psi_i \rangle) \, p( | \psi \rangle = | \psi_i \rangle ) = \\
  & = \sum_i \langle \psi_i | m_{\mu} \rangle \langle m_{\mu} | \psi_i \rangle \, p_i = \\
  & = \sum_i \langle \psi_i | \hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} | \psi_i \rangle \, p_i \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having introduced the orthogonal projector over the \(\mu^{th}\) eigenfunction of the operator \(\hat{M}\), i.e. \(\hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} = | m_{\mu} \rangle \langle m_{\mu} |\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s define the \sphinxstylestrong{density operator} as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\rho} = \sum_i p_i | \psi_i \rangle \langle \psi_i | \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using an orthonormal basis \(\{ | e_k \rangle \}_k\), it’s easy to show that

\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & := \sum_k \langle e_k | \hat{\rho} \hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} | e_k \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{k,i} p_i \langle e_k | \psi_i \rangle \langle \psi_i | \hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} | e_k \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{i} p_i \langle \psi_i | \hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} \underbrace{\sum_k | e_k \rangle \langle e_k |}_{ = \hat{\mathbf{1}} } \psi_i \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{i} p_i \langle \psi_i | \hat{\Pi}_{m_{\mu}} | \psi_i \rangle = \\

\end{equation*}

\sphinxstylestrong{Expected value.}

 \mathbb{E}[ M ]
