\chapter{Decoherence}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:decoherence}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:quantum-mechanics-decoherence}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence::doc}}

\section{Example: two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional system interacting with a large\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional environment}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:example-two-dimensional-system-interacting-with-a-large-dimensional-environment}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:quantum-mechanics-decoherence-example}}

\subsection{State of the system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:state-of-the-system}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:quantum-mechanics-decoherence-example-state}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional system is interacting with a large\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional environment. The state of the 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional system is identified by the wave function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_S \rangle = c_0 | 0 \rangle + c_1 | 1 \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the state of the environment by the wave function \(| \Psi_E \rangle\), and the state of the whole system (S+E) by the tensor product of the two,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_{S+E} \rangle = | \Psi_S \rangle \otimes | \Psi_E \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Evolution of the system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:evolution-of-the-system}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:quantum-mechanics-decoherence-example-evolution}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The evolution of the system is governed by the Schrodinger equation, with the Hamiltonian of the whole system
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi_{S+E} \rangle = \hat{H}_{S+E} | \Psi_{S+E} \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose evolution can be represented by an unitary operator \(\hat{U}_{S+E; t,0}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_{S+E} \rangle_t = U_{S+E; t,0} | \Psi_{S+E} \rangle_0  = \dots = \alpha | 0 \rangle \otimes | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle + \beta | 1 \rangle \otimes | \Psi_{E;1} \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Density operator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\rho} := | \Psi_{S+E} \rangle \langle \Psi_{S+E} | \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tracing out the environment states,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\rho}_E 
  & = \text{Tr}_E \left( \hat{\rho} \right) = \\
  & = \sum_{k} \left( \alpha | 0 \rangle \langle \phi_k | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle + \beta | 1 \rangle \langle \phi_k | \Psi_{E;1} \rangle \right)  \left( \alpha^* \langle 0 | \langle \Psi_{E;0} | \phi_k  \rangle + \beta^* \langle 1 | \langle \phi_k | \Psi_{E;1} \rangle  \right) = \\
  & = |\alpha|^2 | 0 \rangle \langle 0 | \langle \Psi_{E;0} | \underbrace{\sum_k | \phi_k \rangle \langle \phi_k}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}}} | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle + 
      \alpha \beta^* | 0 \rangle \langle 1 | \langle \Psi_{E;0} | \underbrace{\sum_k | \phi_k \rangle \langle \phi_k |}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}} } \Psi_{E;1} \rangle + \\
  & \quad + 
      \alpha^* \beta | 1 \rangle \langle 0 | \langle \Psi_{E;1} | \underbrace{\sum_k | \phi_k \rangle \langle \phi_k}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}}} | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle + 
      |\beta|^2 | 1 \rangle \langle 1 | \langle \Psi_{E;1} | \underbrace{\sum_k | \phi_k \rangle \langle \phi_k |}_{= \hat{\mathbf{1}} } \Psi_{E;1} \rangle = \\
  & = |\alpha|^2 | 0 \rangle \langle 0 | + \alpha \beta^* \langle \Psi_{E;0} | \Psi_{E;1} \rangle | 0 \rangle \langle 1 | + 
    + \alpha^* \beta \langle \Psi_{E;1} | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle | 1 \rangle \langle 0 | + |\beta|^2 | 1 \rangle \langle 1 | \ . 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The components of the reduced density operator in the system basis are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} |\alpha|^2  & \alpha \beta^* \langle \Psi_{E;0} | \Psi_{E;1} \rangle \\ \alpha^* \beta \langle \Psi_{E;1} | \Psi_{E;0} \rangle & |\beta|^2 \end{bmatrix} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Decoherence time}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/decoherence:decoherence-time}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\chapter{Interaction picture, perturbation theory and Einstein coefficients}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:interaction-picture-perturbation-theory-and-einstein-coefficients}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:quantum-mechanics-einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture::doc}}

\section{Interaction picture}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:interaction-picture}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:quantum-mechanics-einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture-interaction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Interaction picture is a common and useful description of a system whose Hamiltonian cna be written as the sum of a term \(\hat{H}_0\) that’s well known and solvable, and \(\hat{H}_1\) that’s a perturbation to the system \(0\), and it’s usually either time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and/or hard to solve analytically,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \hat{H}_1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\hat{H}_0\) is time\sphinxhyphen{}independent, the corresponding unitary evolution operator is \(U^{(0)} = \exp\left[ i \dfrac{\hat{H}_0}\hbar t \right]\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A state vector in interaction picture, \(| \Psi_I(t) \rangle\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi_{I} (t) \rangle = U^{(0) \, \dagger} | \Psi_S(t) \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(| \Psi_S(t) \rangle\) the state vector in Schrodinger picture.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If one requires that the expectation value of operators is the same using different pictures,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \hat{A}_I \rangle
  & = \langle \Psi_I | \hat{A}_I | \Psi_I \rangle = \\
  & = \langle \Psi_S | \underbrace{U^{(0)} \hat{A}_I U^{(0) \, \dagger}}_{=\hat{A}_S} | \Psi_S \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows that \(\hat{A}_I(t) = U^{(0) \, \dagger}(t,t_0) \hat{A}_S U^{(0)}(t,t_0)\). From the commutation of \(\hat{H}_0\) with \(U^{(0)}\), it follows that it has the same expression in Schrodinger and interaction picture, \(H^{(0)}_I = H^{(0)}_S\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Time evolutions.}
\subsubsection*{Time evolution of a state \protect\(\ | \Psi_I(t) \rangle\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi_I \rangle 
  & = \hat{H}^{(1)}_I | \Psi_I \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi_I \rangle 
  & = i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} \left[ U^{(0) \, \dagger}(t,t_0) | \Psi_S \rangle  \right] = \\
  & = i \hbar \left[ \partial_t U^{(0) \, \dagger}(t,t_0) | \Psi_S \rangle + U^{(0) \, \dagger} \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi_S \rangle  \right] = \\
  & = - U^{(0) \, \dagger} \hat{H}_0 | \Psi_S \rangle + U^{(0) \, \dagger} \left( \hat{H}^{(0)} + \hat{H}^{(1)} \right) | \Psi_S \rangle = \\
  & = \underbrace{U^{(0) \, \dagger} \hat{H}^{(1)} U^{(0)}}_{\hat{H}^{(1)}_I} \, \underbrace{U^{(0) \, \dagger} | \Psi_S \rangle}_{| \Psi_I \rangle} = \\
  & = \hat{H}^{(1)}_I | \Psi_I \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
recalling that \(\hat{H}^{(0)} = i \hbar \, \partial_t U^{(0)} U^{(0) \, \dagger} = - i \hbar U^{(0)} \partial_t U^{(0) \, \dagger}\), and that the Hamiltonian operator is Hermitian, \(\hat{H} = \hat{H}^{\dagger}\).
\subsubsection*{Time evolution of an operator \protect\(\hat{A}_I(t)\protect\)}
\subsubsection*{Details}


\section{Perturbation theory}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:perturbation-theory}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:quantum-mechanics-einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture-perturbation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For an isolated system with time\sphinxhyphen{}independent Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}_0\), the state of the system can be written as a linear combination of the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi(t) \rangle = | n \rangle a_n(t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(a_n(t) = a_n(0) \exp\left( - i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t \right) = \langle n | \Psi(0) \rangle \exp\left( - i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t \right) \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Time varying perturbation theory.} The state of the perturbed system is can be written as a linear combination of the eigenstates of the unperturbed Hamiltonian as well \sphinxhyphen{} here explicitly writing a factor \(e^{-i E_n t / \hbar}\) in the coefficient,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi(t) \rangle = | n \rangle c_n(t) e^{-i E_n t / \hbar} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that for unperturbed systems \(c_n(t) = a_{n,0}\) constant. Inserting this expression in the Schrodinger equation of the system provides dynamical equations for the coefficients \(c_n(t)\), i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0
 & = - i \hbar \dfrac{d}{dt} | \Psi \rangle + \left( \hat{H}_0 + \hat{H}_1(t) \right) | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \sum_n \left[ \left( - i \hbar \dot{c}_n - c_n \, E_n + c_n \, E_n \right) | n \rangle + \hat{H}_1 | n \rangle c_n \right] e^{-i E_n t/\hbar} \\
 & = \sum_n \left[ - i \hbar \dot{c}_n |  n \rangle + \hat{H}_1 | n \rangle c_n \right] e^{-i E_n t/\hbar} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Projecting on \(\langle m |\), a system of an infinite number of equations follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{c}_m = - \frac{i}{\hbar} \sum_{n} \langle m | \hat{H}_1 | n \rangle c_n \, e^{i \frac{E_m - E_n}{\hbar} t} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Einstein coefficients}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:einstein-coefficients}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:quantum-mechanics-einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture-einstein-coeffs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perturbation theory is applied to an electron around a steady positive nucleus, subject to time\sphinxhyphen{}varying electric field. The classical counterpart of the governing equation of a point charge subject to Coulomb potential and a travelling wave in the electric field
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r},t) = 2 \mathbf{E}_0 \cos( \omega t - \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} ) = q \mathbf{E}_0 ( e^{i(\omega t - \mathbf{k}\cdot \mathbf{r})} + c.c. ) \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m \ddot{\mathbf{r}} + \dfrac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} = 2 q \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(\omega t - \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dipole approximation} assumes that the displacement of the charged particle is small compared to the wave\sphinxhyphen{}length of the radiation, \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} = \frac{ \hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{r} }{2 \pi \lambda} \ll 1\), and thus the dynamic equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m \ddot{\mathbf{r}} + \dfrac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} = 2 q \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(\omega t) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The total force is the sum of the Coulomb force and the force due to the incoming electric field. This sum can be written as a gradient of a scalar function, a potential \(V\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{F} 
  & = - \dfrac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} + 2 q \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(2 \pi \, \nu \, t) = \\
  & = \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \left[ \dfrac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\dfrac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} + 2 q \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(2 \pi \, \nu \, t) \right] = \\
  & = - \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \left( V_0(\mathbf{r}) + V_1(\mathbf{r},t) \right) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that can be written as the stationary potential \(V_0\) from Coulomb force and the time\sphinxhyphen{}varying perturbation \(V_1(\mathbf{r},t)\). The vector \(q \mathbf{r}\) is usually defined as the \sphinxstylestrong{electric dipole}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Schrodinger equation follows from the promotion of the Hamiltonian function \(H = K + V\) to the Hamiltonian operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \hat{H}_1(t) = \hat{H}_0 + 2 \mathbf{E}_0 \cdot q \hat{\mathbf{r}} \, \cos(2 \pi \nu t ) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Topics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics:topics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics:quantum-mechanics-history-topics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Atomic models.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1891, J.J.Thomson find electrons in cathodic rays. He found out that cathodic rays are made of negatively charged particles%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
While J.J.Thomson won the Nobel prize in Physics (1906) for having found the first sub\sphinxhyphen{}atomic particle, the electron, his son G.P.Thomson won the Noble prize (1937) for its discovery of the diffraction of electrons by crystals in 1927, thus showing wave behavior. Particle\sphinxhyphen{}wave duality never ends…
%
\end{footnote}, deflected by a transverse electromagnetic field. He:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
evaluated the ratio \(\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{el.charge}}\) of these particles. See \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-hs/ch/modern/experiments-matter.html\#scoperta-dell-elettrone-j-j-thomson}{Scoperta dell’elettrone \sphinxhyphen{} J.J.Thomson}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
proposed the pudding atomic model, with negatively charged particles in a positive cloud.

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1909, Rutherford scattering experiment and Rutherford atomic model: electrons around a compact nucleus

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1913, Bohr…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1916, Sommerfeld
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
relativistic model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
elliptial orbits

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
introduced another quantum number and degeneracy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
describe energy level split by magnetic field (Zeeman effect)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1925, Heisenberg and Schrodinger first theories about QM; Pauli solution of the \(\text{H}\) atom system

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectroscopy.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1707, Newton “Optics” described his experiments about diffraction of light with glass prisms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second half of the XIX century, experimental studies on the emission/absorption spectra in chemistry. Each element showed characteristics black lines in otherwise continuous absoprtion spectra (and corresponding bright lines in emission spectra, “hot spectra”)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Empirical laws for the refractive index followed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1836, Cauchy proposed a relation between the refractive index \(n\) of a material and the wave\sphinxhyphen{}length of the radiation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 = a + \frac{b}{\lambda^2} + \frac{c}{\lambda^4} + \dots \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with material\sphinxhyphen{}dependent parameters \(a\), \(b\), \(c\),…This model proposed \(n(\lambda)\) as a continuous function

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1870, Christiansen observed anomalous dispersion, with apparently discountinuous refractive index at wave lengths that are characteristics of the element under investigation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1872, Sellmeier proposed that anomalous dispersion should be described in the context of light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction, in terms of resonance modes of the matter and proposed his law for the refractive index
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 - 1 = \sum_{k} \frac{a_k \lambda_k^2}{\lambda^2 - \lambda^2_k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1875, Helmholtz modified Sellmeier formula, introducing a (wrong, this was not a dampening factor, as the one shown by Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model) dampening factor.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical-drude-lorentz}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model}}}}. Following the idea of Sellmeier, P.Drude (1900) and then H.Lorentz (1905) proposed a theoretical model for the refractive index of a medium, using a second\sphinxhyphen{}order damped oscillator, forced by the electric field of an incoming electromagnetic wave, and evaluated the transmitted wave as the sum of the incident wave and the one generated by the oscillating charges of the matter.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generalization of the Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model for systems with multiple modes became the general semi\sphinxhyphen{}empirical classical model for light dispersion
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n(\omega)-1 = \frac{q^2}{2 \varepsilon_0 m} \sum_k \frac{N_k}{\omega_k^2 - \omega^2 + i \gamma_k \omega_k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2(\omega) - 1 \simeq 2 \delta .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dispersion becomes quantum:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1905, Einstein explanation of photoelectric effect

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1906\sphinxhyphen{}1908, \sphinxstylestrong{Ladenburg} and Loria began experiments about spectral lines, anomalous dispersion, and the microstructure of the light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction. They found a way to measure the number density of the electrons responsible for spectral lines in absorption spectra in \(\text{H}\) atom (\(\text{H}_{\alpha}\) line only, while they had not enough accuracy for other weaker lines). Only few electrons resonate while the majority appear to be unaffected. They then focused on \(\text{Na}\) for better resolution. They came back to \(\text{H}\) few years later (1911), to find \(\frac{N_{\text{H}_{\alpha}}}{N_{\text{H}}} \sim \frac{1}{50.000}\), \(\frac{N_{\text{H}_{\beta}}}{N_{\text{H}}} \sim \frac{1}{200.000}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1913, Bohr model (incompatible with classical mechanics, no \(e^-\) fast collapse on the nucleus, due to classical radiation):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
circular stable orbits with quantized angular momentum \(n h\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines are generated by quantum jumps, with \(\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
results compatible with the empirical Rydberg formula (1888)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ladenburg: how do both Bohr model and Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model work so well in atomic spectra?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1914, H.Kohn: experimental confirmed radiation emitted by incandescent bodies can be treated as thermal radiation. Ladenburg then used thermodynamics to explain thermal radiation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Still Ladenburg
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1914, procedure to compute the density of dispersion electrons

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1921, quantum counterpart of the classical dispersion, and link with Einstein coefficients (1916)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{physical atom is replaced by a representation of oscillators}: only frequencies and intensities of spectral lines can be observed. They abandoned the idea of building a “physical model of the atom” following the electron along an orbit, and built a model that’s just compatible with the phhysical quantities they can measure

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1924, \sphinxstylestrong{Kramers} (with theoretical derivation from Born, 1924, and Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rule for \sphinxstylestrong{polarization} with transition frequencies (both to higher and lower energy levels, modeling both emission and absorption)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kramers formula and the idea of virtual oscillators are used by Heisenberg in his formulation of matrix mechanics: this formula set the origin for the non\sphinxhyphen{}commutativity of physical quantities and, thus, Heisenberg uncertainty principle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tested by Ladenburg, 1928

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radiation and Light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1896, Wien’s law

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1900, Planck described the \sphinxstylestrong{continuous spectrum} of black\sphinxhyphen{}body radiation, introducing of \(h\), and the idea that light radiation with frequency \(\nu\) have discrete amount of energy, \(h \nu\). He first introduced \(h\) as a trick for matching experimental results of the spectrum \(\rho(\nu, T)\); a model of statistical mechanics of radiation with discrete levels of energy followed, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/notes:statistical-mechanics-notes-distributions-be}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Black\sphinxhyphen{}body ratiation using Bose\sphinxhyphen{}Einstein statistics}}}}, even though that was the original way Planck first found a theoretical model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1905, Einstein explained the photolectric effects using Planck constant \(h\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1916, Einstein
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
derived Planck’s law from Bohr’s atomic model, using a (quantum) statistical approach to the interaction of atoms (and thier electrons) and electromagnetic radiation in a box. He postulated the existence of three processes, introducing proportionality \sphinxstylestrong{Einstein coefficients}, for transition probability (of a \(e^-\)) between states: \sphinxstyleemphasis{absorption} (rate: \(B_{kj} N_k \rho(\nu)\)) \sphinxstyleemphasis{spontaneous emission} (rate: \(-A_{jk} N_j\)), and \sphinxstylestrong{stimulated emission} (rate: \(- B_{jk} N_j \rho(\nu)\)). Stimulated emissions was found to be necessary in order for this model to be compatible with Planck’s law \(\rho \propto \frac{1}{e^{h\nu/k T}-1}\) for the system at thermal equilibrium (and not with Wien’s law \(\rho(\nu) \propto e^{-h \nu/ k T}\), the law one would get without stimulated emission)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Einstein couldn’t calculate his coefficients but he was positive that they could be computed once a theory about the atom had been be established

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
recognized that light quanta have momentum, \(p = \hbar k = h \frac{\nu}{c}\), then found by Compton (1923) in experiments about X\sphinxhyphen{}rays scattering

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in 1927, Dirac calculated Einstein coefficients (The Quantum Theory of Emission and Absorption of Radiation)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Origin of quantum mechanics.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix mechanics.} (Heisenberg, Born, Jordan), three papers in 1925

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ondulatory mechanics.} (Schrodinger)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1923, L.\({}\)de Broglie: idea of guiding wave for matter particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1925, E.Schrodinger: wave equation. If matter behaves as a wave, a wave equation should be the governing equation of the system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1923\sphinxhyphen{}1927, C.Davisson and L.Germer found a diffraction pattern in an experiment about electron scattering

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equivalence.} (Dirac)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxstepscope


\section{Origins of Matrix and Wave Quantum Mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:origins-of-matrix-and-wave-quantum-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:quantum-mechanics-history-origins}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins::doc}}

\subsection{Origins of Matrix Mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:origins-of-matrix-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:quantum-mechanics-history-origins-matrix-mechanics}}\subsubsection*{Quantization of radiation energy.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Planck (1900), Einstein photoelectric effect (1905) and heat capacity of the solids: introduction and evidences of \(h\), \(E = h \nu\)
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:eq:history:planck-radiation-formula}
\begin{split}u(\nu, T) = \dots\end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction and light dispersion.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
First experimental evidences: Cauchy; Sellmeier (1872) proposed an empirical law for the refraction index \(n\) taking into account resonances of matter; {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical-drude-lorentz}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}Drude}}}} (1900\sphinxhyphen{}1905) provided a theoretical model of Sellmeier formula, using Maxwell equations for electromagentism,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:eq:history:lorenz-drude}
\begin{split}n - 1 = \dfrac{q^2 N}{2 \varepsilon m} \dfrac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + i \gamma \omega} \approx \dfrac{q^2 N}{2 \varepsilon m} \dfrac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}  \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(m\) and \(q\) the mass and the charge of a particle, \(N\) the number density of the charged particles, \(\omega_0\) the natural frequency and \(\gamma\) a damping coefficient of the dynamical equation governing the dynamics of the particle, \(m \ddot{x} + m \gamma \omega \dot{x} + m \omega_0^2 x = q E(t)\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Einstein (1916): quantum theory of the radiation interacting with matter.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Statistics of the equilibrium of radiation and matter, with the processes of absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emissions. He introduced Einstein coefficiens as proportionality constants

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
E. theory connected Bohr’s atomic with Planck’s radiation formula \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:eq:history:planck-radiation-formula}: matching Planck’s formula induces relationss between Einstein coefficients,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
    \dfrac{A_{jk}}{B_{kj}} \dfrac{g_j}{g_k} = \dfrac{8 \pi \nu^3}{c^3}
    \qquad , \qquad                        
    \dfrac{B_{jk}}{B_{kj}} \dfrac{g_j}{g_k} = 1 \ .
    \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Einstein didn’t know how to compute \(A_{ik}\), \(B_{jk}\), \(B_{kj}\), but he was confident that it would have been possible to do so, once a theory of quanta was established.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ladenburg (1914\sphinxhyphen{}24)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a material may have more than one resonance. The generalization of the formula \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origins:eq:history:lorenz-drude} for the refractive index \(n\) from Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}Drude model reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n - 1 = \dfrac{q^2}{2 \varepsilon m} \sum_{k} \dfrac{N_k}{\omega_k^2 - \omega^2} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(N_k\) the “number density of particles”%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
This should be interpreted as a weight representing the contribution of mode \(k\).
%
\end{footnote} with natural frequency \(f_k = \dfrac{\omega_k}{2 \pi}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
But what’s the meaning of \(N_k\)? Ladenburg compared the averaged emitted power from {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:moving-charge-radiation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{Larmor’s formula}}}}} \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:eq:larmor:quadratic:power-energy} \sphinxhyphen{} the classical model \sphinxhyphen{} and the emitted power by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,std,std-doc}{\sphinxstylestrong{Planck’s formula}}}}}, or by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc,std,std-doc}{\sphinxstylestrong{Einstein quantum theory of interaction of radiation and matter}}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} the quantum model, for a frequency \(\nu_{ij}\). The power emitted by \(R\) resonators per unit volume is

\sphinxAtStartPar
…


\subsubsection*{Dimensional analysis}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
[ \langle \Phi_1 \rangle ] & = \dfrac{\text{power}}{\text{n.parts}} \\
[ R ] & = \dfrac{\text{n.parts}}{\text{length}^3} \\
[ \langle P \rangle ] & = \dfrac{\text{power}}{\text{length}^3} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(\nu) = \dots\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
–>

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Particle\sphinxhyphen{}wave duality.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {}

Einstein (1909): radiation has wave and particle behavior

\section{Origin of matrix mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-matrix-mechanics:origin-of-matrix-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-matrix-mechanics:quantum-mehcanics-history-origin-matrix-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-matrix-mechanics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Experiences:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Quantization in light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1900, Planck radiation law: \(h\) as a mathematical trick to fit experimental data of black\sphinxhyphen{}body radiation; thermodynamics model followed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1905, Einstein work on photoelectric effect: \(h\) is not a mathematical trick

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Light dispersion, as a light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction process:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1900, Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}Drude model for classical dispersion

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1913, Bohr atomic model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1917, Einstein derived Planck law from thermodynamic equilibrium between atoms and radiation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1914\sphinxhyphen{}24, Ladenburg work on quantization of dispersion law, matching Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}Drude (classical model) and Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Einstein (quantum model) in the classical limit

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Heisenberg matrix mechanics
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{First experiences}

\subsubsection{Classical dispersion}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:classical-dispersion}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical}}

\paragraph{Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:drude-lorentz-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical-drude-lorentz}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n(\omega)-1 = \frac{q^2 N}{2 \varepsilon_0 m} \frac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + i \gamma \omega}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The refractive index \(n\) is a complex number, with
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \text{re} \{ n \}(\omega) & = 1 + \Delta n_0 \omega^2_0 \frac{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega)^2 + \gamma^2 \omega^2} \\
  \text{im} \{ n \}(\omega) & = - \Delta n_0 \omega^2_0 \frac{\gamma \omega}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega)^2 + \gamma^2 \omega^2} \ \le 0 \ , \quad \forall \omega \ge 0 \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here the condition \(\omega \ge 0\) is required by the condition that the incoming wave travels from left to right.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, a travelling wave
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(x,t) = e^{i (\omega t - k x)} = e^{i \omega \left( t - \frac{x}{c} \right)} = e^{i \omega \left( t - n \frac{x}{c_0} \right)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
thus contains both a oscillating and a dampening contribution by \(n = \text{re}\{ n \} + i \, \text{im}\{ n \}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(x,t) = e^{\frac{\omega}{c_0} \text{im}\{ n(\omega) \} x} e^{i \omega \left( t - \text{re}\{ n(\omega) \} \frac{x}{c_0} \right)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the imaginary part of the refractive index is negative for all the positive frequencies, than the real exponential represents a damping term. The minimum value of \(\text{im}\{ n \}(\omega)\) for a slightly damped second\sphinxhyphen{}order oscillator occurs approximately at the natural frequency, \(\omega_{max damp} \simeq \omega_0\). This represents an \sphinxstylestrong{absorption of radiation} by the matter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model in the form \(n - 1 = \delta\) is compatible with empirical formulas in the form \(n^2 - 1 = \widetilde{\delta}\), as the correction is “small enough” for a linear approximation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 = ( 1 + \delta )^2 \simeq 1 + 2 \delta \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Einstein}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:einstein}}

\paragraph{Ladenburg}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:ladenburg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ladenburg wrote the energy balance at thermodynamical equilibrium, from transitions between each pair of states \(i\), \(k > i\), using \sphinxstylestrong{Einstein’s coefficients} from his {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:quantum-mehcanics-history-light-matter-einstein}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{quantum theory of radiation interacting with matter}}}}.
The total amount of energy emitted by \(N_k\) molecules in the state \(k\) transitioning to a lower state \(i\) is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J = \underbrace{h \nu_{ik}}_{\Delta E_{ik}} N_k \left[ A_{ki} + B_{ki} u(\nu_{ik}) \right] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At thermal equilibrium, this energy is equal to the energy absorbed by \(N_i\) molecules in the state \(i\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A = h \nu_{ik} N_i B_{ik} u(\nu_{ik}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exploiting the relations between Einstein coefficients \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:eq:einstein-coeffs:relations}, Ladenburg wrote the emitted and absorbed energy as a function of the spontaneous emission foefficient \(A_{ki}\) (allowing to relate dispersion with other phenomena involving emission),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J = A = h \nu_{ik} u(\nu_{ik}) N_i B_{ik} \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Light matter interaction}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:light-matter-interaction}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:quantum-mehcanics-history-light-matter}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck::doc}}

\subsubsection{Einstein: quantum theory of radiation interacting with matter}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:einstein-quantum-theory-of-radiation-interacting-with-matter}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:quantum-mehcanics-history-light-matter-einstein}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Three mechanisms, whose probabilities are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Spontaneous emission of radiation, for a photon going from level \(j\) to level \(i\) (\(E_j > E_i\)),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \frac{d n_{ij}}{d t} \right)_{spont} = A_{ji} n_j \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Stimulated emission of radiation, for a photon going from level \(j\) to level \(i\) (\(E_j > E_i\)),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \frac{d n_{ij}}{d t} \right) = B_{ji} n_j \rho(\nu_{ji}) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\nu_{ji} = \frac{E_j - E_i}{h}\), and \(\rho(\nu)\) the density of radiation in the system at frequency \(\nu\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Absorption, for a photon going from level \(j\) to level \(i\) (\(E_j > E_i\)),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \frac{d n_{ij}}{d t} \right) = - B_{ij} n_i \rho(\nu_{ij}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The overall rate reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{d n_i}{d t} = \sum_{j, E_j > E_i} \dfrac{d n_{ij}}{d t} = \sum_{j, E_j > E_i} \left\{ A_{ji} n_j + B_{ji} n_j \rho(\nu_{ij}) - B_{ij} n_i \rho(\nu_{ij}) \right\} \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At thermodynamic equilibriumm between all the states
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \dfrac{d n_{ij}}{d t} = A_{ji} n_j + B_{ji} n_j \rho(\nu_{ij}) - B_{ij} n_i \rho(\nu_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Boltzmann distribution
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{n_i}{n} = \frac{g_i e^{-\frac{E_i}{kT}}}{Z} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the expression of the radiation density follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \rho(\nu_{ij})
  & = \frac{A_{ji} n_j}{n_i B_{ij} - n_j B_{ji}} = \\
  & = \frac{A_{ji} g_j}{B_{ij} g_i} \frac{ \exp(-E_j/kT) }{ \exp(-E_i/kT) - \frac{g_j B_{ji}}{g_i B_{ij}} \exp(-E_j/kT)} = \\
  & = \frac{A_{ji} g_j}{B_{ij} g_i} \frac{ 1 }{ \exp((E_j-E_i)/kT) - \frac{g_j B_{ji}}{g_i B_{ij}}} = \\
  & = \frac{A_{ji} g_j}{B_{ij} g_i} \frac{ 1 }{ \exp(h \nu_{ji}/kT) - \frac{g_j B_{ji}}{g_i B_{ij}}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparing with Planck’s law (with the \sphinxstylestrong{radiance}?) \(\rho(\nu, T) = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^3} \frac{1}{\exp(h \nu /kT) - 1}\), the relations between Einstein coefficients \((E_j > E_i)\) follows
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/einstein-planck:eq:einstein-coeffs:relations}
\begin{split}\frac{g_j A_{ji}}{g_i B_{ij}} = \frac{2 h \nu_{ji}^3}{c^3} \quad , \quad \frac{g_j B_{ji}}{g_i B_{ij}} = 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Planck’s law}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Spectral energy density (energy per unit volume, per unit frequency):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u_{\nu}(\nu, T) = \frac{8 \pi h \nu^3}{c^3} \frac{1}{\exp(h \nu/kT) - 1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dimensional analysis:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[u] = \frac{[h][\nu]^3}{[c]^3} = \frac{J s \cdot s^{-3}}{ m^3 c^{-3}} = \frac{J}{ m^3 \cdot \text{Hz}} = \frac{\text{energy}}{\text{length}^3 \cdot \text{freq.}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Radiance, \(B_{\nu}(\nu, T) = \frac{c}{4 \pi} u_{\nu}(\nu, T)\) \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Justify this relation. Is this right? Or should the factor be \(\frac{c}{8 \pi}\)}%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Taltavull, Rudolf Ladenburg and the first quantum interpretation of optical dispersion, Eur. Phys. J. H.
%
\end{footnote}. Thus

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}B_{\nu}(\nu, T) = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2} \frac{1}{\exp(h \nu/kT) - 1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dimensional analysis
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[B] = \frac{\text{power}}{\text{solid angle} \cdot \text{surface} \cdot \text{Hz}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Radiation of moving charges \sphinxhyphen{} Larmor’s formula}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:radiation-of-moving-charges-larmor-s-formula}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:moving-charge-radiation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula::doc}}

\subsubsection{Green’s function solution of wave equations: Liénard\sphinxhyphen{}Wiechert potential}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:green-s-function-solution-of-wave-equations-lienard-wiechert-potential}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:moving-charge-radiation-lienard-wiechert}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Wave equations in electromagmetism.} See \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-electromagnetism/ch/waves-equation.html}{Classical Electromagnetism: Wave Equations in Electromagnetism}. Using \sphinxstylestrong{Lorentz gauge}, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{c^2}\partial_t \varphi = 0\), the wave equations for the mathbftor potential \(\mathbf{a}\) and the scalar potential \(\varphi\) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} \mathbf{a} - \Delta \mathbf{a} & = \mu \mathbf{j} \\
  \frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} \varphi - \Delta \varphi & = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Solution of wave equation with Green’s function}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The solution of a wave equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} u - \Delta u = f \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
can be written using \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/pde/bem-poisson-helmholtz-waves.html\#wave-equation}{Math: Green’s function method} (with assumptions of causality, and no contribution from i.c. and b.c.),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  u(\mathbf{r},t) 
  & = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \int_{t' \in T} \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in V} \dfrac{ \delta \left( t' - t + \frac{|\mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r}|}{c} \right) }{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |} f (\mathbf{r}', t') d \mathbf{r}' d t' = \\
  & = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in V} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |} f\left( \mathbf{r}', t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t; \mathbf{r}') \right)  d \mathbf{r}' \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the retarded time \(t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t; \mathbf{r}') = t - \frac{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |}{c} \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The solution of the wave equations reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r},t) & = \frac{\mu}{4 \pi} \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in V} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |} \mathbf{j} \left( \mathbf{r}', t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t; \mathbf{r}') \right)  d \mathbf{r}' \\
  \varphi(\mathbf{r},t) & = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \int_{\mathbf{r}' \in V} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |} \rho \left( \mathbf{r}', t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t; \mathbf{r}') \right)  d \mathbf{r}' \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the retarded time \(t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t; \mathbf{r}') = t - \frac{| \mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r} |}{c} \).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Point charge.} The charge density and the current density of a point charge with electrical charge \(q\), position \(\mathbf{r}_s(t)\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}_s = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_s\) are respectively
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \rho(\mathbf{r},t) & = q \, \delta ( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t) ) \\
  \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r},t) & = q \mathbf{v}_s(t) \, \delta ( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t) ) \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the electromagnetic potentials generated by a point charge are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r},t) & = \frac{\mu}{4 \pi} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) - \mathbf{r} |} q \mathbf{v}_s(t_{ret}) \\
  \varphi(\mathbf{r},t) & = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) - \mathbf{r} |} q  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Derivatives of the retarded time}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t t_{ret} & = \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \\   
  \nabla     t_{ret} & = - \frac{1}{c} \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Time derivative
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t t_{ret}(\mathbf{r}, t, \mathbf{r}_s(t)) 
  & = \partial_t \left( t - \frac{|\mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}(\mathbf{r},t, \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret})) - \mathbf{r}|}{c} \right) = \\
  & = 1 - \frac{1}{c} \frac{d |\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}|}{d t_{ret}} \partial_t t_{ret} = \\
  & = 1 + \frac{x_{k} - x_{s,k}}{|\mathbf{r}_s - \mathbf{r}|} \frac{v_{s,k}}{c} \partial_t t_{ret} = \\
  & = 1 + \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta \, \partial_t t_{ret} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t t_{ret} = \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Space derivatives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that

\begin{split}\partial_k t_{ret} = - \frac{1}{c} \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \frac{r_k - r_{s,k}(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) - \mathbf{r}|} \end{split}

or, using vector notation,

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now,

  \partial_t ( r_{i} - r_{s,i}(t_{ret}))

\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) |^n
  & = \partial_t \left[ ( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) ) \cdot ( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) ) \right]^{\frac{n}{2}} = \\

\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_k | \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) |^n

\begin{equation*}

It’s easy to realize that \(\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{c} \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{e}\).
\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}

  \mathbf{e} 
  & = - \partial_t \mathbf{a} - \nabla \varphi = \\
  & = - \partial_t \left( \frac{\mu}{4 \pi} \frac{q \mathbf{v}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) - \mathbf{r}|} \right) - \nabla \left( \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{q}{|\mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret}) - \mathbf{r}|}  \right) = \\
  & = - \frac{q \mu}{4 \pi} \left[ \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret}) \, \partial_t t_{ret} + \mathbf{v}_s |\mathbf{r}|^{-2} \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} c \right] - \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} |\mathbf{r}|^{-2} \left( - 1 - \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right) \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \\
  & = - \frac{q \mu c^2}{4 \pi} \left[ \frac{\mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2} \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}  + \frac{\boldsymbol\beta}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right] + \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|^{2}} \left( 1 + \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right) \hat{\mathbf{r}}= \\
  & = - \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{\mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2} \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} + \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \left( \frac{ -\boldsymbol\beta (\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta) + \hat{\mathbf{r}} (\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta) }{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} + \hat{\mathbf{r}} \right) = \\
  & = - \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{\mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2} \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} + \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \left( \frac{ \hat{\mathbf{r}} - \boldsymbol\beta (\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta) }{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{b} 
  & = \nabla \times \mathbf{a} = \\
  & = \nabla \times \left( \frac{\mu}{4 \pi} \frac{q \mathbf{v}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret})|} \right) = \\
  & = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_k \varepsilon_{klm} \partial_l \left( \frac{\mu}{4 \pi} \frac{q v_{s,m}(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret})|} \right) = \\
  & = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_k \varepsilon_{klm} \frac{\mu q}{4 \pi} \partial_l \left( \frac{v_{s,m}(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_s(t_{ret})|} \right) = \\

  & = \frac{q \mu c^2}{4 \pi} \frac{1}{c^2} \left[ -\frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c} \frac{1}{1-\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} - \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \times \mathbf{v}_s(t_{ret}) \left( 1 + \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right) \right] = \\
  & = \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{c} \left[ -\frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2} \frac{1}{1-\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} - \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \times \boldsymbol\beta \left( 1 + \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right)  \right] = \\
  & = \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{c} \left[ -\frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{a}_s(t_{ret})}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2} \frac{1}{1-\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} - \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \times \boldsymbol\beta \left( \frac{1}{1 - \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \boldsymbol\beta} \right)  \right] \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Larmor formula}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:larmor-formula}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/larmor-formula:moving-charge-radiation-larmor}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Poynting vector reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r},t) := \frac{ \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r},t) \times \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{r},t) }{\mu} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus, using the electromagnetic field of a moving charge,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{s} = \frac{1}{\mu} \mathbf{e} \times \mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{c \mu} \mathbf{e} \times \left( \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{e} \right) = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left[ |\mathbf{e}|^2 \hat{\mathbf{r}} - ( \mathbf{e} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} ) \mathbf{e} \right] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Far\sphinxhyphen{}field approximation} (also assuming that \(\boldsymbol\beta \sim \mathbf{0}\). \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{slow charge? Non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic limit?}),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{e} \sim - \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{\mathbf{a}_{s,ret}}{|\mathbf{r}| c^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{s}
  & = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}| c^2} \right)^2 \, \mathbf{a} \times \left( \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{a} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}| c^2} \right)^2 \left( |\mathbf{a}|^2 \hat{\mathbf{r}} - ( \mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} ) \mathbf{a} \right) = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The elementary power flux at \(\mathbf{r} = R \hat{\mathbf{r}}\), assuming that the motion is ina region much smaller than \(R\), so that \(t_{ret} = t - \frac{R}{c}\), is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{s} 
  & = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon R c^2} \right)^2 \left( |\mathbf{a}|^2 - ( \mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} )^2 \right) = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s define the direction of \(\mathbf{a}_{ret} = a \hat{\mathbf{t}}\), and sperical coordinates so that \(\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{\mathbf{t}} = \cos \theta\). Integration over the sphere of radius \(R\) gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \Phi
  & := \int_{S} \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{s} = \\
  & = \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi} \int_{\phi = 0}^{2 \pi}  \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon R c^2} \right)^2 \left( 1 - \cos^2 \theta \right)^2 |\mathbf{a}|^2 R^2 \sin \theta \, d \theta \, d \phi = \\
  & = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q |\mathbf{a}|}{4 \pi \varepsilon c^2} \right)^2 \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi} \int_{\phi = 0}^{2 \pi} ( 1 - \cos^2 \theta) \sin \theta \, d \theta \, d \phi = \\
  & = \frac{1}{\mu c} \left( \frac{q |\mathbf{a}|}{4 \pi \varepsilon c^2} \right)^2 \cdot \frac{4}{3} \cdot 2 \pi = \\
  & = \frac{q^2 |\mathbf{a}_{s,ret}|^2}{6 \pi \varepsilon c^3} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Average power.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \Phi \rangle = \frac{q^2}{6  \pi \varepsilon c^3} \langle |\mathbf{a}|^2 \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}

\subsection{Spin}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/spin:spin}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/spin:quantum-mechanics-history-spin}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/spin::doc}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Early 1910s: Experiments about emission spectra of alkali metals (transition between levels obey selection rules) and the Zeeman effect (strong magnetic fields can influence atomic spectra)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1924: W.Pauli proposed an additional degree of freedom, the spin, a “two\sphinxhyphen{}valuedness without a classical counterpart”. This physical quantity is related to angular momentum. This physical quantity was also required to formulated the Pauli exclusion principle, and linking this quantity to symmetry properties of the wave function of systems with many indentical bodies.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
W.Pauli first introduced the new degree of freedom in the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic Schrodinger equation, later shown to be the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic limit of the relativistic quantum mehcanics equation by Dirac (1928).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1922\sphinxhyphen{}1927: Stern\sphinxhyphen{}Gerlach experiment. First performed to test Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld atomic model, then used to verify and investigate the properties of spin.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Modern reinterpretation of Heisenberg mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:modern-reinterpretation-of-heisenberg-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation::doc}}

\subsubsection{Heisenberg Equations of Motion in the Heisenberg Picture}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:heisenberg-equations-of-motion-in-the-heisenberg-picture}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-eoms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Time derivative of an operator \(\hat{A}_H\) in Heisenberg picture satisfies the relation \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:eq:qm:heisenberg:dAdt},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{d \hat{A}_H}{dt} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[ \hat{A}_H , \hat{H}_H \right] + \left( \partial_t \hat{A} \right)_H \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Applying this relation to the position and momentum operators, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_H\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_H\), Heisenberg found the quantum mechanics counterpart of the equations of motion in classical mechanics,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:eoms-1}
\begin{split}\left\{
\begin{aligned}
  \dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}_H & = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_H , \hat{H}_H \right] = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_H}{m} \\
  \dot{\hat{\mathbf{p}}}_H & = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}_H , \hat{H}_H \right] = - \left( \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} V\left( \hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \right)_H \\
\end{aligned}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\hat{H} = \frac{|\hat{\mathbf{p}|}^2}{2 m} + V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right)\),
\subsubsection*{\protect\(\left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_H, \hat{H}_H \right] = i \hbar \frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_H}{m}\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_H, \hat{H}_H \right] 
  & = \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0}^{\dagger} \left( \left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \frac{\left|\hat{\mathbf{p}}\right|^2}{2m} \right] + \left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}, V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \right] \right) \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0} = \\
  & = \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0}^{\dagger} \left( i \hbar \frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}}{m} \right) \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0} = \\
  & = i \hbar \frac{\hat{\mathbf{p}}_H}{m} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and \(V(\hat{\mathbf{r}})\) commute, as it can be proved using power expansion \sphinxhyphen{} if required \sphinxhyphen{} of \(V(\hat{\mathbf{r}})\);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the commutator of \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and the kinetic contribution of the Hamiltonian operator reads (sum over \(b\) repeated index),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
      \left[ \hat{x}_a, \hat{p}_b \hat{p}_b \right] 
      & = \hat{x}_a \hat{p}_b \hat{p}_b - \hat{p}_b \hat{x}_a \hat{p}_b + \hat{p}_b \hat{x}_a \hat{p}_b - \hat{p}_b \hat{x}_b \hat{p}_a = \\
      & = \left[ \hat{x}_a , \hat{p}_b \right] \hat{p}_b + \hat{p}_b \left[ \hat{x}_a , \hat{p}_b \right] = \\
      & = 2 i \hbar \delta_{ab} \hat{p}_b = \\
      & = 2 i \hbar \hat{p}_a \ .
    \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
\subsubsection*{\protect\(\left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}_H, \hat{H}_H \right] = - i \hbar \left( \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} V\left( \hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \right)_H\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}_H, \hat{H}_H \right] 
  & = \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0}^{\dagger} \left( \left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}, \frac{\left|\hat{\mathbf{p}}\right|^2}{2m} \right] + \left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}, V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \right] \right) \mathscr{U}_{t,t_0} = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since, the commutator of the momentum and potential energy operator reads \(\left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}, V(\hat{\mathbf{r}}) \right] = \)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \left[ \hat{\mathbf{p}}, V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \right] | \Psi \rangle
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) | \Psi \rangle - \langle \mathbf{r} | V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = - i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} | V\left(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\right) | \Psi \rangle - V\left(\mathbf{r}\right) \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = - i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \left( V(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) \right) + i \hbar V(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) = \\
  & = - i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} V(\mathbf{r}) \, \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \\
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | - i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} V\left( \hat{\mathbf{r}} \right) | \Psi \rangle \ . 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} \rangle = - i \hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} |\), and \(V\left( \hat{\mathbf{r}} \right) | \mathbf{r} \rangle = V( \mathbf{r} ) | \mathbf{r} \rangle\), and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  f(x) \Psi(x,t)
  & = \int_{x'} f(x) \Psi(x', t) \delta(x-x') \, dx' = \\
  & = \int_{x'} f(x) \langle x' | \Psi \rangle \langle x | x' \rangle \, dx' = \\
  & = \int_{x'} \langle x | f(x) | x' \rangle \langle x' | \Psi \rangle \, dx' = \\
  & = \langle x | f \left(\hat{x}\right) \underbrace{\int_{x'} | x' \rangle \langle x' | dx'}_{=\hat{\mathbf{1}}} | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = \langle x | f\left(\hat{x}\right) | \Psi \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Matrix components in energy basis of the equations of motion}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:matrix-components-in-energy-basis-of-the-equations-of-motion}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-eoms-matrix-components}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The matrix components in energy basis of the equations of motion \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:eoms-1} read
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:eoms-2}
\begin{split}\left\{
\begin{aligned}
 i \omega_{jk} X_{jk}^H & = \frac{P_{jk}^H}{m} \\
 i \omega_{jk} P_{jk}^H & = - \left( \nabla V \right)^{H}_{jk} \\
\end{aligned}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\omega_{jk} := \frac{E_j - E_k}{\hbar}\).
\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the Hamiltonian is not an explicit function of time, \(\mathscr{U}_{t,0} = \exp\left[ -i \frac{\hat{H}}{\hbar} t \right]\), and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left( \hat{\mathbf{x}}_H  \right)
  & = \left( | j \rangle \langle j | \hat{\mathbf{x}}_H | k \rangle \langle k | \right) = \\
  & = \left( | j \rangle \langle j | \mathscr{U}_{t,0}^{\dagger} \hat{\mathbf{x}} \mathscr{U}_{t,0} | k \rangle \langle k | \right) = \\
  & = | j \rangle \langle k | \left[ \exp\left(- i \frac{E_k-E_j}{\hbar} t  \right) \langle j | \hat{\mathbf{x}} | k \rangle  \right] 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}X^{H}_{jk}(t) = X^{S}_{jk} \exp\left( i \frac{E_j - E_k}{\hbar} t \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The time\sphinxhyphen{}derivative of the matrix elements of the position operator in Heisenber picture reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{X}^{H}_{jk} = i \omega_{jk} X^{S}_{jk} \exp\left( i \omega_{jk} t \right) = i \omega_{jk} X^H_{jk} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\omega_{jk} := \frac{E_j - E_k}{\hbar}\).


\subsubsection{Equations of motion as Hamilton’s equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:equations-of-motion-as-hamilton-s-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-hamilton-eqns}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The equations of motion \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:eoms-1}, or \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:eoms-2}, can be recast in the form of Hamilton’s equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
  \dot{\hat{\mathbf{q}}}_H & = \dfrac{\partial \mathsf{H}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}_H} \\
  \dot{\hat{\mathbf{p}}}_H & =-\dfrac{\partial \mathsf{H}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{q}}_H} \\
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
  \dot{X}^{H}_{jk} & = \dfrac{\partial \mathsf{H}}{\partial P^{H}_{jk}} \\
  \dot{P}^{H}_{jk} & =-\dfrac{\partial \mathsf{H}}{\partial Q^{H}_{jk}} \\
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathsf{H} = \text{tr} \left( \hat{H} \right) = \sum_a \langle a | \hat{H} | a \rangle \).
\subsubsection*{Details}


\subsubsection{CCR and quantization rule}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:ccr-and-quantization-rule}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-ccr-quantization-rule}}

\paragraph{Modern approach. Matrix form of the CCR}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:modern-approach-matrix-form-of-the-ccr}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-ccr-quantization-rule-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the CCR
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} \right] = i \hbar \mathbb{I} \qquad , \qquad \left[ \hat{x}_a, \hat{p}_b \right] = i \hbar \delta_{ab} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
its matrix components are
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:ccr-matrix}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \delta_{ab} \delta_{jk} 
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ X^{a}_{j \ell} P^{b}_{\ell k} - P^{b}_{j \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \delta_{ab} \delta_{jk} 
  & = \langle j | i \hbar \delta_{ab} | k \rangle = \\
  & = \langle j | \left[ \hat{x}_a , \hat{p}_b \right] k \rangle = \\
  & = \langle j | \hat{x}_a \hat{p}_b - \hat{p}_b \hat{x}_a | k \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ \langle j | \hat{x}_a | \ell \rangle \langle \ell | \hat{p}_b | k \rangle - \langle j | \hat{p}_b | \ell \rangle \langle \ell | \hat{x}_a | k \rangle \right\} = \\
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ X^{a}_{j \ell} P^{b}_{\ell k} - P^{b}_{j \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{From Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld quantization to CCR}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:from-bohr-sommerfeld-quantization-to-ccr}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-ccr-quantization-rule-sommerfeld-to-ccr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In old quantum mechanics \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. quantum mechanics before a quantum mechanics theory \sphinxhyphen{} Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld quantization rule was
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J = n h = \oint p_n d q_n = \oint p_n \dot{q}_n \, dt \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Classical trajectory.} Using Fourier series of a periodic trajectory,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}q_n(t) = \sum_{\alpha} q_\alpha(n) e^{i \alpha \omega_n t} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the time derivative of \(q_n(t)\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{q}_n(t) & = \sum_{\alpha} i \alpha \omega_n q_{\alpha}(n) e^{i \alpha \omega_n t} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while momentum can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n(t) = \sum_{\beta} p_\beta(n) e^{i \beta \omega_n t} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using these expression in the Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld quantization rule,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  J
  & = \dots = \\
  & = i \, 2 \pi \sum_{\alpha} \alpha p^*_{\alpha}(n) q_{\alpha}(n) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the derivative w.r.t. \(J\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 = i \, 2 \pi \sum_{\alpha} \alpha \dfrac{\partial}{\partial J} \left( p^*_{\alpha}(n) q_{\alpha}(n) \right) \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quantum reinterpretation.} Let a function \(\Phi(n,\alpha)\), then
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \Phi(n, \alpha) - \Phi(n - \alpha, \alpha) 
  & \sim \alpha \partial_n \Phi(n, \alpha) + o(\alpha) = \\
  & = \alpha h \partial_J \Phi(n, \alpha) + o(\alpha) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the \sphinxstylestrong{Born\sphinxhyphen{}Kramers correspondence principle follows},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\Phi(n, \alpha) - \Phi(n - \alpha, \alpha) }{ h } \sim \alpha \dfrac{\partial \Phi}{\partial J} (n, \alpha) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(p_\alpha(n) = p(n,\alpha) = p_{n+\alpha,n}\), then the reinterpretation of the classical quantization rule gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  1
  & = i \, \frac{2 \pi}{h} \sum_{\alpha} \left\{ p^*_{n+\alpha,n} q_{n+\alpha,n} - p^*_{n,n-\alpha} q_{n,n-\alpha} \right\} = \\
  & = i \, \frac{2 \pi}{h} \sum_{\alpha} \left\{ p^*_{n+\alpha,n} q_{n+\alpha,n} - \sum_\alpha p^*_{n,n-\alpha} q_{n,n-\alpha} \right\} = \\
  & = i \, \frac{2 \pi}{h} \sum_{\alpha} \left\{ p_{n,n+\alpha} q_{n+\alpha,n}   - \sum_\alpha q_{n,n-\alpha} p_{n-\alpha,n}  \right\} = \\
  & = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \sum_{\alpha} \left\{  q_{n,\alpha} p_{\alpha,n} - p_{n,\alpha} q_{\alpha,n} \right\}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These relations are nothing but the diagonal components of the matrix form \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:ccr-matrix} of the CCR. The out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal components are identically zero, as P.Jordan proved with the following trick
\subsubsection*{How P.Jordan proved that out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal components of the CCR are identically zero}

\sphinxAtStartPar
…


\subsubsection{CCR in Energy Basis and Ladenburg Dispersion Formula}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:ccr-in-energy-basis-and-ladenburg-dispersion-formula}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-ccr-ladenburg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing the expression of matrix components of the momentum \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_H = m \dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}_H\), \(P^a_{jk} = i m \omega_{jk} X^{a}_{jk}\) into the matrix form \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:eq:qm:heisenberg:ccr-matrix} of the CCR relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \delta_{ab} \delta_{jk} 
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ X^{a}_{j \ell} P^{b}_{\ell k} - P^{b}_{j \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} = \\
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ i m \omega_{\ell k} X^{a}_{j \ell} X^{b}_{\ell k} - i m \omega_{j \ell} X^{b}_{j \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The diagonal components \(j = k\) are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \delta_{ab} 
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ i m \omega_{\ell k} X^{a}_{k \ell} X^{b}_{\ell k} - i m \omega_{k \ell} X^{b}_{k \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(a = b\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar 
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ i m \omega_{\ell k} X^{a}_{k \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} - i m \omega_{k \ell} X^{a}_{k \ell} X^{a}_{\ell k} \right\} = \\
  & = \sum_{\ell} \left\{ i m \omega_{\ell k} X^{a}_{k \ell} X^{a \, *}_{k \ell} - i m \omega_{k \ell} X^{a}_{k \ell} X^{a \, *}_{k \ell} \right\} = \\
  & = i 2 m \, \sum_{\ell} \omega_{\ell k} \left| X^{a}_{k \ell} \right|^2  \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 \frac{2 m}{\hbar} \, \sum_{\ell} \omega_{\ell k} \left| X^{a}_{k \ell} \right|^2  = 1 \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{CHECK if there’s a factor \(3\), summing over all the components indexed by \(a\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Connection to Ladenburg Dispersion Formula.}
In classical optics/early quantum theory, Ladenburg’s quantum dispersion formula for the oscillator strength \(f_{km}\) associated with a transition \(k \to m\) is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f_{km} = \frac{2m \omega_{km}}{\hbar} |x_{km}|^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The diagonal CCR condition directly yields the \sphinxstylestrong{Thomas\sphinxhyphen{}Reiche\sphinxhyphen{}Kuhn (TRK) sum rule}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_m f_{km} = 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This showed that Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics naturally incorporated the empirically validated dispersion theory of Ladenburg, Kramers, and Kronig.


\subsubsection{Application: The Linear Harmonic Oscillator}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:application-the-linear-harmonic-oscillator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-linear-harmonic-oscillator}}\subsubsection*{Linear harmonic oscillator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian \(\hat{H} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \frac{1}{2}m\omega_0^2 \hat{x}^2\):

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equations of Motion.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  \dot{\hat{x}} & = \frac{\hat{p}}{m} \\
  \quad \dot{\hat{p}} & = -m\omega_0^2 \hat{x}
\end{aligned} \right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Taking the derivative of the first equation and replacing the second equation for \(\dot{\hat{p}}\), a second\sphinxhyphen{}order equation for \(\hat{x}\) follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ddot{\hat{x}} + \omega_0^2 \hat{x} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In matrix components:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(-\omega_{mn}^2 + \omega_0^2) x_{mn} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, non\sphinxhyphen{}zero matrix elements \(x_{mn}\) can only exist if \(\omega_{mn} = \pm \omega_0\), meaning transitions only occur between adjacent levels: \(m = n \pm 1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix Elements \& Energy Spectrum.}
Using the diagonal CCR \(\frac{2m}{\hbar} \sum_m \omega_{mn} |x_{nm}|^2 = 1\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{2m\omega_0}{\hbar} \left( |x_{n, n+1}|^2 - |x_{n, n-1}|^2 \right) = 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With the boundary condition \(x_{0,-1} = 0\) for the ground state:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|x_{n, n+1}|^2 = \frac{\hbar}{2m\omega_0} (n+1)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy matrix elements give the discrete eigenvalues:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n = \hbar \omega_0 \left( n + \frac{1}{2} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Transition Probabilities as Dipole Matrix Elements}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:transition-probabilities-as-dipole-matrix-elements}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-transition-dipole-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When an atom interacts with an electromagnetic field, the interaction Hamiltonian is dominated by the electric dipole coupling:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{V}(t) = - \hat{\mathbf{d}} \cdot \mathbf{E}(t) = - q \hat{\mathbf{x}} \cdot \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(\omega t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The probability amplitude for a transition from state \(|n\rangle\) to state \(|m\rangle\) is dictated by the matrix element of the position/dipole operator:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}x_{mn} = \langle m | \hat{x} | n \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The transition rate \(W_{n \to m}\) (spontaneous emission / absorption probability) is proportional to the square of the dipole matrix element:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W_{n \to m} \propto |\mathbf{d}_{mn}|^2 = q^2 |\langle m | \hat{\mathbf{x}} | n \rangle|^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Perturbation Theory for Transition Probabilities in Weak Electric Fields}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:perturbation-theory-for-transition-probabilities-in-weak-electric-fields}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-transition-perturbation-theory}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider a time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent perturbation \(\hat{V}(t) = \hat{W} \cos(\omega t) = -q \hat{\mathbf{x}} \cdot \mathbf{E}_0 \cos(\omega t)\).


\paragraph{First\sphinxhyphen{}Order Amplitude}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:first-order-amplitude}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Writing state expansion \(|\psi(t)\rangle = \sum_n c_n(t) e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}E_n t} |n\rangle\), the equations for \(c_m(t)\) are:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i\hbar \dot{c}_m(t) = \sum_n \langle m | \hat{V}(t) | n \rangle c_n(t) e^{i \omega_{mn} t}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming the system starts in initial state \(c_k(0) = 1\) and \(c_m(0) = 0\) for \(m \neq k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_m^{(1)}(t) = -\frac{i}{\hbar} \int_0^t V_{mk}(t') e^{i \omega_{mk} t'} dt'\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Substituting \(V_{mk}(t') = -q E_0 x_{mk} \frac{e^{i\omega t'} + e^{-i\omega t'}}{2}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_m^{(1)}(t) = \frac{q E_0 x_{mk}}{2\hbar} \left[ \frac{1 - e^{i(\omega_{mk} + \omega)t}}{\omega_{mk} + \omega} + \frac{1 - e^{i(\omega_{mk} - \omega)t}}{\omega_{mk} - \omega} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Resonant Approximation (Rotating Wave Approximation)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:resonant-approximation-rotating-wave-approximation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Near resonance (\(\omega \approx \omega_{mk}\) with \(E_m > E_k\)):

\sphinxAtStartPar
The term with denominator \((\omega_{mk} - \omega)\) dominates:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|c_m^{(1)}(t)|^2 \approx \frac{q^2 E_0^2 |x_{mk}|^2}{4\hbar^2} \frac{\sin^2\left(\frac{(\omega_{mk} - \omega)t}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\omega_{mk} - \omega}{2}\right)^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Second\sphinxhyphen{}Order Expansion for \protect\(|c_n(t)|^2\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:second-order-expansion-for-c-n-t-2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To compute probability to second order without assuming immediate resonance, we expand \(c_k(t)\) and \(c_m(t)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|c_k(t)|^2 = 1 + c_k^{(1)}(t) + c_k^{(1)*}(t) + |c_k^{(1)}(t)|^2 + \dots\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(V_{kk} = 0\) for parity\sphinxhyphen{}symmetric unperturbed states (\(x_{kk} = 0\)), the first\sphinxhyphen{}order correction to the initial state \(c_k^{(1)}(t) = 0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The conservation of total probability yields:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|c_k(t)|^2 = 1 - \sum_{m \neq k} |c_m^{(1)}(t)|^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This confirms that weak external monochromatic fields cause probability transitions whose rates are directly dictated by matrix elements \(x_{mk}\) of Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics.

\sphinxstepscope

\sphinxstylestrong{A. Ultrashort / Arbitrary Pulses.} For a general pulse (such as a Gaussian envelope centered at \(t_0\) with bandwidth \(\Delta \omega\)):
