\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the numerical solver, you simply update the field definition in \(V_{mn}(t)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V_{mn}(t) = -e \, D_{mn} \, E(t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{B. Broad\sphinxhyphen{}Spectrum / Thermal Light (Fermi’s Golden Rule \& Rate Equations).} If the field is incoherent broadband light characterized by a spectral energy density \(\rho(\omega)\) (\(\text{J}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}\cdot\text{Hz}^{-1}\)), phase coherence between states drops out on fast timescales.Instead of tracking coherent state amplitudes \(c_n(t)\) via the TDSE, the dynamics transition to Einstein Rate Equations for populations \(P_n(t) = \vert{}c_n(t)\vert{}^2\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{d P_b}{dt} = -\frac{d P_a}{dt} = B_{ab} \, \rho(\omega_{ba}) \, (P_a - P_b) - A_{ba} \, P_b\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where Fermi’s Golden Rule gives the absorption rate \(W_{a \to b}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W_{a \to b} = \frac{2\pi}{\hbar^2} \vert{}\langle b \vert{} V_0 \vert{} a \rangle\vert{}^2 \delta(E_b - E_a - \hbar\omega) \implies B_{ab} = \frac{\pi e^2}{\epsilon_0 \hbar^2} \vert{}D_{ab}\vert{}^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Origin of wave theory of quantum mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-wave-mechanics:origin-of-wave-theory-of-quantum-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-wave-mechanics:quantum-mehcanics-history-origin-wave-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/origin-wave-mechanics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Main contributions from:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/de-broglie:quantum-mehcanics-history-wave-mechanics-de-broglie}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{L. de Broglie}}}}, (1922\sphinxhyphen{}24): matter waves

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/schrodinger:quantum-mehcanics-history-wave-mechanics-schrodinger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{E. Schrodinger}}}}, (1926) “An Undulatory Theory of the Mechanics of Atoms and Molecules”:  wave equation. “if a phenomenon behaves like a wave, it must be governed by a wave equation”

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Experimental verifications:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Davisson\sphinxhyphen{}Germer experiment (1923\sphinxhyphen{}27) confirmed the hypothesis of L. de Broglie: \(e^-\) scattered by a surface of a metal crystal showed a diffraction pattern, a characteristic phenomenon of wave processes, consistent with the relation postulated by de Broglie linking the wave vector and the momentum \(\mathbf{k} = \frac{\mathbf{p}}{\hbar}\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}

\section{Bohr model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:bohr-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-bohr}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assumption:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Electron moves on circular orbits

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All the possible orbits are identified by discrete values of the angular momentum, \(L = n \hbar\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Light emission/absorption occurs when an electron transitions between two orbits

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some mathematical details, using the equations of classical mechanics. The problem of determining the orbit of an electron around the positive nucleus is a two\sphinxhyphen{}body problem, subject to a force \(\vec{F} \propto \frac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|^3}\) (here the assumption of the center of mass in the nucleus; otherwise change of coordinates, and equivalent masses…). For an electrically neutral atom with one electron only (\(H\) atom?) the dynamical equation governing the motion of the electron
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m \ddot{\vec{r}} = - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|^3} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(q\) the charge of the electron.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using polar coordinates, \(\vec{r} = r \hat{r}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Taking time derivative of the position vector \(\vec{r}\) identifying the position of the electron w.r.t. the nucleus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( r \hat{r} \right ) & = \dot{r} \hat{r} + r \dot{\theta} \hat{\theta} \\
     \dfrac{d^2}{dt^2} \left( r \hat{r} \right ) & = \left( \ddot{r} - r \dot{\theta}^2 \right) \hat{r} +  \left( 2 \dot{r} \dot{\theta} + r \ddot{\theta} \right) \hat{\theta} \\
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming circular orbits, \(\dot{r} = 0\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the radial and angular components of the dynamical equation read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  r      & : \quad - m r \dot{\theta}^2 = - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r^2} \\
  \theta & : \quad \ddot{\theta} = 0 \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The angular momentum and the energy of the system are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Angular momentum,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     n \hbar = L_n 
     & = m r_n^2 \dot{\theta}_n =  && \text{(radial component)} \\
     & = m r_n^2 \left( \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon r_n^3 m} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \\
     & =  \frac{\sqrt{m} q}{\sqrt{ 4 \pi \varepsilon}} r^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
     \rightarrow \quad r_n & = 4 \pi \varepsilon \frac{n^2 \hbar^2}{m q^2}
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:eq:atom:bohr:energy}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
    E_n 
    & = \frac{1}{2} m |\dot{\vec{r}}_n|^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r_n} =  && \text{(radial component of the eom)} \\
    & = \frac{q^2}{8 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r_n} - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r_n} = \\
    & = - \frac{q^2}{8 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r_n} = && \text{($r_n$ from angular momentum)} \\
    & = - \frac{m q^4}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon^2 \hbar^2} \frac{1}{n^2} = && \text{($h = 2 \pi \hbar$)} \\
    & = - \frac{m q^4}{8 \varepsilon^2 h^2}\frac{1}{n^2} \ .
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The value of energy \(E_n\) of Bohr model coincides with the value \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:eq:atom:schrodinger:energy} of the energy produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Schrodinger model}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From the relation \(\Delta E = \nu h\), the relation between the frequency of the emitted (if \(E_{n} > E_{m}\), \(n\) initial state, \(m\) final state) or absorbed (if \(E_n < E_m\), \(n\) initial state, \(m\) final state) radiation, follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nu_{nm} = \frac{E_n - E_m}{h} = - \frac{m q^4}{8 \varepsilon^2 h^3} \left( \frac{1}{n^2} - \frac{1}{m^2} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Sommerfeld model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:sommerfeld-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-sommerfeld}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a revolutionary model of the atom that successfully explained the spectral lines of hydrogen. Bohr’s model combined classical mechanics with quantum concepts, asserting that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed, circular orbits with quantized angular momentum:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L = n \hbar = n \frac{h}{2\pi}, \quad n \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
While the Bohr model was a monumental step forward, high\sphinxhyphen{}resolution spectroscopy soon revealed several limitations:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fine Structure:} Spectral lines that initially appeared singular actually split into closely spaced multiplet lines under high resolution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Complex Atoms:} The model failed to accurately predict the spectra of multi\sphinxhyphen{}electron atoms (like helium).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Zeeman Effect:} It could not explain the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of a magnetic field.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To resolve these shortcomings, German physicist \sphinxstylestrong{Arnold Sommerfeld} extended Bohr’s theory in 1916 by:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
relaxing the restriction of purely circular orbits.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
introducing relativistic corrections

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Key Postulates and Mathematical Framework}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:key-postulates-and-mathematical-framework}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sommerfeld generalized Bohr’s circular orbit condition using the \sphinxstylestrong{Wilson\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld Quantization Rule} for periodic systems:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint p_i \, dq^i = n_i h\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(p_i\) is the generalized momentum corresponding to coordinate \(q^i\), \(n_i\) is an integer quantum number, and \(h\) is Planck’s constant.


\subsubsection{Elliptical Orbits}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:elliptical-orbits}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sommerfeld proposed that electron orbits are generally \sphinxstylestrong{elliptical}, with the nucleus residing at one of the foci of the ellipse. To describe an ellipse in polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\), two generalized coordinates are required, leading to two quantization conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Azimuthal Quantization},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint p_\theta \, d\theta = n_\theta h \implies L = n_\theta \hbar\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radial Quantization},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint p_r \, dr = n_r h \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(n_\theta\) is the azimuthal quantum number (also denoted as \(k\)) and \(n_r\) is the radial quantum number. The total principal quantum number \(n\) is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n = n_r + n_\theta\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The geometry of the ellipse—specifically the ratio of the semi\sphinxhyphen{}minor axis \(b\) to the semi\sphinxhyphen{}major axis \(a\)—is governed by these quantum numbers:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{b}{a} = \frac{n_\theta}{n} = \frac{n_\theta}{n_r + n_\theta}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When \(n_\theta = n\), \(b = a\), yielding a circular orbit (Bohr’s original case).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When \(n_\theta < n\), \(b < a\), producing an elliptical orbit.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Relativistic Correction and Energy Splitting}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:relativistic-correction-and-energy-splitting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic mechanics, the energy of an electron in an elliptical orbit depends \sphinxstylestrong{only} on the principal quantum number \(n\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n = -\frac{m_e e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This means all orbits with the same \(n\) would have identical energy (degeneracy).

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, Sommerfeld recognized that an electron moves faster when it passes closer to the nucleus in a highly elliptical orbit. Applying Einstein’s special relativity, the electron’s mass \(m\) varies with velocity \(v\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When relativistic effects are accounted for, the ellipse undergoes \sphinxstylestrong{precession} (perihelion precession), breaking the energy degeneracy. The modified energy expression becomes dependent on both \(n\) and \(n_\theta\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{n, n_\theta} = -\frac{R_y h c Z^2}{n^2} \left[ 1 + \frac{\alpha^2 Z^2}{n} \left( \frac{1}{n_\theta} - \frac{3}{4n} \right) \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(R_y\) is the Rydberg constant,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(Z\) is the atomic number,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 \hbar c} \approx \dfrac{1}{137}\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{Fine\sphinxhyphen{}Structure Constant}.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Major Achievements}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:major-achievements}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Explanation of Fine Structure:} The dependence of energy levels on \(n_\theta\) alongside \(n\) successfully explained the small energy differences responsible for the fine splitting of hydrogen spectral lines.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Introduction of Spatial Quantization:} Sommerfeld added a third quantum number \(m\) (magnetic quantum number) to describe the orientation of orbits in 3D space, providing a framework for the Zeeman effect.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Introduction of \(\alpha\):} It introduced the fine\sphinxhyphen{}structure constant \(\alpha\), a fundamental constant in modern physics representing the coupling strength of electromagnetic interactions.

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Limitations and Transition to Quantum Mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/sommerfeld:limitations-and-transition-to-quantum-mechanics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Despite its empirical success, the Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld model was a \sphinxstylestrong{semi\sphinxhyphen{}classical (or “Old Quantum Theory”)} construction. Its limitations ultimately spurred the transition to modern quantum mechanics:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ad\sphinxhyphen{}hoc Assumptions:} It blended classical electrodynamics (planetary orbits) with arbitrary quantization rules without an underlying wave mechanism.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intensity and Selection Rules:} It could not predict the transition probabilities (intensities of spectral lines) accurately.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Failure for Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Electron Systems:} Like Bohr’s model, it could not be extended reliably to helium or larger atoms.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The model was eventually superseded by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic atomic model using \sphinxstylestrong{Schrödinger’s Wave Mechanics}}}}} (1926) and \sphinxstylestrong{Dirac’s Relativistic Quantum Mechanics} (1928), where \(n_\theta\) was replaced by the orbital angular momentum quantum number \(l = n_\theta - 1\).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Analytical mechanics \sphinxhyphen{} short notes}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:analytical-mechanics-short-notes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:analytical-mechanics-short}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To understand the theoretical justification behind the \sphinxstylestrong{Wilson\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld Quantization Rule}, we must examine the formal framework of classical analytical mechanics. Old Quantum Theory did not apply quantization conditions to arbitrary coordinates; rather, it relied on the natural canonical coordinates provided by \sphinxstylestrong{action\sphinxhyphen{}angle variables}.


\subsubsection{Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:lagrangian-and-hamiltonian-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:analytical-mechanics-short-lagrange-hamilton}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Lagrangian mechanics.} Consider a classical physical system with \(f\) degrees of freedom described by generalized coordinates \(\mathbf{q} = (q_1, q_2, \dots, q_f)\) and generalized velocities \(\mathbf{\dot{q}} = (\dot{q}^1, \dot{q}^2, \dots, \dot{q}^f)\). The equations of motion can be derived from the principle of stationariety of the action, \(S\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \delta S = \delta \int_{t_0}^{t_1} L \left( \dot{\mathbf{q}}(t), \mathbf{q}(t), t \right) \, dt \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with prescribed ends \(\delta \mathbf{q}(t_0) = \delta \mathbf{q}(t_1) = \mathbf{0}\), and \(L(\dot{\mathbf{q}}(t), \mathbf{q}(t), t)\) the Lagrangian function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  L(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{\dot{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{\dot{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q}) \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical (or conjugate) momentum associated with coordinate \(q_i\) is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
p_i = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Hamiltonian mechanics.} Via a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Legendre transformation}, we transition from the \((\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{\dot{q}})\) state space to the canonical phase space \((\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p})\), introducing the \sphinxstylestrong{Hamiltonian}, nothing but the mechanical energy of the system as a function of generalized coordinates and momenta,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}, t) = \sum_{i=1}^f p_i \dot{q}_i - L(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{\dot{q}}, t)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Taking the differential of \(H\), the equations of motion follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ 
\begin{aligned}
  \dot{q}_i & =  \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} \\
  \dot{p}_i & = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}
\end{aligned} \right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while \(\partial_t H = - \partial_t L\).


\subsubsection{Canonical Transformations and Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi Theory}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:canonical-transformations-and-hamilton-jacobi-theory}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:analytical-mechanics-short-canonical-transformations}}\subsubsection*{Canonical transformations and invariance}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Transformation \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}) \leftrightarrow  \mathbf{Z} = (\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P})\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  \dot{\mathbf{q}} & = \partial_{\mathbf{p}} H \\
  \dot{\mathbf{p}} & =-\partial_{\mathbf{q}} H \\
\end{aligned} \right.
\qquad , \qquad
\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  \dot{\mathbf{Q}} & = \partial_{\mathbf{P}} K \\
  \dot{\mathbf{P}} & =-\partial_{\mathbf{Q}} K \\
\end{aligned} \right.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
 \dot{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{J} \nabla_{\mathbf{z}} H
 \qquad , \qquad
 \dot{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{J} \nabla_{\mathbf{Z}} K \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \\ -\mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{Z},t)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{z}_i        & = \dot{Z}_k \, \partial_{Z_K} z_i + \partial_t z_i \\
  \partial_{z_i} f & = \partial_{z_i} Z_k \, \partial_{Z_k} f
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
for a regular transformation, with non\sphinxhyphen{}singular gradient \(\partial_{Z_k} z_i \, \partial_{z_i} Z_j = \delta_{kj}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{Z}_j
  & = \partial_{z_i} Z_j \left( \dot{z}_i - \partial_t z_i \right) = \\
  & = \partial_{z_i} Z_j \left( J_{il} \partial_{z_l} H - \partial_t z_i \right) = \\
  & = \partial_{z_i} Z_j \, J_{il} \, \partial_{z_l} Z_{m} \, \partial_{Z_m} H -  \partial_{z_i} Z_j \, \partial_t z_i \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or with matrix formalism

\begin{split}\dot{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{G}^T \mathbf{J} \mathbf{G} \nabla_{\mathbf{Z}} H - \mathbf{G}^T \, \partial_t \mathbf{z} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

…

\sphinxstyleemphasis{Fix and uncomment}

\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Invariance of Poisson brackets

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{todo}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Determinant of \(\mathbf{G}^T \mathbf{J} \mathbf{G} = \mathbf{J}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{G} |^2 |\mathbf{J}| = |\mathbf{J}| \quad \rightarrow \quad | \mathbf{G} | = \mp 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The orientation\sphinxhyphen{}preserving transformation is the one with \(| \mathbf{G} | = 1\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Elementary volume in the phase space
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|d \mathbf{q} d \mathbf{p}| = | \mathbf{G}| \, | d \mathbf{Q} \, d \mathbf{P} | = | d \mathbf{Q} \, d \mathbf{P} |\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A transformation from coordinates \((\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p})\) to new variables \((\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P})\) is \sphinxstylestrong{canonical} if it preserves the form of Hamilton’s equations under a new Hamiltonian \(K(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P}, t)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using two sets of coordinates, the principle of stationary action reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \delta \int_{t_0}^{t_1} L(\dot{\mathbf{q}}, \mathbf{q},t) \, dt = \delta \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \mathcal{L}(\dot{\mathbf{Q}}, \mathbf{Q},t) \, dt \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The two Lagrangian functions can differ by a time\sphinxhyphen{}derivative \(\dfrac{d}{dt} F_{1}(\mathbf{q}(t), \mathbf{Q}(t),t)\) at most. Thus, using the relation between the Lagrangian and the Hamiltonian function, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{q}} - H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) = \mathbf{P} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{Q}} - K(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P}, t) + \frac{d}{dt} F_1(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{Q},t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Moving \( \frac{d F_1}{dt}\) on one side, and expanding the time derivative,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dfrac{d F_1}{dt}
  & = \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{Q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{Q}} F_1 + \partial_t F_1 = \\
  & = \mathbf{p} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{q}} - \mathbf{P} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{Q}} - H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) + K(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P}, t)
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exploiting the arbitrariness of the functions involved, the following relations hold
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{p} = \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 \qquad , \qquad
  \mathbf{P} =-\partial_{\mathbf{Q}} F_1 \qquad , \qquad
  K - H      = \partial_{t} F_1 \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Another \sphinxstyleemphasis{Legendre transformation} introduces a type\sphinxhyphen{}2 generating function \(F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t) := F_1(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{Q}, t) + \mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{P} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that allows to go from the independent pair of variables \((\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{Q})\) to \((\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P})\), as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d_t F_2 
  & = \partial_t F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{Q}} \cdot \underbrace{\left( \partial_{\mathbf{Q}} F_1 + \mathbf{P} \right)}_{= \mathbf{0}} + \dot{\mathbf{P}} \cdot \mathbf{Q} = \\
  & =\partial_t F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{P}} \cdot \mathbf{Q} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_2 = \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 = \mathbf{p} \qquad , \qquad
  \partial_{\mathbf{P}} F_2 = \mathbf{Q} \qquad , \qquad
  \partial_t F_2 = \partial_{t} F_1 = K - H \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{The Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi Equation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:the-hamilton-jacobi-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:analytical-mechanics-short-hamilton-jacobi-equation}}\subsubsection*{Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the canonical transformation so that the Hamiltonian function in \(\mathbf{Q}\), \(\mathbf{P}\) is identically zero, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}K(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P}, t) := 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} This is not a 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional constraint between \(\mathbf{Q}\), \(\mathbf{P}\). This is the expression of the function, like the function \(f(x) := 0 \) is a real function whose value is \(0\) for all the \(x\) of the domain. Thus, all the derivatives of the function w.r.t. the independent variables are identically zero as well,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_{\mathbf{Q}} K = \mathbf{0} \qquad , \qquad \partial_{\mathbf{P}} K = \mathbf{0} \qquad , \qquad \partial_t K = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If these relations hold, from the Hamiltonian equations, it follows that \(\mathbf{Q}\) and \(\mathbf{P}\) are constant in time.
Thus,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = K(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{P}, t) = \\
  & = H(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p},t) + \partial_t F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t) = \\
  & = H(\mathbf{q}, \partial_\mathbf{q} F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t) ,t) + \partial_t F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t) = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(H\) is not explicitly dependent on \(t\), and thus the system is conservative as \(d_t H = \partial_t H = 0\), it follows \(H(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}) = E\), constant. Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi equation thus becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = H\left( \mathbf{q}, \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_2 \right) + \partial_t F_2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(H\) doesn’t explicitly depends on time, it’s possible to look for a solution of the equation \(F_2(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}, t) = S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}) - T(t)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = H \left( \mathbf{q}, \partial_{\mathbf{q}} S \right) + \dot{T} = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H \left( \mathbf{q}, \partial_{\mathbf{q}} S \right) = - \dot{T} = E \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  T(t) & = - E t + T_0 \\
  H \left( \mathbf{q}, \partial_{\mathbf{q}} S \right) & = E \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ultimate goal of Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi theory is to find a canonical transformation to a set canonical variables \((\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{J})\) with \sphinxstylestrong{constant} momentum variables \(\mathbf{J}\) and making the new Hamiltonian identically zero (\(K = 0\)). Hamilton equations read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{\begin{aligned}
  \dot{\mathbf{w}} & = \partial_{\mathbf{J}} K \\
  \dot{\mathbf{J}} & =-\partial_{\mathbf{w}} K \\
\end{aligned}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\mathbf{J}\) is constant, thus \(\dot{\mathbf{J}} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\partial_{\mathbf{Q}} K = 0\). Thus \(K(\mathbf{J}, t)\). As \(K(\mathbf{J}, t) = 0\), and \(\mathbf{J}\) constant, thus \(0 = d_t K = \partial_t K\). Then it follows that \(K(\mathbf{J}) = 0\). As \(\mathbf{J}\) are constant, then \(\partial_{\mathbf{J}} K\) is constant as well. The first Hamilton equation implies \(\mathbf{w}(t) = \partial_{\mathbf{J}} K \cdot t + \mathbf{w}_0\).
\subsubsection*{old}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Time derivative of Type\sphinxhyphen{}1 generating function, \(F_1(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{Q},t)\), becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d_t F_1 
  & = \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \mathbf{p} - \underbrace{ \dot{\mathbf{w}} }_{=\partial_{\mathbf{J}} K} \cdot \mathbf{J} + \underbrace{ K }_{=0} - H(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}, t) = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Time derivative of Type\sphinxhyphen{}2 generating function, \(F_2(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{P},t)\), becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d_t F_2 
  & = \partial_t F_1 + \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{q}} F_1 + \underbrace{\dot{\mathbf{J}} \cdot \mathbf{w}}_{=\mathbf{0}} = \\
  & = - H(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}, t) + \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \mathbf{p} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Choosing \(F_2(\mathbf{q}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, t) = S(\mathbf{q}, \boldsymbol{\alpha}) - E t\), where \(S(\mathbf{q}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is \sphinxstylestrong{Hamilton’s characteristic function}, Hamilton’s principal equation reduces to the time\sphinxhyphen{}independent \sphinxstylestrong{Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi Equation}:

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(H(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}\), then the system is conservative. Exploiting separation of variables, \(F_{2}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J}, t) = S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J}) - E t\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H\left(\mathbf{q}, \partial_{\mathbf{q}} S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J}) \right) = E \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\dot{\mathbf{J}} = 0\), the time derivative of \(S\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{S} = \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{q}} S + \underbrace{\dot{\mathbf{J}} \cdot \partial_{\mathbf{J}} S}_{= \mathbf{0}} = \dot{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system is \sphinxstylestrong{separable}, \(S(\mathbf{q}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})\) splits into independent single\sphinxhyphen{}variable functions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J}) = \sum_{i=1}^f S_i(q^i, \mathbf{J})
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that its time derivative reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{S} = \dot{q}^i \, S'_i(q_i, \mathbf{J}) = \dot{q}^i \, p_i(q^i, \mathbf{J}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Action\sphinxhyphen{}Angle Variables}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:action-angle-variables}}\subsubsection*{Anction\sphinxhyphen{}angle variables}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the canonical transformation \(\mathbf{w}\), \(\mathbf{J}\), so that \(\mathbf{J}\) is constant. From Hamilton equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{
\begin{aligned}
  \dot{\mathbf{w}} & = \partial_{\mathbf{J}} K \\
  \dot{\mathbf{J}} & =-\partial_{\mathbf{w}} K = \mathbf{0} \\
\end{aligned}
\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(K\) is a function of \(\mathbf{J}, t\) only, \(K(\mathbf{J},t)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bound, periodic systems whose Hamilton\sphinxhyphen{}Jacobi equations are separable, the most suitable coordinate system consists of \sphinxstylestrong{Action\sphinxhyphen{}Angle Variables} \((\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{J})\).


\paragraph{Definition of Action Variables}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:definition-of-action-variables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Action Variable} \(J_i\) associated with the \(i\)\sphinxhyphen{}th degree of freedom is defined as the line integral of momentum over one complete cycle of motion in phase space:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
J_i \equiv \oint p_i \, dq_i = \oint \frac{\partial S_i(q_i, \boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\partial q_i} \, dq_i
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, the loop \(\oint\) denotes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A complete libration (back\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}forth oscillation between turning points), or

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \(2\pi\) rotation for angular coordinates.

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Angle Variables and Frequencies}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:angle-variables-and-frequencies}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the action variables \(J_i\) are constants of motion, we can express the total Hamiltonian purely as a function of the action variables: \(H = H(J_1, J_2, \dots, J_f)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical conjugates to \(J_i\) are the \sphinxstylestrong{Angle Variables} \(w_i\), defined via the generating function \(S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J})\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
w_i = \frac{\partial S(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{J})}{\partial J_i}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Hamilton’s equations of motion in action\sphinxhyphen{}angle variables simplify to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\dot{J}_i = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial w_i} = 0 \implies J_i = \text{constant}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\dot{w}_i = \frac{\partial H(J_1, \dots, J_f)}{\partial J_i} \equiv \nu_i (\mathbf{J}) \implies w_i(t) = \nu_i t + w_i(0)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(\nu_i\) is the exact \sphinxstylestrong{fundamental frequency} of the classical motion along coordinate \(q_i\).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{4. The Wilson\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld Quantization Postulate}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:the-wilson-sommerfeld-quantization-postulate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The central insight of William Wilson (1915) and Arnold Sommerfeld (1916) was that quantization should \sphinxstylestrong{not} be applied arbitrarily to any set of phase space coordinates. Instead, quantization conditions must be invariant under canonical transformations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The integral invariants of Poincaré show that the total phase space volume element \(\sum_i \oint p_i dq_i\) is a canonical invariant. Therefore, quantization must be imposed directly onto the adiabatic invariants of the classical motion: \sphinxstylestrong{the Action Variables \(J_i\)}.


\paragraph{The Quantization Rule}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:the-quantization-rule}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Wilson\sphinxhyphen{}Sommerfeld quantization rule dictates that each action variable \(J_i\) is restricted to integer multiples of Planck’s constant \(h\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
J_i = \oint p_i \, dq_i = n_i h, \quad n_i \in \mathbb{N}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Summary of Connection to Quantum Mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/analytical-mechanics-short:summary-of-connection-to-quantum-mechanics}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Separability:} The classical system must be separable in coordinates \((q_1, \dots, q_f)\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Phase Space Loops:} The integral \(\oint p_i dq_i\) measures the area enclosed by the periodic trajectory in the \((q_i, p_i)\) 2D projection of phase space.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Discretization:} Quantizing \(J_i = n_i h\) slices phase space into discrete cells of volume \(h^f\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy Spectrum:} Inverting \(H(J_1, \dots, J_f)\) with \(J_i \to n_i h\) yields the quantized energy levels \(E(n_1, n_2, \dots, n_f)\).

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Schrodinger model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:schrodinger-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger::doc}}\subsubsection*{Contents}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-analytical-sln}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mathematical details of the analytical solution}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Gallery of orbitals}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Auxiliary notes}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Schrodinger equation.} Schrodinger equation in space basis for the electron in a \(\text{H}\) atom reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \partial_t \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the Hamiltonian is the sum of the kinetic energy and a Coulomb potential contribution, \(\hat{V}\), so that \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}|} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t)\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectral decomposition of the Hamiltonian operator.} The stationary states, and the corresponding energy levels \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the eigenfunctions, and the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) \sphinxhyphen{} are the result of the eigenvalue problem, \(\hat{H} | \Psi \rangle = E | \Psi \rangle\), or using space basis,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r}) = E \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quantum numbers.} The stationary states depend on \sphinxstylestrong{three} \sphinxhyphen{} in this model, no spin exists \sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstylestrong{quantum numbers}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{principal} quantum number \(n \in \{ 1, 2, \dots \}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{azimuthal} quantum number \(\ell \in \{ 0, 1,\dots, n-1 \} \)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{magnetic} quantum number \(m_{\ell} \in \{ -\ell, -\ell+1, \dots, \ell \}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy levels only depend on the principal quantum number, \(E(n)\). Thus, Schrodinger model of the atom has \sphinxstylestrong{degenerate} stationary states, i.e. stationary states with the same energy value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutation of \(\hat{H}\), \(\hat{L}^2\), \(\hat{L}_z\).} As angular momentum operators \(\hat{L}^2\), \(\hat{L}_z\) commute with the Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) of the \(\text{H}\) atom, these three operators share common eigenvectors. These relations are proved in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{note section}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Schrodinger model \sphinxhyphen{} Mathematical details of the analytical solution}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:schrodinger-model-mathematical-details-of-the-analytical-solution}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-analytical-sln}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Schrodinger equation} for the hydrogen atom in space basis reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \left[ - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon} \frac{1}{r} \right] \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{eigenproblem of the Hermitian operator} (projected onto space basis, as well) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon r} \Psi_n(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the symmetries of the system, the solution of the eigenproblem is evaluated using spherical coordinates \(\{ r, \theta, \varphi \}\), and the method of separation of variables. Using \sphinxstylestrong{spherical coordinates},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}- \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left\{ \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r \left( r^2 \partial_r \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin\theta} \partial_\theta \left( \sin\theta \partial_\theta \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} \right\} \Psi_n - \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \Psi_n = E_n \Psi_n\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Separation of variables, \protect\(\ \Psi_{nlm}(r, \theta, \varphi) = R_n(r) Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) \ \protect\) }

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstylestrong{method of separation of variables}, we look for solutions in product form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi_{nlm}(r, \theta, \varphi) = R_n(r) Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and substituting into the Schrödinger equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( E_n + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right) R_n Y_{lm} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left[ \frac{1}{r^2} \left( r^2 R_n' \right)' Y_{lm} + R_n \left( \frac{1}{r^2 \sin\theta} \partial_\theta \left( \sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm} \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right) \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing by \(R_n Y_{lm}\), and multiplying by \(r^2 \frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \underbrace{\frac{1}{R_n} (r^2 R_n')' + \frac{2m r^2}{\hbar^2} \left( E_n + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right)}_{f(r)} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{Y_{lm}} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \partial_\theta (\sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm}) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right\}}_{g(\theta, \varphi)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(f(r) + g(\theta, \varphi) = 0\), both terms must equal equal\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}opposite constant \(C\) for all valid domains \(r \in (0, +\infty)\), \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\), \(\varphi \in (0, 2\pi)\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C = f(r) = - g(\theta, \varphi) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Radial equation, and energy levels}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The radial component determines the energy level,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:eq:atom:schrodinger:energy}
\begin{split}E_n = - \frac{m q^4}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2} \frac{1}{n^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(n \in \{ 1, 2, \dots \}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The radial distribution of the energy state functions is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = e^{-\rho/2} \rho^{\ell} L^{2 \ell+1}_{n-\ell-1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\rho = r \frac{\sqrt{-8 m E_n}}{\hbar}\) the non dimensional radius, \(\ell \in \{ 0, 1, \dots, n-1 \}\), and \(L_{p}^{k}(x)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre differential equation \(x y'' + ( k + 1 - x ) y' + p y = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Change of variables, and asymptotic behavior}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining \(C = \ell(\ell+1)\), and dividing the equation \(f(r) = C\) by \(r^2\), for the states with \(E_n <0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr} \left( r^2 R' \right) + \left[ \frac{2m}{\hbar^2} \left( E + \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r} \right) - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{r^2} \right] R = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining the \sphinxstylestrong{dimensionless radial variable} \(\rho = \kappa r\), so \(\frac{d}{dr} = \kappa \frac{d}{d\rho}\), and factoring out \(\kappa^2\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \kappa^2 \left\{ \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 \frac{dR}{d\rho} \right) + \left( \frac{2m E}{\hbar^2 \kappa^2} + \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \kappa \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0 \rho} - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} \right) \right\} R\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By choosing \(\kappa^2 = -\frac{8 m E}{\hbar^2}\) (where \(\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{-8 m E}}{\hbar}\) for \(E < 0\)), the first term inside the parentheses becomes \(-1\). Defining the constant parameter \(\rho_0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_0 = \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \kappa \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0} = \frac{2m q^2}{\hbar^2 \sqrt{-8 m E} \cdot 4\pi \varepsilon_0} = \frac{q^2}{8\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar} \sqrt{\frac{2m}{-E}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the dimensionless radial equation simplifies to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 \frac{dR}{d\rho} \right) + R \left[ - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\rho_0}{\rho} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Boundary conditions required for regular wavefunctions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho = 0) < \infty, \quad R(\rho \to +\infty) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior for \protect\(\ r \rightarrow 0\protect\), and \protect\(\ r \rightarrow +\infty\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large Distance Limit (\(\rho \to +\infty\)).} For large \(\rho\), terms proportional to \(\frac{1}{\rho}\) and \(\frac{1}{\rho^2}\) become negligible:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 R' \right) = R'' + \frac{2}{\rho} R' \sim R''\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The equation reduces to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R'' - \frac{1}{4} R \sim 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
General solution:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = A e^{-\rho/2} + B e^{\rho/2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To satisfy the non\sphinxhyphen{}divergent boundary condition at infinity, set \(B = 0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) \sim e^{-\rho/2} \quad \text{as } \rho \to +\infty\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Small Distance Limit (\(\rho \to 0\)).} For \(\rho \to 0\), the centrifugal term \(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{\rho^2}\) dominates over the constant and \(\frac{1}{\rho}\) terms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R'' + \frac{2}{\rho} R' - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} R \sim 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Proposing a power\sphinxhyphen{}law ansatz \(R(\rho) \sim \rho^s\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s(s - 1) \rho^{s-2} + 2s \rho^{s-2} - \ell(\ell + 1) \rho^{s-2} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s^2 + s - \ell(\ell + 1) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Solving the quadratic characteristic equation for \(s\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_{1,2} = \frac{-1 \mp \sqrt{1 + 4\ell(\ell + 1)}}{2} = \frac{-1 \mp (1 + 2\ell)}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_1 = \ell, \quad s_2 = -(\ell + 1)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(\ell \ge 0\), \(s_2 = -(\ell + 1)\) leads to divergence at the origin \(\rho \to 0\). Retaining only the physically acceptable solution \(s = \ell\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) \sim \rho^\ell \quad \text{as } \rho \to 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Transformation \& Differential Equation for \(v(\rho)\).} Combining both asymptotic behaviors, we represent the full radial solution as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = \rho^\ell e^{-\rho/2} v(\rho)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Writing out derivatives of \(R(\rho)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R' = \left( \ell \rho^{\ell-1} - \frac{1}{2} \rho^\ell \right) e^{-\rho/2} v + \rho^\ell e^{-\rho/2} v'\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After expanding \(\frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{d}{d\rho} \left( \rho^2 R' \right) + R \left[ - \frac{\ell(\ell + 1)}{\rho^2} - \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\rho_0}{\rho} \right] = 0\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}= e^{-\rho/2} \Big\{ \rho^\ell v'' + v' \left[ 2\ell \rho^{\ell-1} - \frac{1}{2} \rho^\ell + 2 \rho^{\ell-1} \right] + v \left[ \rho^\ell \ell(\ell+1) - \rho^{\ell+1} \left( \ell + 1 \right) + \frac{1}{4} \rho^{\ell+2} - \ell(\ell+1) \rho^{\ell} - \frac{1}{4} \rho^{\ell+2} + \rho_0 \rho^{\ell+1} \right] \Big\} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing out non\sphinxhyphen{}zero factor \(\rho^{\ell-1} e^{-\rho/2}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho v''(\rho) + [2(\ell + 1) - \rho] v'(\rho) + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) v(\rho) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polynomial expansion, energy quantization \protect\(\ E_n \ \protect\) and radial distribution \protect\(\ R_n(\rho)\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting from the transformed radial equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho v''(\rho) + [2(\ell + 1) - \rho] v'(\rho) + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) v(\rho) = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Looking for a power series solution:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
    v(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k \rho^k  \\
   v'(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k c_k \rho^{k-1} \\
  v''(\rho) & = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k(k-1) c_k \rho^{k-2} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Substituting into the differential equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k(k-1) c_k \rho^{k-1} + \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2(\ell + 1) k c_k \rho^{k-1} - \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} k c_k \rho^k + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_k \rho^k = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Shift indices to group terms by power \(\rho^k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \Big\{ (k+1)(k) c_{k+1} + 2(\ell + 1)(k+1) c_{k+1} - k c_k + (\rho_0 - \ell - 1) c_k \Big\} \rho^k = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Recurrence Relation.} Equating coefficients to zero yields the recurrence relation for \(c_k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_{k+1} = c_k \frac{k + \ell + 1 - \rho_0}{(k + 1)(k + 2\ell + 2)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Asymptotic Behavior \& Series Termination.} If the power series does not terminate, as \(k \to +\infty\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{c_{k+1}}{c_k} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This asymptotic behavior matches that of the exponential expansion \(e^\rho \sim \sum \frac{\rho^k}{k!}\) and thus \(\frac{c_{k+1}}{c_k} = \frac{1}{k+1} \sim \frac{1}{k}\).
Thus, an infinite series \(v(\rho) \sim e^\rho\), would lead to \(R(\rho) \sim e^{-\rho/2} e^\rho = e^{\rho/2}\), which diverges as \(\rho \to +\infty\).
Thus, in order to maintain physical normalizability, the series must terminate at a maximum power \(k_{\max} = N\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_{N+1} = 0 \implies N + \ell + 1 - \rho_0 = 0 \implies \rho_0 = N + \ell + 1 \equiv n\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N \ge 0\) is the radial quantum number.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n = N + \ell + 1\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{Principal Quantum Number} (\(n \ge 1\)).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\forall n\), the orbital angular momentum quantum number satisfies \(0 \le \ell \le n - 1\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy Quantization.} Recalling the definition of \(\rho_0\), \(n = \rho_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2m}{-E}} \frac{q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar}\), and solving for the bound state energies \(E_n\) (\(E < 0\)), the relation between the energy \(E_n\) of the \(n^{th}\) energy level and the principal quantum number \(n\) follows
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-analytical-sln:eq:atom:schrodinger:energy:details}
\begin{split}E_n = - \frac{m q^4}{32 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 \hbar^2} \frac{1}{n^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The value of energy \(E_n\) of Schrodinger model coincides with the value \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:eq:atom:bohr:energy} of the energy produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/bohr:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-bohr}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bohr model}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radial solution.} Putting everything together, the radial part of the solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R(\rho) = e^{-\rho/2} \rho^{\ell} L^{2 \ell+1}_{n-\ell-1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(L_{p}^{k}(x)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre differential equation \(x y'' + ( k + 1 - x ) y' + p y = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Azimuthal and polar equations}
\subsubsection*{Further separation of variables, \protect\(\ Y_{\ell m}(\theta, \varphi) = \Theta(\theta) \Phi(\varphi) \ \protect\) }

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(Y(\theta, \varphi) = \Theta(\theta) \Psi(\varphi)\), the equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{1}{Y_{lm}} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \partial_\theta (\sin\theta \partial_\theta Y_{lm}) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \partial_{\varphi\varphi} Y_{lm} \right\} = - \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \ . 
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
becomes \sphinxhyphen{} after multipyling by \(\sin^2 \theta\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underbrace{\frac{\sin \theta}{\Theta} \left( \sin \theta \, \Theta' \right)' + \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \, \sin^2 \theta}_{F(\theta)} = -\underbrace{\frac{\Phi''}{\Phi}}_{G(\varphi)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F(\theta) = - G(\varphi) = m_\ell^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with a non\sphinxhyphen{}negative constant \(m_{\ell}^2\) in order to match periodic conditions for \(\Phi(\varphi = 0) = \Phi(\varphi = 2 \pi)\).
\subsubsection*{Azimuthal equation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi'' + m_\ell^2 \Phi = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution is \(\Phi(\varphi) \propto \exp \left( \mp i m_{\ell} \varphi \right)\). In order to satisfy periodic conditoins, \(m_{\ell} \in \mathbb{Z}\). This parameter will be furthered constrained later, in the solution of the polar equation, to be \(m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, -\ell+1, \dots, \ell \}\), with \(\ell \in \mathbb{N}\). Thus, selecting only the independent solutions, the azimuthal distribution of the eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi(\varphi) \propto \exp\left( i m_{\ell} \varphi \right) \ , \quad m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, -\ell+1, \dots \ell \} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polar equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiplying the equation \(F(\theta) = m_{ell}^2\) by \(\Theta\), the polar equation becomes,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \sin \theta \left( \sin \theta \, \Theta' \right)' + \left[ \ell ( \ell + 1 ) \, \sin^2 \theta - m_{\ell}^2 \right] \Theta = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Polar equation as an associated Legendre equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing by \(\sin^2 \theta= 1 - \cos^2 \theta\), the second term can be immediately recast as the second term in the associated Legendre equation, if \(x = \cos \theta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\frac{d x}{d \theta} = - \sin \theta\), then \(\frac{d}{d\theta} = \frac{d x}{d \theta} \frac{d}{d x} = - \sin \theta \frac{d}{d x}\), the first term \sphinxhyphen{} divided by \(\sin^2 \theta\) \sphinxhyphen{} becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\frac{1}{\sin^2 \theta} \sin^2 \theta \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( - \sin^2 \theta \dfrac{d}{dx} \Theta \right) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ ( 1 - x^2) \dfrac{d}{dx} \Theta \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the polar equation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1 - x^2 ) \dfrac{d \Theta}{dx} \right] + \left[ \ell(\ell+1) - \frac{m_\ell^2}{1 - x^2} \right] \Theta  \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. as the associated Legendre equation whose solution (see below) is \(\Theta(x) = P_\ell^{m_{\ell}}(x)\), for \(m_{\ell} \in \{ - \ell, \dots, \ell\}\), \(\ell \in \mathbb{N}\).
\subsubsection*{Legendre differential equation and associated Legendre equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Legendre differential equations} read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = (1- x^2) P_n''(x) - 2 x P_n'(x) + n(n+1) P_n(x) =  \quad , \qquad x \in [-1, 1] \\
  & = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1-x^2 ) P_n'(x) \right] + n(n+1) P_n(x) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the solution \(P_n(x)\) be the Legendre polynomial. The \sphinxstylestrong{associated Legendre differential equations} are defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ ( 1-x^2 ) P_n'(x) \right] + \left[ n(n+1) - \frac{m^2}{1-x^2} \right] P_n(x) \quad , \qquad x \in [-1, 1] \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the solution reads \(P_{n}^{m}(x) = (-1)^{m} \left( 1 - x^2 \right)^{\frac{m}{2}} \dfrac{d^m}{dx^m} P_{n}(x)\), for \(m \ge 0\).
The soutions for \(m < 0\) are defined via symmetry conditions, or Rodrigues’ formula, as \(P_{\ell}^{-m} = (-1)^{m} \frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!} P_{\ell}^{m}(x)\), see \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated\_Legendre\_polynomials}{Wikipedia: associated Lagendre polynomials}.

\sphinxstepscope

\subsubsection{Stationary states}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:stationary-states}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery-stationary-states}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_{n,\ell,m_\ell}(r, \theta, \phi) = R_{n\ell}(r) \, Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta, \phi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radial Wavefunctions, \(R_{n\ell}(r)\).} Using the dimensionless variable \(\rho = \frac{2r}{n a_0}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_{n\ell}(r) = -\sqrt{\left(\frac{2}{n a_0}\right)^3 \frac{(n-\ell-1)!}{2n [(n+\ell)!]^3}} e^{-\rho/2} \rho^\ell L_{n-\ell-1}^{2\ell+1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(a_0 = \frac{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e e^2}\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{Bohr radius}, and \(L^k_p(\rho)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre equation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spherical Harmonics, \(Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta, \phi) = \Theta_{\ell, m_{\ell}}(\theta) \Phi_{m_{\ell}}(\phi)\).}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta, \phi) = (-1)^{m_\ell} \sqrt{\frac{(2\ell+1)}{4\pi} \frac{(\ell-m_\ell)!}{(\ell+m_\ell)!}} P_\ell^{m_\ell}(\cos\theta) \, e^{i m_\ell \phi}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(P^{m_{\ell}}_{\ell}\) the associated Legendre polynomials. The polar functions are real\sphinxhyphen{}valued and by definition \(\Theta_{\ell,-m_\ell}(\theta) = (-1)^{m_\ell} \Theta_{\ell,m_\ell}(\theta)\).

\subsubsection{Some details}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:some-details}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery-details}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\Theta_{\ell, -m_\ell} = (-1)^{m_{\ell}} \Theta_{\ell, m_\ell}\), it follows that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  Y_{\ell}^{m_\ell} + (-1)^{m_{ell}} Y_{\ell}^{-m_\ell}
  = \Theta_{\ell, m_{\ell}}(\theta) \left[ e^{i m_{\ell} \phi} + e^{-i m_{\ell} \phi} \right] \propto \cos( m_{\ell} \theta ) \\
  Y_{\ell}^{m_\ell} - (-1)^{m_{ell}} Y_{\ell}^{-m_\ell}
  = \Theta_{\ell, m_{\ell}}(\theta) \left[ e^{i m_{\ell} \phi} - e^{-i m_{\ell} \phi} \right] \propto i \sin( m_{\ell} \theta ) \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus the real orbitals as the linear combinations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_{n,\ell,m_\ell, \text{real}} = \begin{cases}  \psi_{n,\ell,0} & \text{for } m_\ell = 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \psi_{n,\ell,-\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}} + (-1)^{m_\ell} \psi_{n,\ell,\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}} \right) \propto \cos(\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}\phi) & \text{for } \text{real orbital } (x, xy, x^2-y^2, \dots) \\ \frac{i}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \psi_{n,\ell,-\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}} - (-1)^{m_\ell} \psi_{n,\ell,\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}} \right) \propto \sin(\vert{}m_\ell\vert{}\phi) & \text{for } \text{real orbital } (y, yz, \dots) \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Radial and spherical factors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:radial-and-spherical-factors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery-r-spherical}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_{n,\ell,m_\ell}(r, \theta, \phi) = R_{n\ell}(r) \, Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta, \phi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subparagraph{Radial wavefunctions, \protect\(R_{n, \ell}(r)\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:radial-wavefunctions-r-n-ell-r}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery-r-spherical-r}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radial Wavefunctions, \(R_{n\ell}(r)\).} Using the dimensionless variable \(\rho = \frac{2r}{n a_0}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_{n\ell}(r) = -\sqrt{\left(\frac{2}{n a_0}\right)^3 \frac{(n-\ell-1)!}{2n [(n+\ell)!]^3}} e^{-\rho/2} \rho^\ell L_{n-\ell-1}^{2\ell+1}(\rho) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(a_0 = \frac{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e e^2}\) is the \sphinxstylestrong{Bohr radius}, and \(L^k_p(\rho)\) the solution of the associated Laguerre equation.


\subparagraph{Polar and azimuthal wavefunctions, \protect\(Y^{m_\ell}_{\ell}(\theta,\phi) = \Theta_{\ell, m_\ell}(\theta) \Phi_{m_\ell}(\phi)\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:polar-and-azimuthal-wavefunctions-y-m-ell-ell-theta-phi-theta-ell-m-ell-theta-phi-m-ell-phi}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-gallery:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-gallery-r-spherical-spherical}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta, \phi) = (-1)^{m_\ell} \sqrt{\frac{(2\ell+1)}{4\pi} \frac{(\ell-m_\ell)!}{(\ell+m_\ell)!}} P_\ell^{m_\ell}(\cos\theta) \, e^{i m_\ell \phi}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(P^{m_{\ell}}_{\ell}\) the associated Legendre polynomials. The first associated Legendre polynomials are

\subsection{Auxiliary Results on Operators for the Schrödinger Model of the Hydrogen Atom}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:auxiliary-results-on-operators-for-the-schrodinger-model-of-the-hydrogen-atom}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes::doc}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the kinetic term \(\frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m}\) and with \(\hat{L}^2\), {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-p2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{proof}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{p}^2, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the potential \(\hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}\), {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-v}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{proof}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Therefore, all components of \(\hat{\mathbf{L}}\) commute with the \(\text{H}\) atom Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \hat{V}_{\text{Coulomb}}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}_b] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simultaneous Commutative Set:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boxed{[\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}^2] = 0, \quad [\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}, \hat{L}_a] = 0, \quad [\hat{L}^2, \hat{L}_a] = 0}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{\text{H-atom}}\), total angular momentum squared \(\hat{L}^2\), and any component \(\hat{L}_a\) all mutually commute, and thus share a set of common eigenvectors. For the commutation relation \([\hat{L}^2, \hat{L}_a] = 0\), see the section about {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spatial:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spatial}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{spatial angular momentum}}}}.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Hamiltonian \& Basic Definitions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:hamiltonian-basic-definitions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian of the electron in the Hydrogen atom with Coulomb potential is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + \hat{V}_{Coulomb} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that in space basis becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{H} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 \langle \mathbf{r} | - \frac{q^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon |\mathbf{r}|} \langle \mathbf{r} | \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Space Basis Representations}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle = \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{r} \langle \mathbf{r} | \quad \implies \quad \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{r}} | \Psi \rangle = \mathbf{r} \, \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} = -i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \langle \mathbf{r} | \quad \implies \quad \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Angular Momentum Operator}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \times \hat{\mathbf{p}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In Levi\sphinxhyphen{}Civita component notation, using Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{L}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \hat{L}_a =  \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, \hat{r}_b \hat{p}_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the space (position) basis (Cartesian coordinates):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{L}} | \Psi \rangle 
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \hat{L}_a | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, r_b (-i\hbar \partial_c \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle) = \\
  & =-i\hbar \hat{\mathbf{e}}_a \varepsilon_{abc} \, r_b \, \partial_c \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = \\
  & = - i \hbar \mathbf{r} \times \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi \rangle = \int \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | \Psi \rangle \, d\mathbf{r}' = \int \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}') \left(-i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi(\mathbf{r}', t)\right) d\mathbf{r}' = -i\hbar \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_b \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_b \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \partial_b \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{r}_a | \Psi \rangle  = -i\hbar \partial_b \left( r_a \langle \mathbf{r} | \Psi \rangle \right) = - i \hbar \partial_b \left( r_a \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \right) = -i\hbar (\delta_{ab} \Psi + r_a \partial_b \Psi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Canonical Commutation Relations (CCR)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:canonical-commutation-relations-ccr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using postion basis and Cartesian coordinates, the CCR \([ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{P}} ] = i \hbar \mathbb{I}\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, p_b] \Psi = r_a (-i\hbar \partial_b \Psi) - (-i\hbar \partial_b (r_a \Psi)) = i\hbar \, \delta_{ab} \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, p_b] = i\hbar \, \delta_{ab}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Commutators of Angular Momentum with Position and Momentum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutators-of-angular-momentum-with-position-and-momentum}}

\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([r_a, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-r-a-l-b}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_a L_b \Psi = r_a (-i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \Psi) = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_a r_c \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L_b r_a \Psi = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d (r_a \Psi) = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \delta_{ad} \Psi - i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c r_a \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subtracting the two expressions gives:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, L_b] \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \delta_{ad} \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{bca} \, r_c \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[r_a, L_b] =-  i \hbar \, (\mathbf{r} \times)_{a b} \, \Psi \quad \left(\text{in general } \neq 0\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(Recall: \((\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_i = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j b_k = \{ \mathbf{a}_{\times} \}_{ik} \cdot \{ \mathbf{b} \}_k\), i.e. \(\{ \mathbf{a}_{\times} \}_{ik} = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j\))}


\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([p_a, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-p-a-l-b}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_a L_b \Psi = -i\hbar \partial_a \left(-i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \Psi\right) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, \partial_a (r_c \partial_d \Psi) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bad} \, \partial_d \Psi - \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_a \partial_d \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L_b p_a \Psi = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d (-i\hbar \partial_a \Psi) = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \partial_d \partial_a \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subtracting the two expressions gives:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p_a, L_b] \Psi = -\hbar^2 \varepsilon_{bad} \, \partial_d \Psi = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{abd} \, \partial_d \Psi = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} \, p_c \Psi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cartesian coordinates.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_x] \equiv 0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_y] = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{xyz} \, \partial_z \Psi = i\hbar p_z\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\([p_x, L_z] = \hbar^2 \varepsilon_{xzy} \, \partial_y \Psi = -\hbar^2 \partial_y \Psi = -i\hbar p_y\)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\paragraph{Commutator \protect\([\hat{p}^2, L_b]\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-hat-p-2-l-b}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-p2}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_b] = \sum_a p_a p_a L_b - L_b \sum_a p_a p_a = \sum_a \Big( p_a [p_a, L_b] + [p_a, L_b] p_a \Big)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \([p_a, L_b] = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_a \left( p_a (i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c) + (i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} p_c) p_a \right) = i\hbar \varepsilon_{abc} (p_a p_c + p_c p_a)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(p_a p_c = p_c p_a\) (symmetric in \(a, c\)) and \(\varepsilon_{abc}\) is antisymmetric in \(a, c\), the sum vanishes identically:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_b] = 0 \quad \text{for all components } b\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example.} For \(b = x\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[p^2, L_x] = -i\hbar^3 \Big[ 1 \cdot \partial_z \partial_y \Psi - 1 \cdot \partial_y \partial_z \Psi \Big] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Commutator of Coulomb Potential \protect\(\hat{V}\protect\) with Angular Momentum \protect\(\hat{L}_b\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:commutator-of-coulomb-potential-hat-v-with-angular-momentum-hat-l-b}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/atom-models/schrodinger-notes:quantum-mechanics-atom-models-schrodinger-notes-commutation-l-v}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In space basis, the Coulomb potential reads:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = -\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{r} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t) = -k \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s evaluate whether \(\hat{V}\) and \(\hat{L}_b\) commute:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Action of \(\hat{V} \hat{L}_b\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{V} \hat{L}_b | \Psi \rangle = -k \frac{1}{\sqrt{x_a x_a}} \left( -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \, \partial_d \Psi \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Action of \(\hat{L}_b \hat{V}\), with \(|\mathbf{r}| = \sqrt{ x_a x_a }\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{L}_b \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \, \partial_d \left( -k \frac{\Psi}{\sqrt{x_a x_a}} \right) = i\hbar k \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \left[ -\frac{\partial_d |\mathbf{r}|}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \Psi + \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \partial_d \Psi \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \(\partial_d | \mathbf{r}| = \partial_d \sqrt{x_a x_a} = \frac{x_d}{|\mathbf{r}|}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{L}_b \hat{V} | \Psi \rangle = i\hbar k \varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c \left[ -\frac{r_d}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} \Psi + \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}|} \partial_d \Psi \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Commutator \([\hat{V}, \hat{L}_b]\):}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | [\hat{V}, \hat{L}_b] | \Psi \rangle = -i\hbar k \, \frac{\varepsilon_{bcd} \, r_c r_d}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} \Psi = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Why?} The product \(r_c r_d\) is \sphinxstylestrong{symmetric} under swapping \(c \leftrightarrow d\), while \(\varepsilon_{bcd}\) is \sphinxstylestrong{antisymmetric} under swapping \(c \leftrightarrow d\). Summing over \(c, d\) gives zero!

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example for \(b = x\).} \(\varepsilon_{xcd} r_c r_d = \varepsilon_{xyz} y z + \varepsilon_{xzy} z y = yz - zy = 0\).

\end{enumerate}
