\section{Dirac equation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:dirac-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:quantum-mechanics-relativistic-dirac-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation::doc}}

\subsection{Klein\sphinxhyphen{}Gordon equation for a free particle}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:klein-gordon-equation-for-a-free-particle}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:quantum-mechanics-relativistic-dirac-equation-klein-gordon-free}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The relation between energy and momentum for a massive particle in {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/relativity-special/notes:relativity-special-notes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{special relativity}}}}
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:eq:dirac-eq:einstein:en-mom}
\begin{split}m^2 c^2 = \frac{E^2}{c^2} - | \mathbf{p} |^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
can be seamlessly promoted to a operator equation, \(\mathbf{p} \rightarrow \hat{\mathbf{p}}\), \(E \rightarrow \hat{H}t\), to only get Klein\sphinxhyphen{}Gordon equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \frac{m^2}{c^2}{\hbar^2} = \frac{\hat{H}^2}{c^2} - |\hat{\mathbf{p}}|^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in position representation, where \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{\mathbf{p}} = - i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} |\), \(\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{H} = i \hbar \partial_t \langle \mathbf{r} |\), applied to a wave function \(| \Psi \rangle\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \square + \frac{m^2 \hbar^2}{c^2} \right\} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Dirac equation for a free particle}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:dirac-equation-for-a-free-particle}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:quantum-mechanics-relativistic-dirac-equation-dirac-free}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dirac’s equation follows from the expression of the Hamiltonian operator as a linear combination of the components of the momentum operator and the \(m c\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \alpha_0 m c + \sum_{k=1}^{3} \alpha_k \hat{p}_k \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that satisfies the relation \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:eq:dirac-eq:einstein:en-mom}.
\subsubsection*{Details of the solution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo}…

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian operator becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = m c^2 \beta + c \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}} = m c^2 \beta - i \hbar c \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \nabla \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the position representation of Dirac’s equation can be written using 3+1 formalism (space+time) as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  i \hbar \partial_t \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) 
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle = \\
  & = - i \hbar c \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) + m c^2 \beta \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the set of \(4 \times 4\) complex matrices \(\beta = \gamma^0\), \(\gamma^k = \beta \alpha_k\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  \gamma^0 = \begin{bmatrix} I_2 & \cdot \\ \cdot & -I_2 \end{bmatrix}
  \quad , \quad
  \gamma^k = \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & \sigma_k \\ -\sigma_k & \cdot \end{bmatrix} \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
built with \(2 \times 2\) identity and {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/angular-momentum/angular-momentum-spin:quantum-mechanics-angular-momentum-spin-pauli-matrices}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Pauli matrices}}}} \(\sigma_k\). Dirac’s equation can be recast in the 4\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional formalism of special relativity, after multiplication by \(\beta\), as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \left( i \hbar \gamma^\mu \partial_\mu - m c \right) \Psi = 0 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0
 & = i \hbar \left( \beta \partial_t + c \beta \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \nabla \right) \Psi - m c^2 \Psi = \\
 & = i \hbar c \gamma^\mu \partial_\mu \Psi - m c^2 \Psi \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Elementary solutions of Dirac equation for a free particle}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:elementary-solutions-of-dirac-equation-for-a-free-particle}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\left\{
i \frac{\hbar}{c} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & & & \\ & 1 & & \\ & & -1 & \\ & & & -1 \end{bmatrix} \partial_t
+ i \hbar \begin{bmatrix} & & & 1 \\ & & 1 & \\ & -1 & & \\ -1 & & &  \end{bmatrix} \partial_x
+ i \hbar \begin{bmatrix} & & & -i \\ & & i & \\ & i & & \\ -i & & &  \end{bmatrix} \partial_y
+ i \hbar \begin{bmatrix} & & 1 & \\ & & & -1 \\ -1 & & & \\ & 1 & &  \end{bmatrix} \partial_z
- m c \right\} \Psi(t, \mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{0} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Dimensional Reduction to 1D and Component Decoupling}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:dimensional-reduction-to-1d-and-component-decoupling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To better understand the internal dynamics of the spinor, we can study a simplified scenario by assuming homogeneity along the \(y\) and \(z\) axes, setting spatial derivatives to zero (\(\partial_y = \partial_z = 0\)). Dirac’s equation reduces to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\left\{
i \frac{\hbar}{c} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & & & \\ & 1 & & \\ & & -1 & \\ & & & -1 \end{bmatrix} \partial_t
+ i \hbar \begin{bmatrix} & & & 1 \\ & & 1 & \\ & -1 & & \\ -1 & & &  \end{bmatrix} \partial_x
- m c \right\} \Psi(t, x) = \mathbf{0} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Expanding the matrix equation for a four\sphinxhyphen{}component spinor \(\Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \psi_1 & \psi_2 & \psi_3 & \psi_4 \end{pmatrix}^T\), the system splits naturally into \sphinxstylestrong{two independent pairs of coupled equations}:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A coupling between \sphinxstylestrong{\(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_4\)}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A coupling between \sphinxstylestrong{\(\psi_2\) and \(\psi_3\)}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the first pair (\(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_4\)), the system reads:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
\frac{i\hbar}{c} \partial_t \psi_1 - mc \, \psi_1 + i\hbar \partial_x \psi_4 = 0 \\[6pt]
-i\hbar \partial_x \psi_1 - \frac{i\hbar}{c} \partial_t \psi_4 - mc \, \psi_4 = 0
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reduction to Klein\sphinxhyphen{}Gordon Equation for individual components.}
By isolating \(\partial_x \psi_4\) from the first equation and substituting it into the second, the mixed temporal\sphinxhyphen{}spatial derivative terms cancel out, demonstrating that each individual component satisfies the relativistic dispersion relation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \square + \frac{m^2 c^2}{\hbar^2} \right) \psi_1 = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\square = \frac{1}{c^2}\partial_t^2 - \partial_x^2\) is the d’Alembertian operator.
\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_x \psi_4 = \frac{1}{i\hbar} \left( m c \psi_1 - \frac{i \hbar}{c} \partial_t \psi_1 \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 
  & = -i \hbar \partial_{xx} \psi_1 - \left( \frac{i \hbar}{c} \partial_t + m c \right) \partial_x \psi_4 = \\
  & = -i \hbar \partial_{xx} \psi_1 + \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left( \frac{i \hbar}{c} \partial_t + m c \right) \left( \frac{i \hbar}{c} \partial_t - m c  \right) \psi_1 = \\
  & = - i \hbar \partial_{xx} \psi_1 - \frac{i}{\hbar} \left( - \frac{\hbar^2}{c^2} \partial_{tt} - m^2 c^2 \right) \psi_1 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus, after dividing by \(i \hbar\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} - \partial_{xx} + \frac{m^2 c^2}{\hbar^2} \right) \psi_1 = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Plane Wave Solutions and Component Relations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:plane-wave-solutions-and-component-relations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming a plane wave ansatz for the components of the form \(\psi_1 = K_{\mathbf{p}} e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}(Et - p_x x)}\), the \sphinxstylestrong{dispersion relation} \(- \frac{E^2}{\hbar^2 c^2} + \frac{p_x^2}{\hbar^2} + \frac{m^2 c^2}{\hbar^2} = 0\) is found between the energy and the momentum of the free particle, or after multiplying by \(\hbar^2\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E^2 = p_x^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4 = 0 \quad \rightarrow \quad E = \mp c \sqrt{ p_x^2 + m^2 c^2 } \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the very same Einstein energy\sphinxhyphen{}momentum equation \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:eq:dirac-eq:einstein:en-mom}. Convert the differential coupling into an algebraic relation between the “large” and “small” components, the first equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i\hbar \partial_x \psi_4 = \left( \frac{i\hbar}{c} \partial_t - mc \right) \psi_1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \cdot i \frac{p_x}{\hbar} \psi_4 = \left( \frac{i\hbar}{c} \left(- \frac{i E}{\hbar} \right) - mc \right) \psi_1 \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the relation between \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_4\) is the ratio
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_4 = \frac{mc^2 - E}{c \, p_x} \psi_1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An identical decoupling procedure applies symmetrically to the second pair (\(\psi_2\) and \(\psi_3\)).
\subsubsection*{Physical Insights and Interpretation}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large vs. Small Components:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The upper pair \((\psi_1, \psi_2)\) represents the \sphinxstylestrong{large components}, which in the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic limit (\(v \ll c\)) reduce to the standard two\sphinxhyphen{}component Pauli spinor describing spin.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The lower pair \((\psi_3, \psi_4)\) represents the \sphinxstylestrong{small components}, suppressed by a factor of \(v/c\), which carry the relativistic corrections responsible for spin\sphinxhyphen{}orbit coupling and magnetic moments.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Emergence of Spin:}
Unlike non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic quantum mechanics where spin is added ad\sphinxhyphen{}hoc via Pauli matrices, spin emerges naturally in the Dirac equation as a direct consequence of the linearization required for Lorentz covariance, combining with orbital angular momentum into a conserved total angular momentum \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{L} + \mathbf{S}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Antimatter and Negative Energies:}
The dispersion relation permits both positive (\(E = +\sqrt{c^2p^2 + m^2c^4}\)) and negative (\(E = -\sqrt{...}\)) energy solutions. In modern quantum field theory, these negative energy states are reinterpreted through second quantization as antiparticles (such as the positron), resolving historical vacuum stability issues.

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Dirac equation for a particle in the EM field}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/relativistic-qm/dirac-equation:dirac-equation-for-a-particle-in-the-em-field}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the \sphinxstylestrong{minimal coupling}, the momentum of a free particle is replaced by the momentum of a charged particle in a EM field,%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
\sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/calculus-variations/examples.html\#lagrange-equations-in-special-relativity}{Math: Calculus of Variations: Examples: Lagrange Equations in Special Relativity Using Tensor Formalism}
%
\end{footnote}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{P} \rightarrow  \mathbf{P} + q \mathbf{A} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathbf{P} = m \mathbf{U} = \gamma m ( c, \mathbf{v} ) = \left( \frac{E}{c}, \mathbf{p} \right)\), and \(\mathbf{A} = \left( \frac{\varphi}{c}, \mathbf{a} \right)\), so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \mathbf{P} + q \mathbf{A} \right\}^{\mu} = \left( \frac{E + q \varphi}{c}, \mathbf{p} + q \mathbf{a} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \mathbf{P} + q \mathbf{A} \right\}_{\mu} = \left( \frac{E + q \varphi}{c}, -\mathbf{p} - q \mathbf{a} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the Hamiltonian in space representation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{H} & = m c^2 \beta - i \hbar c \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \nabla \\
\quad \rightarrow \quad \hat{H} & = m c^2 \beta + q \varphi + c \boldsymbol\alpha \cdot \left( - i \hbar \nabla + q\mathbf{a} \right)
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = i \hbar \beta \partial_t \Psi - \beta \hat{H} \Psi = \\
  & = i \hbar \beta \partial_t \Psi - m c^2 - q \beta \varphi \Psi + i c \hbar \beta \alpha_k \partial_k \Psi - c q \beta \alpha_k a_k \Psi = \\
  & = i \hbar c \gamma^0 \frac{1}{c}\partial_t \Psi + i \hbar c \gamma^k \partial_k \Psi - m c^2 \Psi + q c \gamma^0 \frac{\varphi}{c} \Psi - q c \gamma^k a_k \Psi = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus, after dividing by \(c\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( i \hbar \gamma^\mu \left( \partial_{\mu} - q A_\mu \right) - m c^2 \right) \Psi = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Identical systems}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-identical}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:identical-systems}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let a system be composed of \(N\) identical indistinguishable sub\sphinxhyphen{}systems. The state of the subsystem \(k\) is described by a single\sphinxhyphen{}system wave function \(| \psi_k \rangle\) belonging to the single\sphinxhyphen{}system Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_1\). Thus, the state of the many\sphinxhyphen{}body subsystem is described by a wave function \(| \Psi \rangle\) belonging to the \(N\) tensor product space
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{H}^{\otimes N} = \underbrace{\mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathcal{H}_1}_{n \text{ times}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\{ | \alpha \rangle \}\) be an orthonormal basis for \(\mathcal{H}_1\). A basis for \(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes N}\) is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle = | \alpha_1 \rangle \dots | \alpha_N \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Indistinguishability.} Applying a permutation operator once
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P_{ij} \Psi( \dots, \mathbf{r}_i, \dots, \mathbf{r}_j, \dots ) = \Psi( \dots, \mathbf{r}_j, \dots, \mathbf{r}_i, \dots )\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Applying it twice
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P_{ij} P_{ij} \Psi( \dots, \mathbf{r}_i, \dots, \mathbf{r}_j, \dots ) = \Psi( \dots, \mathbf{r}_i, \dots, \mathbf{r}_j, \dots ) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows that \(P_{ij} P_{ij} = 1\). Thus, two solutions are possible, corresponding to two different nature of the subsystems
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bosons, \(P_{ij} = 1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(\dots, \ \mathbf{r}_j, \dots, \ \mathbf{r}_i, \dots) = \Psi(\dots, \ \mathbf{r}_i, \dots, \ \mathbf{r}_j, \dots)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fermions, \(P_{ij} = -1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(\dots, \ \mathbf{r}_j, \dots, \ \mathbf{r}_i, \dots) = - \Psi(\dots, \ \mathbf{r}_i, \dots, \ \mathbf{r}_j, \dots)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}


\subsection{Symmetrization and anti\sphinxhyphen{}symmetrization}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:symmetrization-and-anti-symmetrization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-identical-symmetrization}}

\subsubsection{Symmetric basis for bosons}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:symmetric-basis-for-bosons}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-identical-symmetrization-bosons}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(| \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle_S := \sqrt{ \dfrac{\prod_k n_k!}{N!} } \sum_{\hat{P} \in S_N} \hat{P} | \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(n_k\) the occupation number of the single\sphinxhyphen{}body state \(k\). The factor before the summation is required for normalization of the symmetric state, as it’s the square root of the inverse of the number of permutations with repetitions, see \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea-hs/ch/statistics/combinatorics.html\#permutazioni-con-ripetizioni}{Combinatorics: Permutations with Repetitions}.
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 23.1.1 (Low\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional example)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Let a 2\sphinxhyphen{}particle system be represented in a Hilbert space thats the product \(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2} = \mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \mathcal{H}_1\). If the two particles are in the same 1\sphinxhyphen{}body state \(| a \rangle\), the state of the system is \(| a , a \rangle\), equal to the symmetric state. If the two particles are in different and orthogonal states \(| a \rangle\), \(| b \rangle\), the symmetric representation of the state reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| a, b \rangle_S = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | a , b \rangle + | b , a \rangle \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This state is unit\sphinxhyphen{}norm, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  {}_S \langle a , b | a, b \rangle_S 
  & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \langle a , b | + \langle b , a | \right) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | a , b \rangle + | b , a \rangle  \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2} \left( \underbrace{\langle a , b | a, b \rangle}_{=\langle a | a \rangle \langle b |b \rangle = 1} + \underbrace{\langle b , a | a, b \rangle}_{\langle b | a \rangle \langle a | b \rangle = 0} + \underbrace{\langle a , b | b, a \rangle}_{=0} + \underbrace{\langle b , a | b, a \rangle}_{=1} \right) = 1 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Anti\sphinxhyphen{}symmetric basis for fermions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:anti-symmetric-basis-for-fermions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-identical-symmetrization-fermions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(| \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \rangle_A := \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{N!}} \left| \begin{matrix} | \alpha_1\rangle_1 & \dots & | \alpha_N \rangle_1 \\ \dots & \dots & \dots \\ | \alpha_1\rangle_N & \dots & | \alpha_N \rangle_N \end{matrix} \right| \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If two bodies were in the same state, two rows of the matrix would be equal and thus the determinant be zero. The factor before the determinant is required for normalization, as it’s the square root of the inverse of the number of simple pertumations of \(N\) objects without repetitions, see \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea-hs/ch/statistics/combinatorics.html\#permutazioni-semplici}{Combinatorics: Permutations with Repetitions}.
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/identical-systems:example-1}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 23.1.2 (Low\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional example)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Let a 2\sphinxhyphen{}particle system be represented in a Hilbert space thats the product \(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2} = \mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \mathcal{H}_1\). If the two particles are in the same 1\sphinxhyphen{}body state \(| a \rangle\), the state of the system is \(| a , a \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| a , a \rangle_A = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left| \begin{matrix} | a \rangle_1 & | a \rangle_2 \\ | a \rangle_1 & | a \rangle_2 \end{matrix} \right| = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the two particles are in different and orthogonal states \(| a \rangle\), \(| b \rangle\), the symmetric representation of the state reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| a , b \rangle_A = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left| \begin{matrix} | a \rangle_1 & | b \rangle_1 \\ | a \rangle_2 & | b \rangle_2 \end{matrix} \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | a, b \rangle - | b, a \rangle \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This state is unit\sphinxhyphen{}norm, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  {}_A \langle a , b | a, b \rangle_A 
  & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \langle a , b | - \langle b , a | \right) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | a , b \rangle - | b , a \rangle  \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2} \left( \underbrace{\langle a , b | a, b \rangle}_{=\langle a | a \rangle \langle b |b \rangle = 1} - \underbrace{\langle b , a | a, b \rangle}_{\langle b | a \rangle \langle a | b \rangle = 0} - \underbrace{\langle a , b | b, a \rangle}_{=0} + \underbrace{\langle b , a | b, a \rangle}_{=1} \right) = 1 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Second quantization. Fock space}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fock-space:second-quantization-fock-space}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fock-space:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-second-quantization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fock-space::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\{ | \alpha \rangle \}\) a basis of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}body system. Let \(n_\alpha\) the number of subsystems in the single\sphinxhyphen{}body state \(| \alpha \rangle\), i.e. the \sphinxstylestrong{occupation number} of the state. The sum of the occupation numbers is equal to the number of particles \(N\), i.e. \(\sum_\alpha n_\alpha = N\). In the second quantization, the state of the system is represented in the occupation number state
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{n} \rangle := | n_1, n_2, \dots, n_{\alpha}, \dots \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ground state.} \(| \mathbf{0} \rangle = | 0_1, 0_2, \dots \rangle\). By definition \(\langle 0 | 0 \rangle = 1\).


\subsection{Fock states}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fock-space:fock-states}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fock-space:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-second-quantization-fock-space}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Properties of Fock states}

\section{Second quantization. Bosons}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:second-quantization-bosons}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-bosons}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The state of a many\sphinxhyphen{}body bosonic system is symmetric under the echange of 2 particles. This condition is represented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-bosons-ccr}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{CCRs}}}}.




\subsection{Creation and annihilation operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:creation-and-annihilation-operators}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-bosons-creation-annihilation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Creation operator, \(\hat{b}_i^{\dagger}\).} The notation with the dagger is justified below, as the creation operator is the adjoint of the annihilation operator \(\hat{b}_i\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{b}_i^{\dagger} | \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle = \sqrt{n+1} | \dots, (n+1)_i, \dots \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A state \(| \mathbf{n} \rangle = | n_1, n_2, \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle\) can be obtained from the vacuum equation as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{n} \rangle = | n_1, n_2, \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\prod_k n_k!}} \left( \hat{b}_1^{\dagger} \right)^{n_1} \dots \left( \hat{b}_i^\dagger \right)^{n_i} \dots | \mathbf{0} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Annihilation operator, \(\hat{b}_i\).}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{b}_i | \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle & = \sqrt{n} | \dots, (n-1)_i, \dots \rangle \ , \qquad \text{if $n_i > 0$} \\
  \hat{b}_i | \dots, 0_i, \dots \rangle & = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{tip}{Tip:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Annihilation and creation operators are not Hermitian.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\subsubsection*{Creation operator is the adjoint of the annihilation operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The adjoint operator of an operator \(\hat{a}: A \rightarrow B\) is defined as the operator \(\hat{a}^\dagger: B \rightarrow A\) so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \phi | \hat{a} | \psi \rangle_B 
  & = \langle \psi | \hat{a}^\dagger | \phi \rangle_A^* = \\
  & = \langle \hat{a}^\dagger \phi | \psi \rangle_A \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
for any \(| \phi \rangle \in B\), \(| \psi \rangle \in  A\). Thus, for the annihilation operator \(\hat{b}_i\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{m} | \hat{b}_i | \mathbf{n} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{n} | \left( \hat{b}_i \right)^{\dagger} | \mathbf{m} \rangle^* \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \mathbf{n} | \left( \hat{b}_i \right)^{\dagger} | \mathbf{m} \rangle^*
  & = \langle \mathbf{m} | \hat{b}_i  | \mathbf{n} \rangle = && {\text{(1)}} \\
  & = \sqrt{n_i} \langle \mathbf{m} | \mathbf{n} - \mathbf{1}_i \rangle = && {\text{(2)}} \\
  & = \sqrt{n_i} \, \delta_{\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}_i} = && {\text{(3)}} \\
  & = \sqrt{m_i + 1} \, \delta_{\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{n}-\mathbf{1}_i} = && {\text{(4)}} \\
  & = \sqrt{m_i + 1} \, \delta_{\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{1}_i, \mathbf{n}} = && {\text{(5)}} \\
  & = \sqrt{m_i + 1} \langle \mathbf{n} | \mathbf{m} + \mathbf{1}_i \rangle = \\
  & = \langle \mathbf{n} | \left( \sqrt{m_i + 1}  | \mathbf{m} + \mathbf{1}_i \rangle \right) = && {\text{(6)}} \\
  & = \langle \mathbf{n} | \hat{b}_i^\dagger | \mathbf{m} \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the Kronecker’s delta acting on all the indices \sphinxhyphen{} just as an example, with \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2)\), \(\mathbf{b} = (b_1, b_2)\), it follows that \(\delta_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}} = \delta_{a_1, b_1} \delta_{a_2, b_2}\) \sphinxhyphen{}, and (1) action of the annihilation operator, (2) orthogonality of Fock states, (3\sphinxhyphen{}4) properties of Kronecker’s delta, (5) orthogonality of Fock states, (6) recognizing the action of the creation operator \(\hat{b}_i^\dagger\) on \(| \mathbf{m} \rangle\). As the result of the inner product is real, its complex conjugate is the value itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Number operator, \(\hat{n}_i = \hat{b}_i^\dagger \, \hat{b}_i\).} Number operator is self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint. This is consistent with postulates of quantum mechanics: physical observables are represented by self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint operators.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{n}_i | \mathbf{n} \rangle
  & = \hat{n}_i | \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle = \\
  & = \hat{b}_i^\dagger \, \hat{b}_i | \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle = \\
  & = \hat{b}_i^\dagger \, \left( \sqrt{n} | \dots, (n-1)_i, \dots \rangle \right) = \\
  & = n_i | \dots, n_i, \dots \rangle = \\
  & = n_i | \mathbf{n} \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}



\subsection{Number operator}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:number-operator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-bosons-number}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Total number operator.} \(\hat{n} = \sum_{i} \hat{n}_i\)


\subsection{Canonical commutation relations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:canonical-commutation-relations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/bosons:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-bosons-ccr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{CCRs.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i, \hat{b}_j^\dagger ] = \delta_{ij} \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i, \hat{b}_j^\dagger ] | \mathbf{n} \rangle = \left( \sqrt{n_j+1} \sqrt{n_i^{(1)}} - \sqrt{n_i} \sqrt{n_j^{(1)}+1} \right) | \dots, (n-1)_i, \dots, (n+1)_j, \dots \rangle \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the \(n^{(1)}_j\) the state after the application of the first operator. If \(i \ne j\), then \(n^{(1)}_{j} = n_j\), and thus the result is zero. If \(i = j\), then \(n_{i}^{(1)} = n_i + 1\), \(n_j^{(1)} = n_j - 1\), and thus the result reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i, \hat{b}_i^\dagger ] | \mathbf{n} \rangle = \left( (n_i + 1) - n_i \right) | \mathbf{n} \rangle = 1 \cdot | \mathbf{n} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i, \hat{b}_j^\dagger ] | \mathbf{n} \rangle = \delta_{ij} | \mathbf{n} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i, \hat{b}_j ] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{b}_i^\dagger, \hat{b}_j^\dagger ] = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Second quantization. Fermions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:second-quantization-fermions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The state of a many\sphinxhyphen{}body fermionic system is anti\sphinxhyphen{}symmetric under the exchange of 2 particles. This is the Pauli exclusion principle, that’s represented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions-car}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{CARs}}}}.


\subsection{Creation and annihilation operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:creation-and-annihilation-operators}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions-creation-annihilation}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\hat c^\dagger_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle & = \theta_k\sqrt{1-n_k}\,|\dots(1-n)_k\dots\rangle \\
\hat c_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle & = \theta_k\sqrt{n_k}\,|\dots(1-n)_k\dots\rangle
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\theta_k=(-1)^{\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} n_j}\).
\subsubsection*{Road to the formalization of creation and annihilation operators}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pauli exclusion principle.} Pauli exclusion principle implies that the occupation number of a state can be either \(0\) or \(1\). Creation and annihilation operators should satisfy the following conditions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{c}_i | 0 \rangle & =   0         &&                                \\
  \hat{c}_i | 1 \rangle & = | 0 \rangle && \hat{c}_i^\dagger | 0 \rangle = | 1 \rangle \\
                        &               && \hat{c}_i^\dagger | 1 \rangle = 0 \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A first \sphinxhyphen{} but wrong, see \sphinxstylestrong{Jordan\sphinxhyphen{}Wigner} solution \sphinxhyphen{} try of the definition of creation \(\hat{c}_i^\dagger\) and annihilation operator \(\hat{c}_i\) for a fermionic field could be
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{c}_k^\dagger | \dots n_k \dots \rangle & = \sqrt{1-n_k} | \dots (1-n)_k \dots \rangle \\
  \hat{c}_k         | \dots n_k \dots \rangle & = \sqrt{  n_k} | \dots (1-n)_k \dots \rangle \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This definition would provide an inconsistent behavior with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions-car}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{canonical anticommuation relations}}}}. As an example, with \(i < j\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_j^\dagger | 0 \rangle = - \hat{c}_j^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger | 0 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Applying the \sphinxhyphen{} wrong \sphinxhyphen{} expression of the creation and annihilation operators given above, the result would be
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| 1_i, 1_j \rangle = - | 1_i, 1_j \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that would imply the state is identically zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jordan\sphinxhyphen{}Wigner, “On the Pauli exclusion principle”.}%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Jordan–Wigner (1928), “On the Pauli exclusion principle”
%
\end{footnote}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\hat c^\dagger_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle & = \theta_k\sqrt{1-n_k}\,|\dots(1-n)_k\dots\rangle \\
\hat c_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle & = \theta_k\sqrt{n_k}\,|\dots(1-n)_k\dots\rangle
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\theta_k=(-1)^{\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} n_j}\). With this definition of the creation and annihilation operators the example above, with \(i < j\) becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_j^\dagger | 0 \rangle & = (-1)^0 \hat{c}_i^\dagger | 1_j \rangle = (-1)^0 | 1_i, 1_j \rangle =   | 1_i, 1_j \rangle \\
  \hat{c}_j^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger | 0 \rangle & = (-1)^0 \hat{c}_j^\dagger | 1_i \rangle = (-1)^1 | 1_i, 1_j \rangle = - | 1_i, 1_j \rangle
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Number operator}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:number-operator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions-number}}

\subsection{Canonical anti\sphinxhyphen{}commutation relations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:canonical-anti-commutation-relations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/fermions:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-fermions-car}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The commutation relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\{ \hat{c}_i^\dagger, \hat{c}_j^\dagger \} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
implies
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger = - \hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger \), and thus \(\left( \hat{c}_i^\dagger \right)^2 = 0\). If \(\hat{c}_i^\dagger\) creates the state \(| 1_i \rangle\) from the vacuum state \(| 0 \rangle\), and a state proportional to \(| 2_i \rangle\) when applied to state \(| 1_i \rangle\), i.e. with 2 applications to \(| 0 \rangle\), then this implies that it’s not possible to get \(| 2_i \rangle\), and states with larger occupation numbers. Thus, the occupation number of each state can be either \(0\) or \(1\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_j^\dagger = - \hat{c}_j^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger \)

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(i < j\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \left( \hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_j^\dagger + \hat{c}_j^\dagger \hat{c}_i^\dagger \right) | \dots n_i \dots n_j \dots \rangle = \\
  & = \sqrt{n_j - 1} \cdot (-1)^{\sum_{k=1}^{j-1} n_k} \hat{c}_i^\dagger | \dots n_i \dots (n-1)_j \dots \rangle + \sqrt{n_i-1} \cot (-1)^{\sum_{l=1}^{i-1} n_l} \hat{c}_j^\dagger | \dots (n-1)_i \dots n_j \dots \rangle   = \\
  & = \sqrt{n_j - 1} \sqrt{n_i - 1 } \cdot \left\{ (-1)^{\sum_{l=1}^{i-1} n_l} \cdot (-1)^{\sum_{k=1}^{j-1} n_k} + (-1)^{\sum_{k=1, l\ne i}^{k-1} n_l} \cdot (-1)^{n_i-1} \cdot (-1)^{\sum_{l=1}^{i-1} n_l}  \right\} | \dots (n-1)_i \dots (n-1)_j \dots \rangle  = \\
  & = \sqrt{n_j - 1} \sqrt{n_i - 1 } \cdot \left\{ \underbrace{\left( (-1)^{n_i} + (-1)^{n_i-1} \right)}_{=0} (-1)^{\sum_{k=1, l\ne i}^{k-1} n_l} \cdot (-1)^{\sum_{l=1}^{i-1} n_l}  \right\} | \dots (n-1)_i \dots (n-1)_j \dots \rangle  = \\
  & = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(j = i\), the equality immediately follows from \(\left( c^\dagger_i \right)^2 = 0\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\{ \hat{c}_i, \hat{c}_j \} = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\section{Quantum fields}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:quantum-fields}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-quantum-fields}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this section, creation and annihilation operators in continuous basis (like space or momentum) are introduced, in terms of creation/annihilation operators in a given (and discrete?) basis \(\{ \nu_a \}_a\)




\subsection{Field creation and annihilation operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:field-creation-and-annihilation-operators}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Creation and annihilation operators in space basis can be written using the basis \(\{ \nu_a \}\) as
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:creation}
\begin{split}\Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_a \nu_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_a}\end{split}
\end{equation}\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:annihilation}
\begin{split}\Psi        (\mathbf{r}) = \sum_a \nu_a  (\mathbf{r}) \hat{a}_{\nu_a}        \end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Creation operator \(\Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{creates a particle} in state \(| \mathbf{r} \rangle\), while annihilation operator \(\Psi(\mathbf{r})\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{destroys a particle} in state \(| \mathbf{r} \rangle\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The inverse relations hold
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:creation:inverse}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_a} 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a(\mathbf{r}) \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:annihilation:inverse}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}_{\nu_a} 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Details. Inverse relations}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_a} 
  & = \sum_b \hat{a}_{\nu_b}^\dagger \langle \nu_b | \nu_a \rangle =  \\
  & = \sum_b \hat{a}_{\nu_b}^\dagger \langle \nu_b | \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} \, | \nu_a \rangle =  \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a(\mathbf{r}) \sum_b \nu^*_b(\mathbf{r}) \hat{a}_{\nu_b}^\dagger \, d \mathbf{r} = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a(\mathbf{r}) \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}_{\nu_a} 
  & = \sum_b \hat{a}_{\nu_b} \langle \nu_a | \nu_b \rangle =  \\
  & = \sum_b \hat{a}_{\nu_b} \langle \nu_a | \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} \, | \nu_b \rangle =  \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \sum_b \nu_b(\mathbf{r}) \hat{a}_{\nu_b} \, d \mathbf{r} = \\
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \nu_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Need to distinguish between bosons and fermions? Or one can just use the proper set of creation/annihilation operators, without any other major change in the formulas}


\subsubsection{CCR}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:ccr}}

\subsubsection{One\sphinxhyphen{}particle system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:one-particle-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Action of \(\hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\) on the vacuum state.} The action of the operator \(\hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\) on the vacuum places a particle in the state \(| \mathbf{r} \rangle\), i.e.
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:second-quantization:field:r-1}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{r} \rangle = \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) | 0 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Discrete basis}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The state \(| \mathbf{r} \rangle\) can be written as a linear combination of the elements of a basis. For a \sphinxstylestrong{discrete basis} \(\{ | \nu_k \rangle \}_k\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{r} \rangle = \sum_k | \nu_k \rangle \langle \nu_k | \mathbf{r} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of the basis of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}body system \(| \nu_k \rangle\) can be built with the creation operator acting on the ground state, \(| \nu_k \rangle = \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_k} | 0 \rangle\), and thus
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:second-quantization:field:r-2}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{r} \rangle = \sum_k \langle \nu_k | \mathbf{r} \rangle \, \hat{a}_{\nu_k}^\dagger | 0 \rangle = \sum_k \nu_k^*(\mathbf{r}) \, \hat{a}_{\nu_k}^\dagger | 0 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparision of \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:second-quantization:field:r-1} and \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:second-quantization:field:r-2} gives the expression of the field creation operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_k \nu_k^*(\mathbf{r}) \hat{a}_{\nu_k}^\dagger \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Equivalent expression of the single\sphinxhyphen{}body wave function}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The single\sphinxhyphen{}body wave function in position representation reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \psi(\mathbf{r}) 
  & = \langle \mathbf{r} | \psi \rangle = \\
  & = \langle 0 | \hat{\Psi}(\mathbf{r}) | \psi \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_k \sum_j \nu_j(\mathbf{r}) \underbrace{\langle 0 | \hat{a}_{\nu_j} | \nu_k \rangle}_{=\delta_{jk} \langle 0 | 0 \rangle = \delta_{jk}} \langle \nu_k | \psi \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_k \nu_k(\mathbf{r}) \langle \nu_k | \psi \rangle = \\ 
  & = \sum_k \langle \mathbf{r} | \nu_k \rangle \langle \nu_k | \psi \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Continuous basis}


\subsubsection{Two\sphinxhyphen{}particle system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:two-particle-system}}

\paragraph{Bosons}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:bosons}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Position state can be expressed either with creation operators
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2 \rangle = \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_2) \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_1) | 0 \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and with as a linear combination of states built with the 1\sphinxhyphen{}body basis \(\{ \nu_k \}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2 \rangle = \sum_{i_1 \le i_2} | \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} \rangle \langle \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} | \mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identity operator.}
\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\mathbf{1}}^{(2)} | \Psi \rangle 
  & = \hat{\mathbf{1}}^{(2)} \sum_{k_1 \le k_2} c_{k_1, k_2} | \nu_{k_1} \nu_{k_2} \rangle = \\
  & = \left( \sum_{i_1 \le i_2} | \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} \rangle \langle \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} | \right) \sum_{k_1 \le k_2} c_{k_1, k_2} | \nu_{k_1} , \nu_{k_2} \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{i_1 \le i_2} \sum_{k_1 \le k_2} | \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} \rangle \delta_{i_1 k_1} \delta_{i_2 k_2} c_{k_1,k_2} = \\
  & = \sum_{i_1 \le i_2} | \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} \rangle c_{i_1,i_2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bosons.} The state \(| \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_2} \rangle\) can be built with creation operators from the vacuum state. If \(i_1 \ne i_2\), then
\begin{equation*}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \nu_{i_1}, \nu_{i_1} \rangle = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_{i_1}} \hat{a}^\dagger_{\nu_{i_1}} | 0 \rangle \qquad '=' \qquad | \dots \underbrace{2}_{i_1} \dots \rangle \ , \end{split}

\end{aligned}\end{split}

\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

\section{Operators in QFT}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:operators-in-qft}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-operators}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One\sphinxhyphen{}body operators act on individual particles. Let \(\hat{o}\) the operator acting on the single\sphinxhyphen{}particle wave function \(| \psi \rangle \in \mathcal{H}\), and \(o_{ab} = \langle \phi_a | \hat{o} | \phi_b \rangle\) its matrix components w.r.t. the vectors of the basis of \(\{ \psi_a \}_a\) of \(\mathcal{H}\), or in \sphinxstylestrong{position representation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
o_{ab} = \langle \psi_a | \hat{o} | \psi_b \rangle = \langle \psi_a |\int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{o} | \psi_b \rangle \, d \mathbf{r} = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \psi_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \, o \psi_b(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(o\) the linear (tipically differential) operator in space representation, and \(o \psi_b(\mathbf{r})\) its action of \(| \psi_b \rangle\) in space representation. Just as an example, the space representation of the action of the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum operator \(\hat{p}_x\) on vector \(| \psi_b \rangle\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{p}_x | \psi_b \rangle = -i \hbar \partial_x \langle \mathbf{r} | \psi_b \rangle = - i \hbar \partial_x \psi_b(\mathbf{r}) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the linear differential operator in space representation acting on the space representation of the wave vector reads \(p_x = - i \hbar \partial_x\), and \(p_x \psi_b(\mathbf{r}) = - i \hbar \partial_x \psi_b(\mathbf{r})\).


\subsection{One\sphinxhyphen{}body operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:one-body-operators}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:quantum-mechanics-second-quantizazion-operators-one-body}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{First quantization.} The operator \(\hat{O}_1\) is the sum of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle operators \(\hat{o}\), each one acting on the corresponding particle,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:first-quantization}
\begin{split}\hat{O}_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \hat{o}(q^i, p_i) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the state of the system \(| \Psi \rangle\) be represented in the basis \(\{ | \psi_{i_1}, \psi_{i_2}, \dots \rangle \}\), with the vectors \(|\psi_i \rangle\) being the eigenvectors of the operator \(\hat{o}\), with eigenvalues \(o_k\). Let the system be in state \(| \Psi \rangle = | \psi_{i_1}, \psi_{i_2}, \dots \rangle\). Then the action of the one\sphinxhyphen{}body operator on the state of the system reads
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:first-quantization:eig}
\begin{split}\hat{O}_1 | \Psi \rangle = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \hat{o}^{(k)} | \Psi \rangle = \sum_{k=1}^N o_{i_k} | \Psi \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the state \(| \psi_{i_1}, \psi_{i_2}, \dots \rangle\) is an eigenstate of the one\sphinxhyphen{}body operator \(\hat{O}_1\), with eigenvalue \(\sum_{k=1}^{N} o_{i_k}\).

\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{O}_1
  & = \sum_{\alpha, \beta} o_{\alpha \beta} \hat{a}_{\alpha}^\dagger \hat{a}_\beta \ , 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\hat{a}^\dagger_{\alpha}\), \(\hat{a}_{\beta}\) the creation and annihilation operators for one particle in states \(| \psi_a \rangle\), and \(| \psi_b \rangle\) respectively, and \(o_{\alpha \beta} = \langle \psi_a | \hat{o} | \psi_b \rangle\), with \(\{ | \psi_a \rangle \}\) vectors of a basis of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle space. The summations in \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) here occur on all the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle eigenstates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the operator is built using the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle eigenstates of the operator \(\hat{o}\), then the matrix \(o_{\alpha \beta}\) is diagonal, and the operator can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{O}_1 = \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \hat{a}_{\alpha}^\dagger \hat{a}_{\alpha}  = \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \hat{n}_{\alpha} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(o_{\alpha}\) the eigenvalues of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle operator \(\hat{o}\) and \(\hat{n}_{\alpha} = \hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\alpha} \hat{a}_{\alpha}\) the number operator of the state \(\alpha\). The action of the operator \(\hat{O}_1\) on the state of the system, represented in the occupation number basis \(| \Psi \rangle = | n_{o_1}, n_{o_2}, \dots \rangle\) built on the 1\sphinxhyphen{}particle eigenstates of the operator \(\hat{o}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{O}_1 | \Psi \rangle 
  & = \left( \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha \beta} \hat{a}_{\alpha}^\dagger \hat{a}_{\alpha} \right) | \Psi \rangle 
    = \left( \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha \beta} \hat{n}_{\alpha} \right) | \Psi \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system is in an eigenstate of the operator \(\hat{O}\), represented by only one vector \(| \Psi \rangle = | \mathbf{n} \rangle = | n_{1}, n_{2}, \dots \rangle\), then
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:second-quantization:eig}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{O}_1 | \mathbf{n} \rangle 
  & = \left( \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \hat{n}_{\alpha} \right) | \mathbf{n} \rangle = \\
  & = \left( \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \hat{n}_{\alpha} \right) | \dots n_\alpha \dots \rangle = \\
  & = \left( \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \, {n}_{\alpha} \right) | \dots n_\alpha \dots \rangle = \\
  & = \underbrace{\left( \sum_{\alpha} {n}_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} \right)}_{=:o_{\mathbf{n}}} | \mathbf{n} \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the state \(| \mathbf{n} \rangle\) of the occupation numbers of the eigenstates of \(\hat{o}\) is an eigenvector of the operator \(\hat{O}\) with eigenvalue \(o_{\mathbf{n}} := \sum_{\alpha} o_{\alpha} n_{\alpha}\).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Operators in first and second quantization}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The action of the operator \(\hat{O}_1\) can be expressed using second quantization formalism with \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:second-quantization:eig} or using the analogous first quantization formalism with \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:first-quantization:eig}: while summation in second quantization runs over the eigenstates, the summation runs over “particles” in first quantization. These two different points of view provide the same result, with the eigenvalue of the eigenstate \(| \mathbf{n} \rangle = | \psi_{i_1}, \psi_{i_2}, \dots \rangle\) (with \(n_1\) of the \(\psi_{i_k}\) in eigenstate \(\psi_{1}\),…) equal to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}o_{\mathbf{n}} = \sum_{\alpha} n_a o_a = \sum_{k} o_{i_k} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This analogy also provides a justification for the expressions \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:first-quantization} and \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:second-quantization} of the one\sphinxhyphen{}body operator \(\hat{O}_1\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Space representation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:space-representation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the relations \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:creation:inverse} and \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/quantum-fields:eq:qft:fields:annihilation:inverse},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}^\dagger_{a} 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \psi_a(\mathbf{r}) \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{a}_{a} 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \psi_a^*(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it’s possible to find another equivalent expression of the expression \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:eq:qft:operator:one-body:second-quantization} of the \(\hat{O}_1\) operator,

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Review these steps. There’s too much free\sphinxhyphen{}style in swapping operators…}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\hat{O}_1
& = \sum_{\alpha, \beta} o_{\alpha \beta} \hat{a}_{\alpha}^{\dagger} \hat{a}_{\beta} = \\
& = \sum_{\alpha, \beta} o_{\alpha \beta} \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}} \psi_a(\mathbf{r}) \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \, d \mathbf{r} \right) \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \psi_\beta^*(\mathbf{r}') \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r}' \right) = \\
& = \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} o_{\alpha \beta}  \psi_a(\mathbf{r}) \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})  \psi_\beta^*(\mathbf{r}') \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \, d \mathbf{r}' = \\
& = \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'}  \psi_a(\mathbf{r}) o_{\alpha \beta} \psi_\beta^*(\mathbf{r}')  \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \, d \mathbf{r}' = && (1) \\
& = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  \langle \mathbf{r} | \psi_a \rangle \langle \psi_a | \hat{o} | \psi_\beta \rangle \langle \psi_\beta | \mathbf{r}' \rangle  \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \, d \mathbf{r}' = \\
& = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{o} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle  \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \, d \mathbf{r}' = && (2) \\
& = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  o_{\mathbf{r}; \partial_{\mathbf{r}}}  \underbrace{\langle \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle}_{\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}')}  \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \, d \mathbf{r}' = \\
& = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \sum_{\alpha, \beta}  \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) o_{\mathbf{r}; \partial_{\mathbf{r}}}  \Psi(\mathbf{r}') \, d \mathbf{r} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/many-body/operators:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 23.6.1 (Kinetic energy)}


\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \hat{T}
 & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \langle \mathbf{r} | \hat{t} \hat{\Psi}(\mathbf{r}) = \\
 & = \dots = \\
 & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \left( - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla^2 \right) \hat{\Psi}(\mathbf{r}) = \\
 & = \int_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \nabla \hat{\Psi}^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla \hat{\Psi}(\mathbf{r}) \ ,

with integration by parts and vanishing operators for \(|\mathbf{r}| \rightarrow + \infty\).

EM field quantization}}}}} Quantization of the EM field. Introduction: Fermi ideal cavity, EM in free space. \sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{Summary}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fock space} is built from commutators (bosons) or anticommutators (fermions) of creation/annihilation operators; Pauli exclusion is the algebraic fact \((c^\dagger)^2=0\), and one\sphinxhyphen{}body operators are \(\sum t_{ij}a_i^\dagger a_j\) for both statistics.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Symmetries} act by unitary operators \(e^{-i\theta T}\) generated by one\sphinxhyphen{}body operators; their eigenvalues are additive over occupied modes. Number conservation of electrons (global \(U(1)\)) versus the absence of such a charge for the photon explains why photons are created singly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Local \(U(1)\) gauge invariance} fixes the electron–photon coupling \(\mathbf p\to\mathbf p+e\mathbf A\), producing both \(H_1\propto\mathbf A\!\cdot\!\mathbf p\) and the seagull \(H_2\propto\mathbf A^2\) with locked coefficients.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The photon field} is a set of oscillators with \([a,a^\dagger]=1\); the classical limit is the coherent state with \(\Delta E/E=1/(2\sqrt{\bar n})\), and radiation by a classical current produces exactly that state.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The electron field} obeys the Schrödinger equation as an operator equation. Free and bound electrons are two different bases of one and the same field, related by a unitary transformation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Emission and absorption}: matrix elements \(\propto\sqrt{n}\) and \(\sqrt{n+1}\) give stimulated and spontaneous emission; in the dipole approximation \(\Gamma=\omega^3|\mathbf d|^2/(3\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3)\), which reproduces the measured hydrogen \(2p\) lifetime of 1.6 ns, equals (oscillator strength) × (classical radiation\sphinxhyphen{}damping rate), and enforces Einstein’s thermal balance.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Free electrons cannot absorb a single photon}; the lowest\sphinxhyphen{}order free\sphinxhyphen{}electron process is Compton scattering. In the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic theory only the seagull contributes for an electron at rest, giving the Thomson cross\sphinxhyphen{}section \(\sigma_{\rm T}=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}r_e^2\) and the Compton shift to leading order in \(\hbar\omega/mc^2\); the relativistic Klein–Nishina result requires the Dirac field.

\end{enumerate}

\section{Harmonic Oscillator}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:harmonic-oscillator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Harmonic oscillator is used as the fundamental element in {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:quantum-mechanics-qft-field-quantization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{field quantization}}}}.


\subsection{Classical model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:classical-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator-classical}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian function of a harmonic oscillator is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2x^2}{2} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{From classical to quantum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:from-classical-to-quantum}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator-quantization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Promoting generalized coordinate and momentum to operators, the Hamiltonian operator of the quantum harmonic oscillator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat{H} = \frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2\hat x^2}{2} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Stationary states}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:stationary-states}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator-quantization-stationary-states}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{stationary states} are defined as the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian operators, whose energy level is the corresponding eigenvalue
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n|\psi_n\rangle=\left(\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2\hat x^2}{2}\right)|\psi_n\rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in position representation, with decaying wave function at infinity,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{\begin{aligned}
& E_n\psi_n=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi_n''+\frac{m\omega^2x^2}{2}\psi_n \\
& \psi\big|_{\pm\infty} \to 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A solution exists only for a set of \sphinxstylestrong{discrete values} of \(E_n\), while for all the other values the b.c. are not satisfied. The feasible solutions of the eigenproblem are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi_n(x)=c_nH_n(x)e^{-\frac12x^2},\qquad E_n=\left(\tfrac12+n\right)\hbar\omega
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The lowest energy is \(\neq0\) because of Heisenberg uncertainty, i.e. a particle can’t be exactly in \(x=0\) with \(p=0\)!
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\subsubsection*{Details of the spectral decomposition of the Hamiltonian operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\xi = a x\). Then, as \(\frac{d}{dx} = \frac{d \xi}{d x} \frac{d}{d \xi} = a \frac{d}{d \xi}\) the equation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_n \psi_n(\xi) = - a^2 \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \psi''_n(\xi) + \frac{m \omega^2 \xi^2}{2 a^2} \psi_n(\xi) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Defining \(a = \sqrt{\frac{m \omega}{\hbar}}\), \(\lambda_n = \frac{2 E_n}{\hbar \omega}\), the equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi''_n(\xi) + (\lambda_n - \xi^2) \psi_n(\xi) = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(|\xi| \rightarrow +\infty\), the elastic term dominates the eigenvalue term, and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0 
 & \simeq - \psi'' + \xi^2 \psi \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The asymptotic behavior reads \(\psi_{n,\infty}(\xi) = e^{-\xi^2/2}\). This can be checked evaluating the first two derivatives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{d}{d\xi} e^{-\xi^2/2} & = - \xi e^{-\xi^2/2} \\
  \frac{d^2}{d\xi^2} e^{-\xi^2/2} & = \left( -1 + \xi^2 \right) e^{-\xi^2/2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and comparing the leading order contributions \(O(\xi^2 e^{-\xi^2/2})\).
\subsubsection*{Full solution}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the solution be \(\psi(\xi) = h(\xi) e^{-\xi^2/2}\), with unknown \(h(\xi)\). Its derivatives read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \psi'  & = \left( h' - \xi h \right) e^{-\xi^2/2} \\
  \psi'' & = \left( h'' - h - 2 \xi h' + \xi^2 h \right) e^{-\xi^2/2} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing this expression in the differential equation, and removing the term \(e^{-\xi^2/2} \ne 0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 
  & = ( \lambda - \xi^2 ) h(\xi) + ( h''(\xi) - h(\xi) - 2 \xi h'(\xi) + \xi^2 h(\xi) ) = \\
  & = \lambda h(\xi) + h''(\xi) - h(\xi) - 2 \xi h'(\xi)  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the power expansion of \(h(\xi)\) be
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}h(\xi) = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} c_k \xi^k \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
thus the equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0 
 & = \lambda \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} c_k \xi^k + \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k (k-1) c_k \xi^{k-2} - \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} c_k \xi^k - 2 \xi \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k \, c_k \xi^{k-1} = \\
 & = \lambda \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} c_k \xi^k + \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} (k+2) (k+1) c_{k+2} \xi^{k} - \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} c_k \xi^k - 2 \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k \, c_k \xi^{k} = \\
 & = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \left\{ - \left( - \lambda + 1 + 2k \right) c_k + \left( k + 2 \right) \left( k + 1 \right) c_{k+2} \right\} \xi^k \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This equation implies the a recursion relation between the coefficients of the power expansion
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:eq:hermite:recurrence}
\begin{split}c_{k+2} = \frac{2k + 1 - \lambda}{(k+2)(k+1)} c_k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Symmetry of the solutions}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The recurrence relation \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:eq:hermite:recurrence} involves coefficients with the same parity, \(c_k\) and \(c_{k+2}\). Thus it’s possible to select:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
even solutions, by setting \(c_1 = 0\), that implies \(c_3 = c_5 = \dots = 0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
odd  solutions, by setting \(c_0 = 0\), that implies \(c_2 = c_4 = \dots = 0\)

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior of the power series}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s discuss even solution here. The discussion for odd solutions is identical.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Even solutions.} Let \(c_1 = 0\). Then the power series of \(h(\xi)\) only contains even powers
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}h(\xi) = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} c_{2m} \xi^{2m} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For “large” \(m\), the recurrence relation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_{2m+2} \sim \frac{2}{2m} c_{2m} = \frac{c_{2m}}{m} \sim \frac{c_{2m}}{m+1} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the asymptotic behavior of the \sphinxstylestrong{infinite power series} becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}h(\xi) = \dots + \sum_{m=1}^{+\infty} c_{2m} \xi^{2m} = \dots + c_0 \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\xi^{2m}}{m!} = \dots + e^{\xi^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the asymptotic behavior of the full solution, \(\psi(\xi) = e^{-\xi^2/2} h(\xi)\), is \(\psi(\xi) \sim e^{-\xi^2/2} e^{\xi^2} = e^{\xi^2/2}\), for \(\xi \rightarrow \mp +\infty\). As the boundary conditions of the original problem implies \(\psi(\xi \rightarrow \mp \infty) \rightarrow 0\), this asymptotic behavior is not allowed, and thus the power series can’t have an infinite number of terms. Thus the recurrence relation provides a \sphinxstylestrong{stopping criterion}.

\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda_n = 2 n + 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Creator and annihilation operators}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:creator-and-annihilation-operators}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator-quantization-creation-annihilation-operators}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s call \(\psi_n(x)=|n\rangle\). It’s possible to prove (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{prove it!}) that there are two operators
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat a^\dagger|n\rangle\to|n+1\rangle\), \sphinxstylestrong{creation operator}, that moves the state \(|n\rangle\) to the state \(|n+1\rangle\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat a|n\rangle\to|n-1\rangle\), \sphinxstylestrong{annihilation operator}, that moves the state \(|n\rangle\) to the state \(|n-1\rangle\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These operators are defined with the following proportionality constants \sphinxhyphen{} whose reason appears in the definition of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator-quantization-number-operator}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{number operator}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\hat a^\dagger|n\rangle & =\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle \\
\hat a|n\rangle & =\sqrt{n}\,|n-1\rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the condition
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat a|0\rangle=0 \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(c=\hbar=1\), creation/destruction in terms of \(\hat x,\hat p\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat a^\dagger=\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\left(\hat x-\tfrac{i\hat p}{m\omega}\right),\qquad
\hat a=\sqrt{\tfrac{m\omega}{2\hbar}}\left(\hat x+\tfrac{i\hat p}{m\omega}\right)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Creation and annihilation operators, and the Hamiltonian}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{H}
  & = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2 m} + \frac{m \omega^2 \hat{x}^2}{2} = \\
  & = \hbar \omega \underbrace{ \sqrt{\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar}} \left( \hat{x} - i \frac{\hat{p}}{m \omega} \right)}_{= \hat{a}^\dagger} \underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{m\omega}{2 \hbar}} \left( \hat{x} + i \frac{\hat{p}}{m \omega} \right)}_{=\hat{a}} - i \hbar \omega \frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} \underbrace{\left( \hat{x} \frac{\hat{p}}{m \omega} - \frac{\hat{p}}{m \omega} \hat{x} \right)}_{\frac{1}{m \omega}[\hat{x}, \hat{p}] = \frac{i \hbar}{m \omega}} = \\
  & = \hbar\omega \left( \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} + \frac{1}{2} \right) \ . 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Commutation of annihilation and creation operator}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left[ \hat{a}, \hat{a}^\dagger \right]
  & = \frac{m\omega}{2\hbar} \left[ \hat{x} + i \frac{\hat{p}}{m\omega}, \hat{x} - i \frac{\hat{p}}{m\omega}\right] = \\
  & = \frac{m\omega}{2\hbar} \left\{ -\frac{i}{m\omega} [ \hat{x}, \hat{p} ] + \frac{i}{m\omega} [ \hat{p}, \hat{x} ] \right\} = \\
  & = - i \frac{1}{2\hbar} \left\{ [ \hat{x}, \hat{p} ] + [ \hat{x}, \hat{p} ] \right\} = \\
  & = - i \frac{1}{2\hbar} \cdot 2 i \hbar = \\
  & = 1 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details about the action of creation and annihilation operators on eigenstates in position basis}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(n\) mode in space basis reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_n(x) = e^{-x^2/2} h_n(x) = e^{-x^2/2} \sum_{k=0}^{n} c_k x^k \ ,\end{split}

\subsubsection{Number operator}

The number operator is defined as \(\hat a^\dagger\hat a=:\hat n\), with \(\hat n|n\rangle=n|n\rangle\).
\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}

All these results apply to a single particle, in a 1\sphinxhyphen{}dim domain, with a single oscillation frequency.

Thus the spectral decomposition of the annihilation operator in Heisenberg picture, \(\hat{a}_H | \alpha \rangle_H = \alpha_H | \alpha \rangle_H\), becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e^{-i \omega t} \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle_H = \alpha_H | \alpha \rangle_H \end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{a} | \alpha \rangle_H = e^{i \omega t} \alpha_H | \alpha \rangle_H \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha \rangle_H = \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…


\paragraph{Classical limit}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The expected value of the position and the momentum of the system starting in a coherent state is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \langle \hat{x} \rangle & = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}} \left( \alpha^* e^{i \omega t} + \alpha e^{-i \omega t} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{2 \hbar} {m \omega}} \left( \text{Re}\{ \alpha \} \cos(\omega t) + \text{Im}\{ \alpha \} \sin(\omega t) \right) \\
 \langle \hat{p} \rangle & = \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \left( i \alpha^* e^{i \omega t} - i \alpha e^{-i \omega t} \right) = \sqrt{2 m \hbar \omega} \left( - \text{Re}\{ \alpha \} \sin(\omega t) + \text{Im}\{ \alpha \} \cos(\omega t) \right) = m \frac{d}{dt} \langle \hat{x} \rangle \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Heisenberg picture, the expected value of the position reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \hat{x} \rangle
  & = \langle \alpha | \hat{x}_H | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \langle \alpha | \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}} \left( \hat{a}^\dagger_H + \hat{a}_H \right) | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}} \langle \alpha | \left( \hat{a}^\dagger e^{i \omega t} + \hat{a} e^{-i \omega t} \right) | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}} \left( \alpha^* e^{i \omega t} + \alpha e^{-i \omega t} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since \(\langle \alpha | \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle = \alpha\), \(\langle \alpha | \hat{a}^\dagger | \alpha \rangle = \alpha^*\) (see the section {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-coulomb-classical-limit-one-mode-coherent}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{One\sphinxhyphen{}mode coherent state, for the EM field}}}}). The expected value of the momentum, \(\hat{p} = i \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \left( \hat{a}^{\dagger} - \hat{a} \right)\), reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \hat{p} \rangle
  & = \langle \alpha | \hat{p}_H | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \langle \alpha | i \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \left( \hat{a}^\dagger_H - \hat{a}_H \right) | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \langle \alpha | i \left( \hat{a}^\dagger e^{i \omega t} - \hat{a} e^{-i \omega t} \right) | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \left( i \alpha^* e^{i \omega t} - i \alpha e^{-i \omega t} \right) = \\
  & = \sqrt{\frac{m \hbar \omega}{2}} \cdot 2 \cdot \text{Re} \{ i \alpha^* e^{i \omega t} \} = \\
  & = \sqrt{ 2 m \hbar \omega} \left( \text{Im}\{ \alpha \} \cos( \omega t ) - \text{Re} \{ \alpha \} \sin(\omega t) \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{old version}
\subsubsection*{Creation and destruction}
\subsubsection*{Motivation}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
EM energy is quantized. These quanta (photons) have \(E=\hbar\omega\), \(\vec p=\hbar\vec k\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Photons can be created/destroyed. Example, \(\gamma\) emission:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
destruction of a high\sphinxhyphen{}energy \(e^-\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
creation of a lower\sphinxhyphen{}energy \(e^-\) + \(\gamma\).

\end{enumerate}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(e^-\) can be represented by wavefunctions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1917, A. Einstein: re\sphinxhyphen{}derived Planck’s law; spontaneous and stimulated emission.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Models for creation and destruction}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Single\sphinxhyphen{}frequency oscillators at frequency \(\nu\)}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
creation → 1 more photon → \(\Delta E = h\nu\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
destruction → 1 photon less → \(\Delta E = -h\nu\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Classical oscillator}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2x^2}{2}\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{Quantum: }\hat H=\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2\hat x^2}{2}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Eigenproblem \(E_n|\psi_n\rangle=\left(\frac{\hat p^2}{2m}+\frac{m\omega^2\hat x^2}{2}\right)|\psi_n\rangle\). In position representation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
E_n\psi_n=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi_n''+\frac{m\omega^2x^2}{2}\psi_n
\quad\text{+ b.c. s.t. } \psi\big|_{\pm\infty}\to0
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A solution exists only for a set of discrete values of \(E_n\); for all the other values the b.c. are not satisfied.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi_n(x)=c_nH_n(x)e^{-\frac12x^2},\qquad E_n=\left(\tfrac12+n\right)\hbar\omega
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The lowest energy is \(\neq0\) because of Heisenberg uncertainty, i.e. a particle can’t be exactly in \(x=0\) with \(p=0\)!
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Creation / destruction operators}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s call \(\psi_n(x)=|n\rangle\).
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat a^\dagger|n\rangle\to|n+1\rangle\): moves from the state \(|n\rangle\) to the state \(|n+1\rangle\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat a|n\rangle\to|n-1\rangle\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The right proportionality constants give:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat a^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle,\qquad
\hat a|n\rangle=\sqrt{n}\,|n-1\rangle,\qquad
\hat a|0\rangle=0
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(c=\hbar=1\), creation/destruction in terms of \(\hat x,\hat p\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat a^\dagger=\sqrt{\tfrac{\omega}{2}}\left(\hat x+\tfrac{i\hat p}{\omega}\right),\qquad
\hat a=\sqrt{\tfrac{\omega}{2}}\left(\hat x-\tfrac{i\hat p}{\omega}\right)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{[}check{]}} the usual convention has the signs the other way round (\(\hat a\propto \hat x+i\hat p/\omega\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Number operator}: \(\hat a^\dagger\hat a=:\hat n\), with \(\hat n|n\rangle=n|n\rangle\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat H=\hbar\omega\left(\tfrac12+\hat a^\dagger\hat a\right),\qquad [\hat a,\hat a^\dagger]=1
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All these results apply to a single particle, in a 1\sphinxhyphen{}dim domain, with a single oscillation frequency.

\sphinxAtStartPar
