\section{Field quantization}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:field-quantization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:quantum-mechanics-qft-field-quantization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First, a {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:quantum-mechanics-qft-field-quantization-classical}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{classical system}}}} governed by a wave equation is discussed, along with its mode decomposition: a general solution can be written as the superposition of modes \(u(x,t) = \sum_k q_k(t) n_k(x)\) whose contribution is modulated by coefficients \(q_k(t)\) satisfying the ODE of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/harmonic-oscillator:quantum-mechanics-qft-harmonic-oscillator}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{“single\sphinxhyphen{}frequency” harmonic oscillator}}}}. Thus, quantization of the system is performed in the modal basis using the same procedure used for the “single\sphinxhyphen{}frequency” harmonic oscillator.


\subsection{Classical system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:classical-system}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:quantum-mechanics-qft-field-quantization-classical}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let a classical field \(u(x,t)\) be governed by the wave equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\partial_t^2u-c^2\partial_{xx}u=f \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
supplied with proper initial and boundary conditions. This equation is usually the continuous model (exploiting \sphinxstylestrong{continuum hypotesis}, or some equivalent principle) of a macroscopic system, made of a huge number \sphinxhyphen{} but \sphinxstylestrong{finite} number \sphinxhyphen{} of sub\sphinxhyphen{}systems at the microscopic level. This is quite a relevant remark, as continuous models have an infinite number of modes, while discrete models with a finite number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}systems have a finite number of modes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The wave equation is a PDE that can be interpreted as the continuous counter\sphinxhyphen{}part of a set of ODE for the sub\sphinxhyphen{}systems of a discrete model, e.g.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\ddot u_i-c^2\frac{u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1}}{\Delta x^2}=f_i \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used centered finite difference for the second\sphinxhyphen{}order space derivative.
As done in \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-continuum-mechanics/ch/solids/intro.html}{mechanics of elastic structures}, the solution of the continuous equation can be written in the modal basis, that is computed as all the possible standing waves of the homogeneous problem
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\partial_t^2u-c^2\partial_{xx}u=0
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
supplied with homogeneous boundary conditions \(u(0) = u(L) = 0\), using the methods of separation of variables. Modes are the set of functions
\(n_k(x) = \sin \left( \frac{k \pi}{L} x \right)\), with \(k \in \mathbb{N}^+\). The general solution can be written as a linear combination of the modes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
u(x,t)=\sum_k q_k(t)\sin\!\left(\frac{k\pi}{L}x\right) \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent coefficients \(q_k(t)\) satisfying the harmonic oscillator uncoupled ODEs
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:eq:field-quantization:classical:mode-ode}
\begin{split}
\ddot q_k+\underbrace{\frac{c^2k^2\pi^2}{L^2}}_{\omega_k^2}q_k=0 \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{energy density} of the system can be defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e(x,t) :=  \frac{|\partial_t u|^2}{2} + c^2 \frac{|\partial_x u|^2}{2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the energy in the whole domain is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 E 
 & = \int_{x=0}^{L} e(x,t) \, dx = \\
 & = \int_{x=0}^{L} \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k, k'} \dot{q}_k \dot{q}_{k'} \sin\left( \frac{k \pi x}{L}\right) \sin\left( \frac{k' \pi x}{L} \right) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k,k'} c^2 q_k q_{k'} \frac{k k' \pi^2}{L^2} \cos \left( \frac{k \pi x}{L} \right) \cos \left( \frac{k' \pi x}{L} \right) \right\} \, dx = \\
 & = \frac{L}{2} \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} \dot{q}_k^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} c^2 \frac{k^2 \pi^2}{L^2} q_k^2 \right\}  = \\
 & = \frac{L}{2} \sum_{k} \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \dot{q}_k^2 + \frac{1}{2} \omega_k^2 q_k^2 \right\}  = \\
 & = \sum_{k} E_k(q^k, \dot{q}^k) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having exploited orthogonality of the modes. The latter expression shows that the total energy can be written as the sum of energy contributions from the different modes. As the amplitudes of the modes satisfy the harmonic oscillator ODE, then they can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  q_k(t)       & = Q_k e^{i ( \omega_k t + \varphi_k)} + c.c. = 2 Q_k \cos( \omega_k t + \varphi_k ) \\
  \dot{q}_k(t) & = i \omega_k Q_k e^{i (\omega_k t + \varphi_k)} + c.c. = - 2 \omega_k Q_k \sin( \omega_k t + \varphi_k ) \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the energy in the domain becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E
  & = \frac{L}{4} \sum_k \left\{ 4 \omega_k^2 Q_k^2 \sin^2( \omega_k t + \varphi_k ) + \omega_k^2 4 Q_k^2 \cos^2( \omega_k t + \varphi_k ) \right\} = \\
  & = L \sum_k \omega_k^2 Q_k^2 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the elementary contribution of the \(k^{th}\) mode to the energy of the system is \(E_k = L \omega^2_k Q_k^2\).


\subsection{From classical to quantum}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:from-classical-to-quantum}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:quantum-mechanics-qft-field-quantization-quantization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The amplitude \(q_k(t)\) of mode \(k\) is governed by the dynamical equation \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:eq:field-quantization:classical:mode-ode}, compatible with the Hamiltonian
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H_k(q^k,p_k) = \frac{p_k^2}{2} + \frac{\omega_k^2 (q^k)^2}{2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Wavefunction of the mode \(k\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi_{n_k}(q^k)\propto H_{n_k}(\cdot)\,e^{-\frac12 (q^k)^2},\qquad E_k=\left(n_k+\tfrac12\right)\hbar\omega_k
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Wavefunction of the system of oscillators:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Psi(q^1,q^2,\dots)=\psi_1(q^1)\,\psi_2(q^2)\cdots
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, using the occupation\sphinxhyphen{}number representation: \(|n_1,n_2,\dots\rangle=|n_1\rangle|n_2\rangle\cdots\)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
creation/destruction and number operators for each individual mode;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for independent modes: energy \(E=\sum_kE_k\), with \(E_k=\hbar\omega_k\left(n_k+\tfrac12\right)\).

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Infinite energy}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/field-quantization:infinite-energy}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Even if \(n_k=0\ \forall k\), then \(E=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\tfrac12\hbar\omega_k=\infty\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{But} physical systems are made of a \sphinxstylestrong{finite number} (even if huge) of particles \(N\), and thus the system has only \(N\) modes: so the zero\sphinxhyphen{}point energy for mechanical systems is non\sphinxhyphen{}\(\infty\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{But} for continuous fields, say \(\vec e(\vec r,t)\), we don’t have this argument: as it’s usually possible to measure only energy differences, zero\sphinxhyphen{}point energy “can be declared by fiat”, i.e. “the vacuum state has zero energy”.

\sphinxstepscope

\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons:fermi-1931-introduction-to-qft-lessons}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-em-field-quantization-fermi}}

\subsubsection{EM Field in free space}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons:em-field-in-free-space}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-em-field-quantization-free-space}}

\paragraph{Field in 1D free space}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons:field-in-1d-free-space}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Travelling wave along \(z\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\vec A(\vec r,t)=\hat u_x\,b\cos(kz-\omega t+\theta)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
b\cos(kz-\omega t+\theta)=b\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t-\theta)+b\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t-\theta)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. a linear combination of 2 standing waves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definitions}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
q(t)=b\cos(\omega t-\theta)\ \ (\text{gen. coord.}),\qquad
\dot q(t)=-b\omega\sin(\omega t-\theta)=:p\ \ (\text{gen. mom.}),\qquad
\ddot q=-\omega^2q
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\vec A=\hat u_x\left[q\cos(kz)-\frac{p}{\omega}\sin(kz)\right]
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In Coulomb gauge:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\vec E=-\partial_t\vec A=-\hat u_x\left[p\cos kz+\omega q\sin kz\right],\qquad
\vec B=\nabla\times\vec A=-\hat u_y\left[kq\sin(kz)+\frac{k}{\omega}p\cos(kz)\right]
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{{[}check{]}} the \(\vec E\) expression above is re\sphinxhyphen{}derived from \(\dot q=p,\ \dot p=-\omega^2q\); the handwriting is hard to read.

\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\dot q=p\), \(\dot p=-\omega^2q\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H=\tfrac12\left(|\vec E|^2+|\vec B|^2\right)
=\tfrac12\left\{2p^2\cos^2(kz)+2\omega^2q^2\sin^2(kz)+4\omega pq\sin(kz)\cos(kz)\right\}

\section{Photons \sphinxhyphen{} EM field quantization with Coulomb gauge}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:photons-em-field-quantization-with-coulomb-gauge}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-coulomb}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb::doc}}



\subsection{Classical fields}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:classical-fields}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-coulomb-classical}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In free space without charge and current densities, the vector potential satisfies the homogeneous wave equation \(\square \vec{a} = \vec{0}\), whose solution can be written as a linear combination of Fourier modes. For finite (or periodic) domains
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{a}(\vec{r},t) = \sum_{\vec{k}} \vec{a}(\vec{k},t) e^{i \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(k_a L_a = n_a 2 \pi\), \(n_a \in \mathbb{Z}\). For infinite domains
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{a}(\vec{r},t) = \dfrac{1}{(2 \pi )^{3/2}} \int_{\vec{k}} \vec{a}(\vec{k},t) e^{i \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r}} \, d \vec{k} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Coulomb gauge.} Exploiting the orthogonality of the base functions \(\frac{e^{i \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r}}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\), Coulomb gauge \(\nabla \cdot \vec{a} = 0\) implies
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \vec{k} \cdot \vec{a}(\vec{k}, t) = 0 \quad , \quad \forall \vec{k} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, as each coefficient \(\vec{a}(\vec{k},t)\) is orthogonal to its corresponding wave vector \(\vec{k}\), it only has 2 independent components (corresponding to \sphinxstylestrong{polarization}). Let \(\{ \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \}_{\mu \in \{1, 2\}}\) an orthogonal basis \sphinxhyphen{} with \(\vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \cdot \vec{k} = 0\) \sphinxhyphen{} for the coefficient \(\vec{a}(\vec{k},t)\), then this coefficient can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{a}(\vec{k}, t) = \sum_{\mu} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}, \mu} a(\vec{k},\mu, t) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Real\sphinxhyphen{}valued field, \(\vec{a}(\vec{r},t)\).} Since \(\vec{a}(\vec{r},t)\) is a real\sphinxhyphen{}valued field, then
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:eq:photons:a:real-value}
\begin{split}\vec{a}(\vec{k},t) = \vec{a}^*(-\vec{k},t) \ . \end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution of the homogeneous wave equation.} Exploiting the orthogonality of the base functions, and the linearity of the wave equation, each coefficient of the Fourier expansion satisfies a linear second\sphinxhyphen{}order equation (simple harmonic oscillator),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_{tt} \vec{a}(\vec{k}, t) + |\vec{k}|^2 \vec{a}(\vec{k},t) = \vec{0} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{a}(\vec{k},t) = \vec{a}_{-}(\vec{k}) e^{i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} + \vec{a}_{+}(\vec{k}) e^{- i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\omega_{\vec{k}} = c | \vec{k} |\), and the coefficients to be determined with the initial conditions for the potential governed by the wave equation. The condition \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:eq:photons:a:real-value} about real\sphinxhyphen{}valued field \(\vec{a}(\vec{r},t)\) implies
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{a}_+(\vec{k},t) = \vec{a}^*_-(-\vec{k},t) \quad , \quad \vec{a}_-(\vec{k},t) = \vec{a}^*_+(-\vec{k},t) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \vec{a}(\vec{k},t) & = \vec{a}_{-}(\vec{k}) e^{i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} + \vec{a}_{+}(\vec{k}) e^{- i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} \\
  \vec{a}^*(-\vec{k},t) & = \left( \vec{a}_{-}(-\vec{k}) e^{i \omega_{-\vec{k}} t} + \vec{a}_{+}(-\vec{k}) e^{- i \omega_{-\vec{k}} t} \right)^* = \\
                        & =        \vec{a}_{-}^*(-\vec{k}) e^{-i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} + \vec{a}^*_{+}(-\vec{k}) e^{i \omega_{\vec{k}} t} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution of the wave equation.} Putting everything together, the solution of the wave equation for the vector potential can be written \sphinxhyphen{} here in a periodic domain \sphinxhyphen{} as
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:eq:photons-coulomb:vector-potential:fourier}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & = \sum_{\vec{k}} \vec{a}(\vec{k},t) e^{i \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r}} = \\

  & = \sum_{\vec{k}} \left[ \vec{a}_{-}(-\vec{k}) e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r} )} + \vec{a}_{+}(\vec{k}) e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r})}  \right] \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}\subsubsection*{Re\sphinxhyphen{}arrangement of the summation}

\sphinxAtStartPar

that can be re\sphinxhyphen{}grouped as

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection*{Schrodinger and Heisenberg picture of annihilation/creation operators. Single simple harmonic oscillator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hamiltonian operator of a single simple harmonic oscillator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2} + \frac{\omega^2 \hat{q}^2}{2} = \hbar \omega \left( \hat{a}^{\dagger} \hat{a} + \frac{1}{2} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Annihilation operator.} Heisenberg equations of motion for the annihilation operator reads
\begin{equation*}

  & = \left[ \hat{a}, \hat{H} \right]_{H} + \cancelto{0}{\left( \partial_t \hat{a} \right)_H} = \\
  & = \left[ \hat{a}, \left( \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} + \frac{1}{2} \right) \hbar \omega \right]_{H} + \cancelto{0}{\left( \partial_t \hat{A} \right)_H} = \\
  & = \left\{ \left( \hat{a} \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} - \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} \hat{a} \right)  \right\}_H \hbar \omega = \\
  & = \left\{ \left[ \hat{a}, \hat{a}^\dagger \right] \hat{a} \right\}_H \hbar \omega = \\
  & = \hbar \omega  \hat{a}_{H} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution provides the relation between the Heisenberg and Schdoringer picture of the annihilation operator,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{a}_H(t) = \hat{a}_H(0) e^{-i \omega t} = \hat{a} e^{-i \omega t} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Creation operator.} Heisenberg equations of motion for the creation operator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & = \left[ \hat{a}^\dagger, \left( \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} + \frac{1}{2} \right) \hbar \omega \right]_{H} + \cancelto{0}{\left( \partial_t \hat{A} \right)_H} = \\
  & = \left\{ \left( \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} - \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} \hat{a}^\dagger \right)  \right\}_H \hbar \omega = \\
  & = \left\{ \hat{a}^\dagger \left[ \hat{a}^\dagger, \hat{a} \right] \right\}_H \hbar \omega = \\
  & = - \hbar \omega  \hat{a}^\dagger_{H} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution provides the relation between the Heisenberg and Schdoringer picture of the creation operator,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{a}^\dagger_H(t) = \hat{a}^\dagger_H(0) e^{i \omega t} = \hat{a}^\dagger e^{i \omega t} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Classical limit}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:classical-limit}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-coulomb-classical-limit}}

\subsubsection{One\sphinxhyphen{}mode coherent state}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:one-mode-coherent-state}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:quantum-mechanics-qft-photons-coulomb-classical-limit-one-mode-coherent}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The state of an electromagnetic field can be written as a linear combination of states in the Fock space, with the occupation numbers of each possible modes \(| \vec{k}, \mu \rangle\). A one\sphinxhyphen{}mode coherent state is defined as the \(| \alpha_{\vec{k},\mu} \rangle\) that’s an eigenstate of the annihilation operator \(\hat{a}_{\vec{k},\mu}\) for the mode \(| \vec{k}, \mu \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{a}_{\vec{k},\mu} | \alpha_{\vec{k},\mu} \rangle = c_{\vec{k}, \mu} | \alpha_{\vec{k},\mu} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The one\sphinxhyphen{}mode coherent state is a linear combination of states in the Fock space
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha_{\vec{k},\mu} \rangle = \sum_{n} b_n^{\vec{k},\mu} | \dots n_{\vec{k},\mu} \dots \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with zero occupation number of any state different from \(|\vec{k}, \mu \rangle\), or dropping the indices,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \alpha \rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} b_n | n \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(b_n = b_0 \frac{c^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\) from the definition and coefficient matching, and \(b_0 = e^{-\frac{|c|^2}{2}}\) from the normalization condition \(\langle \alpha | \alpha \rangle = 1\).
\subsubsection*{Annihilation operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected value when the system is in state \(| \alpha \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \alpha | \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle = c \end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle 
  & = \sum_{n,m=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \langle m | \hat{a} | n \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \sqrt{n} \langle m | n - 1 \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_{n+1} \sqrt{n+1} \underbrace{\langle m | n \rangle}_{=\delta_{mn}} = \\
  & = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} c \cdot |b_n|^2 = \\
  & = c \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \frac{|c|^{2n}}{n!} = \\
  & = c \cdot \underbrace{|b_0|^2 \cdot e^{|c|^2}}_{=1} = c \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since \(\sqrt{n+1} b_{n+1} = c \cdot b_n\).
\subsubsection*{Creation operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected value when the system is in state \(| \alpha \rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle \alpha | \hat{a}^\dagger | \alpha \rangle = c^* \end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{a}^\dagger | \alpha \rangle 
  & = \left( \langle \alpha | \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle \right)^* = \\
  & = \left( \sum_{n,m=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \langle m | \hat{a} | n \rangle \right)^* = \\
  & = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} b_m b_n^* \sqrt{n} \langle m | n - 1 \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} b_m b_{n+1}^* \sqrt{n+1} \underbrace{\langle m | n \rangle}_{=\delta_{mn}} = \\
  & = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} c^* \cdot |b_n|^2 = \\
  & = c^* \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \frac{|c|^{2n}}{n!} = \\
  & = c^* \cdot \underbrace{|b_0|^2 \cdot e^{|c|^2}}_{=1}  = c^* \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Number operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected value of the number operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{n} | \alpha \rangle = |c|^2
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \(\hat{n} = \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} | \alpha \rangle 
  & = \sum_{m,n=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \langle m | \hat{a}^\dagger \hat{a} | n \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{m,n=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \sqrt{n} \langle m | \hat{a}^\dagger | n - 1 \rangle = \\
  & = \sum_{m,n=0}^{+\infty} b_m^* b_n \sqrt{n} \sqrt{n} \underbrace{\langle m | n \rangle}_{=\delta_{mn}} = \\
  & = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} | b_n |^2 \cdot n = \\
  & = |b_0|^2 \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} n \frac{|c|^{2n}}{n!} = \\
  & = |c|^2 \cdot |b_0|^2 \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \frac{|c|^{2n}}{n!}}_{ = e^{|c|^2} = |b_0|^{-2}} = \\
  & = |c|^2 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Potential vector}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expected value of the potential vector field operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{\vec{a}}(\vec{r},t) | \alpha \rangle
  & =  e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r} )} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}, \mu} \, c^*_{\vec{k},\mu} + e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r})} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \, c_{\vec{k},\mu} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle \alpha | \hat{\vec{a}}(\vec{r},t) | \alpha \rangle
  & = \langle \alpha | \sum_{\vec{k}', \mu'} \left[ e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}'} t - \vec{k}' \cdot \vec{r} )} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}', \mu'} \hat{a}^\dagger_{\vec{k}',\mu'} + e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}'} t - \vec{k}' \cdot \vec{r})} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}',\mu'} \hat{a}_{\vec{k}',\mu'} \right] | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & = \langle \alpha | \left[ e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r} )} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}, \mu} \hat{a}^\dagger_{\vec{k},\mu} + e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r})} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \hat{a}_{\vec{k},\mu} \right] | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & =  e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r} )} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}, \mu} \langle \alpha | \hat{a}^\dagger_{\vec{k},\mu} | \alpha \rangle + e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r})} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \langle \alpha | \hat{a}_{\vec{k},\mu} | \alpha \rangle = \\
  & =  e^{i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r} )} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k}, \mu} \, c^* + e^{- i ( \omega_{\vec{k}} t - \vec{k} \cdot \vec{r})} \vec{\epsilon}_{\vec{k},\mu} \, c \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparison with \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/photons-coulomb:eq:photons-coulomb:vector-potential:fourier} identifies the coefficients of the Fourier expansion with the eigenvalue of the annihilation operator corresponding to the coherent state,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\vec{a}_+(\vec{k},\mu) \sim c_{\vec{k},\mu}
\quad , \quad
\vec{a}_-(-\vec{k},\mu) \sim c^*_{\vec{k},\mu} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Multi\sphinxhyphen{}body quantum mechanics and QFT}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:multi-body-quantum-mechanics-and-qft}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:quantum-mechanics-qft-multi-body}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In multi\sphinxhyphen{}body quantum systems the number of identical particles may change in time, and the interactions may occur as non\sphinxhyphen{}smooth dynamics involving creation and destruction of particles. First, the limits of the quantum systems represented with so called first quantization process are discussed: these systems can’t represent systems with a variable number of particles and non smooth interactions. Then, the second quantization of the electron field is introduced, along with the Pauli exclusion principle. Eventually, the properties and the formalism for the second quantization of boson and fermion fields are recalled.


\subsection{First quantization}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:first-quantization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:quantum-mechanics-qft-multi-body-first-quantization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First quantization moves the description of a particle to a wave process, promoting generalized coordinates and momenta \(x\), \(p\) to operators \(\hat{q}\), \(\hat{p}\). The state of a system is described by a wave function \(| \Psi \rangle\) belonging to a Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\), satisfying the Schrodinger equation of the system
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{ | \Psi \rangle } = \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The wavefunction \(| \Psi \rangle\) satisfies the normalization condition \(\langle \Psi | \Psi \rangle = 1\).
If the Hamiltonian operator \(\hat{H}\) is independent from time, its spectral decomposition provides an orthogonal basis for \(\mathcal{H}\) of stationary states \(\{ | \psi_n \rangle \}\) and their energy levels \(\{ E_n \}\). The wavefunction of the system \(| \Psi \rangle\) can be represented in the orthonormal basis as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi(t) \rangle = \sum_n | \psi_n \rangle c_n(t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the coefficients \(c_n\) that can be linked to the probability \(|c_n|^2\) of finding the system whose state is represented by \(| \Psi \rangle\) in the state \(| \psi_n \rangle\), as from normalization condition it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 = \langle \Psi | \Psi \rangle = \sum_{n,m} c_n^* c_m \underbrace{\langle \psi_n | \psi_m \rangle}_{\delta_{nm}} = \sum_n |c_n|^2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Schrödinger equation makes \(c_n(t)\) vary continuously. In energy basis, the coefficients of teh expansion are governed by the ODEs
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{c}_n = E_n c_n \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus they evolve as \(c_n(t) = c_{n,0} \exp\left( - i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t \right)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{But} Interactions between systems may occur as non\sphinxhyphen{}smooth dynamics. As an example, EM radiation absorption or emission by an atom occurs in \sphinxstylestrong{quantum jumps}. As an example, spontaneous emission of EM radiation from an atom involves:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the destruction of a high\sphinxhyphen{}energy \(e^-\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the creation of a lower\sphinxhyphen{}energy \(e^-\) + a \(\gamma\).

\end{enumerate}


\subsection{Second quantization of the electron field}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:second-quantization-of-the-electron-field}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{First quantization.} The wave function describing an electron can be written as a linear combination of the energy eigenstates. In space representation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi(\mathbf{r},t)=\sum_k b_k(t)\psi_k(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_k b_{k0} \psi_k(\mathbf{r}) e^{-i\omega_kt} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\omega_k = \tfrac{E_k}{\hbar}\). The expected value of the energy is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\langle\psi|\hat H|\psi\rangle=\sum_{m,n}\langle m|\hat H|n\rangle\,b^*_{m0}b_{n0}\,e^{+i\omega_mt}e^{-i\omega_nt}
=\sum_nE_n|b_{n0}|^2 \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Second quantization:} \(b_{k0}\to\hat b_k\) (destruction operator). In analogy with multi\sphinxhyphen{}body QM:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat H=\sum_kE_k\hat n_k=\sum_kE_k\hat b_k^\dagger\hat b_k
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Hamiltonian and state of the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting \protect\(e^-\protect\) and radiation fields}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:hamiltonian-and-state-of-the-non-interacting-e-and-radiation-fields}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Electron field.} The state can be represented in the occupation number basis as a linear combination of the basis of the Fock space, namely
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ | \mathbf{n} \rangle \right\} = \left\{ |\mathbf{0} \rangle, |1,0,0,\dots \rangle, |0,1,0,\dots \rangle, \dots, |2,0,0,\dots \rangle, |1,1,0,\dots \rangle, \dots \right\} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
e^-:\ |\phi_e\rangle=|n_{e1},n_{e2},\dots\rangle,\quad \hat H_e=\sum_kE_k\hat b_k^\dagger\hat b_k
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Radiation field
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\text{rad}:\ |\psi_r\rangle=|n_{k\alpha}\dots\rangle,\quad \hat H_{rad}=\sum_{k,\alpha}\hbar\omega_k\hat a^\dagger_{k\alpha}\hat a_{k\alpha}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These are \sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting fields}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{interaction is required} to get quantum jumps of \(e^-\) associated with creation/annihilation of a \(\gamma\).


\subsection{Bosons and fermions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/multi-body:bosons-and-fermions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{(This page of the notes is written upside\sphinxhyphen{}down; the content is transcribed in condensed form.)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bosons} — occupation\sphinxhyphen{}number formalism:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat a^\dagger\) acts on a state by raising it, \(|0\rangle\to|1\rangle\to|2\rangle\to\cdots\), and \(\hat a\) lowers it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number operator: \(\hat n_k=\hat a_k^\dagger\hat a_k\), s.t. \(\hat n_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle=n_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle\).

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat a^\dagger_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle=\sqrt{n_k+1}\,|\dots(n_k+1)\dots\rangle,\qquad
\hat a_k|\dots n_k\dots\rangle=\sqrt{n_k}\,|\dots(n_k-1)\dots\rangle
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
CCR (canonical commutation relations):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
[\hat a_k,\hat a^\dagger_{k'}]=\hat a_k\hat a^\dagger_{k'}-\hat a^\dagger_{k'}\hat a_k=\delta_{kk'}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fermions} — with occupation\sphinxhyphen{}number formalism (Pauli exclusion principle):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat b^\dagger\hat b^\dagger|0\rangle=0\), and \(\hat b\,\hat b|1\rangle=0\) (a second particle cannot be added to an occupied orbital);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\hat b|0\rangle=0\), \(\hat b^\dagger|1\rangle=0\);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
thus \(\{\hat b,\hat b'\}\) and \(\{\hat b^\dagger,\hat b'^\dagger\}\) vanish: \sphinxstylestrong{anticommutators}, \(\{\hat b,\hat b^\dagger\}=1\) (CCR/anticommutation);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
number operator \(\hat n=\hat b^\dagger\hat b\) satisfies \(\hat n^2=\hat b^\dagger\hat b\hat b^\dagger\hat b=\hat b^\dagger(1-\hat b^\dagger\hat b)\hat b=\hat n\) ⟹ \(n=0\) or \(1\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{split}

the Hamiltonian of the electron bound to the atom, and the Hamiltonian of the EM field. Interaction comes from the coupling of the electron dynamics and the EM field: electron may act as a source of the EM field, and its state is influenced by the EM field, as shown…

In classical mechanics the Hamiltonian reads

\begin{split}\mathcal{H} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{|\vec{p}- q \vec{a}|^2}{m} + q \varphi \ ,\end{split}

\subsection{Perturbation theory}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:perturbation-theory}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:quantum-mechanics-qft-interactions-perturbation-theory}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Other sections dealing with perturbation theory:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/heisenberg-reinterpretation:quantum-mechanics-history-heisenberg-reinterpretation-transition-perturbation-theory}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Perturbation theory for transition probabilities in weak electric fields}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture:quantum-mechanics-einstein-coeffs-interaction-picture-perturbation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Interaction picture and perturbation theory}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Need for cleaning}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Perturbation theory applies to systems governed by a Hamiltonian that can be written as the sum
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\hat H = \hat H_0+\hat H_{int} \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\hat H_0\) an easy\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}solve (unperturbed) system, whose spectral decomposition is usually known, and \(\hat H_{int}\) a “small” perturbation, either time independent or time dependent. Let \(| \phi_n \rangle\), and \(E_n\) the eigenstates and the eigenvalues of the unperturbed Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_0\), i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H}_0 | \phi_n \rangle = E_n | \phi_n \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, the perturbation Hamiltonian is explicitly written as the product of a “small” parameter \(\lambda\) and a scaled perturbation Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_1\), with the same order of the unperturbed Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_0\), i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \lambda \hat{H}_1 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and a generic state \(| \psi \rangle\) of the system written as a linear combination of the eigenstates \(\{ | \phi_n \rangle \}_n\) of the unperturbed system,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
|\psi\rangle=\sum_nc_n(t)e^{-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t}|\phi_n\rangle \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inserting this expression in the Schrodinger equation \(i\hbar|\dot\psi\rangle=(\hat H_0+\hat H_{int})|\psi\rangle\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
i\hbar\sum_n\left(\dot c_n-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} c_n \right)e^{-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t}|\phi_n\rangle & = (\hat H_0+\hat H_{int})\sum_nc_ne^{-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t}|\phi_n\rangle \\
 \sum_n i\hbar\dot c_ne^{-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t}|\phi_n\rangle & = \hat H_{int}\sum_n c_n e^{-i \frac{E_n}{\hbar} t}|\phi_n\rangle \ , 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since \(E_n| \phi_n \rangle = \hat{H}_0 | \phi_n \rangle\). Multiplying by \(\langle\phi_m|\), and exploiting orthogonality \(\langle \phi_m | \phi_n \rangle = \delta_{mn}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
i\hbar\dot c_me^{-i\omega_mt}=\sum_nc_ne^{-i\omega_nt}\langle\phi_m|\hat H_{int}|\phi_n\rangle
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the infinite system of equations \sphinxhyphen{} \(m \in \{0,1,2,\dots\}\) \sphinxhyphen{} follows
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:eq:interaction:perturbation}
\begin{split}
\dot c_m=\frac1{i\hbar}\sum_nc_ne^{i(\omega_m-\omega_n)t}\langle\phi_m|\hat H_{int}|\phi_n\rangle
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perturbation theory looks for a solution writing the coefficients \(c_m(t)\) as power expansions in the “small” parameter \(\lambda\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
c_m(t)=c_m^{(0)}(t)+\lambda c_m^{(1)}(t)+\lambda^2c_m^{(2)}(t)+\dots
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inserting this expression in \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:eq:interaction:perturbation},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot c_m^{(0)}+\lambda\dot c_m^{(1)}+\lambda^2\dot c_m^{(2)}+\dots=\frac1{i\hbar}\sum_n\left(c_n^{(0)}+\lambda c_n^{(1)}+\lambda^2c_n^{(2)}+\dots\right) \lambda H^{(1)}_{mn}e^{i(\omega_m-\omega_n)t} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
an (approximate) solution can be found by coefficient matching:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \begin{aligned}
(0): & \quad \dot{c}_m^{(0)} = 0 \\
(k): & \quad \dot{c}_m^{(k)} = \frac{1}{i\hbar} \sum_n c_n^{(k-1)} H^{(1)}_{mn} e^{i ( \omega_m - \omega_n ) t} \\
\end{aligned} \right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{0th\sphinxhyphen{}order solution}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:th-order-solution}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
System starting in \(| n \rangle\), \(c_n(0)=1\), \(c_{m \neq n}(0)=0\). As the \(0^{th}\)\sphinxhyphen{}order equations read \(\dot{c}^{(0)}_m = 0\), then \(0^{th}\)\sphinxhyphen{}order coefficients are constant in time.

else

\subsubsection{Fermi golden rule}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:fermi-golden-rule}}\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:qft:fermi-golden-rule}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 25.6.1 (Fermi golden rule \sphinxhyphen{} infinite time)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(t \rightarrow +\infty\), for a system with unperturbed Hamiltonian \(\hat H_0\), with stationary states \(|\phi_n\rangle_t=|\phi_n\rangle e^{-i\omega_nt}\), an additive “small” perturbation Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{int}\) causes the initial state \(|i\rangle_t=|\phi_i\rangle e^{-i\omega_it}\) to transition to \(|f\rangle=|\phi_f\rangle e^{-i\omega_ft}\) at the rate
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}2\pi\,|H^{int}_{mn}|^2\,\delta(\omega_m-\omega_n)\qquad\text{(to the 1st order)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-perturbation:qft:fermi-golden-rule-finite}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 25.6.2 (Fermi golden rule \sphinxhyphen{} finite time)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
For a system with unperturbed Hamiltonian \(\hat H_0\), with stationary states \(|\phi_n\rangle_t=|\phi_n\rangle e^{-i\omega_nt}\), an additive “small” perturbation Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{int}\) causes the initial state \(|i\rangle_t=|\phi_i\rangle e^{-i\omega_it}\) to transition to \(|f\rangle=|\phi_f\rangle e^{-i\omega_ft}\) at the rate
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
|c_n(t)|^2\sim\lambda^2|H^{(1)}_{mn}|^2\frac{4\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\omega_{mn}t}{2}\right)}{\hbar^2\omega_{mn}^2}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\end{sphinxadmonition}

\subsubsection*{Non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic model of the electron field. Schrodinger equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For an electron in a potential \(V(\mathbf x)\) we impose \(\{\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x),\psi_{\sigma'}^\dagger(\mathbf y)\}=\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)\) and use the one\sphinxhyphen{}body Hamiltonian:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
H_{\rm el}=\sum_\sigma\int d^3x\;\psi_\sigma^\dagger(\mathbf x)\Big[-\frac{\hbar^2\nabla^2}{2m}+V(\mathbf x)\Big]\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Heisenberg equation follows from \([A,BC]=\{A,B\}C-B\{A,C\}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
[\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x),\,\psi^\dagger_{\sigma'}(\mathbf y)\,h\,\psi_{\sigma'}(\mathbf y)]=\delta(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)\,h\,\psi_\sigma(\mathbf y)-\psi^\dagger(\mathbf y)\,h\,\underbrace{\{\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x),\psi_{\sigma'}(\mathbf y)\}}_{=0},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so, integrating over \(\mathbf y\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x,t)=[\psi_\sigma,H_{\rm el}]=\Big[-\frac{\hbar^2\nabla^2}{2m}+V\Big]\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x,t).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{operator} \(\psi\) obeys the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Schrödinger equation}, and the one\sphinxhyphen{}particle wave function is recovered as \(\Phi(\mathbf x,\sigma)=\langle0|\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x)|\Phi\rangle\). “Second quantisation” is therefore not a second quantisation of the same object: what is quantised is a field whose classical equation of motion happens to be the Schrödinger equation.
\subsubsection*{Free electrons}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(V=0\) in the periodic box use plane waves \(\phi_{\mathbf k\sigma}(\mathbf x)=V^{-1/2}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\chi_\sigma\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt V}\sum_{\mathbf k}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}c_{\mathbf k\sigma},\qquad
H_{\rm el}=\sum_{\mathbf k\sigma}\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\,c^\dagger_{\mathbf k\sigma}c_{\mathbf k\sigma},\qquad
\mathbf P=\sum_{\mathbf k\sigma}\hbar\mathbf k\,c^\dagger_{\mathbf k\sigma}c_{\mathbf k\sigma}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A single free electron is \(c^\dagger_{\mathbf k\sigma}|0\rangle\), with energy \(\hbar^2k^2/2m\) and momentum \(\hbar\mathbf k\). The ground state of \(N\) non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting electrons fills the \(N\) lowest \((\mathbf k,\sigma)\) levels, the Fermi sea (a consequence of \((c^\dagger)^2=0\)). The spin label is conserved by \(H_{\rm el}\).
\subsubsection*{Bound electrons}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a hydrogen\sphinxhyphen{}like atom, \(V=-Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0r\), use the orbitals \(\phi_{nlm}(\mathbf x)\chi_\sigma\) with \(E_n=-Z^2\,\text{Ry}/n^2\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\psi_\sigma(\mathbf x)=\sum_{nlm}\phi_{nlm}(\mathbf x)\,c_{nlm\sigma}+\int\!d^3k\;\phi^{(+)}_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf x)\,c_{\mathbf k\sigma},\qquad
H_{\rm el}=\sum_{nlm\sigma}E_n\,c^\dagger_{nlm\sigma}c_{nlm\sigma}+\int\!d^3k\,\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}c^\dagger_{\mathbf k\sigma}c_{\mathbf k\sigma}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The second term, the \sphinxstylestrong{Coulomb scattering states} \(\phi^{(+)}_{\mathbf k}\), completes the basis: bound and continuum states together span \(\mathcal H\). By §1.6 these operators are related to the plane\sphinxhyphen{}wave operators of §4.2 by a unitary transformation, \(c^{\rm plane}_{\mathbf p}=\sum_b\langle\mathbf p|b\rangle c_b+\int\langle\mathbf p|\mathbf k^{(+)}\rangle c_{\mathbf k}\), with the bound\sphinxhyphen{}state momentum distribution \(\langle\mathbf p|b\rangle\) spread over \(|\mathbf p|\sim\hbar/a_0\). \sphinxstylestrong{The Fock space is the same; free and bound electrons differ only by which single\sphinxhyphen{}particle basis diagonalises \(H_{\rm el}\).} A transition \(c^\dagger_{\mathbf k}c_{b}\) is a photoionisation; \(c^\dagger_{b'}c_{b}\) is a bound–bound transition; both are matrix elements of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{same} operator. For an atom with several electrons one adds the two\sphinxhyphen{}body Coulomb term of §1.5 and, in the single\sphinxhyphen{}active\sphinxhyphen{}electron approximation, treats the outermost electron in an effective potential; the light–matter formalism below is unchanged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spin.} Besides the orbital coupling, the electron has a Zeeman\sphinxhyphen{}type term \(H_{\rm spin}=(e\hbar/2m)\,\boldsymbol\sigma\!\cdot\!\mathbf B\) (\(g=2\)). Compared with \(H_1=(e/m)\mathbf A\!\cdot\!\mathbf p\), using \(p\sim\hbar/a_0\) and \(B\sim kA\), the ratio is \(\sim ka_0\sim10^{-3}\) for optical and UV light, so we neglect it; it produces magnetic\sphinxhyphen{}dipole transitions. The fully consistent treatment of spin and its relativistic corrections is given by the Dirac field (§5.6).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Total momentum \(\mathbf P_{\rm el}+\mathbf P_{\rm rad}\) is conserved when \(V=0\), and the total angular momentum and parity in general (§2).

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Transition rates}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-atom-spectrum:transition-rates}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perturbation theory allows to evaluate the transition probability between an initial state \(| i \rangle\) and a final state \(| f \rangle\) of the unperturbed system, with Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(\hat{H}=\hat{H}_0+\hat{H}_I\) with the Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_0=\hat{H}_{\rm el}+\hat{H}_{\rm rad}\) the Hamiltonian of the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting fields. Let the initial and final states be eigenvectors of the unperturbed Hamiltonian, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{H}_0 | i \rangle & = \left( \hat{H}_{\rm el} + \hat{H}_{\rm rad} \right) | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_i \rangle_{\rm el} \otimes | \mathbf{n}^{\rm rad}_i \rangle_{\mathbf{k} \mu} = \left( \sum_{a} n_{a,i}^{\rm el} E_a^{\rm el} + \sum_{\mathbf{k} \mu} n_{\mathbf{k} \mu,i}^{\rm rad} E_{\mathbf{k} \mu} \right) | i \rangle = E_i | i \rangle \\
  \hat{H}_0 | f \rangle & = \left( \hat{H}_{\rm el} + \hat{H}_{\rm rad} \right) | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_f \rangle_{\rm el} \otimes | \mathbf{n}^{\rm rad}_f \rangle_{\mathbf{k} \mu} = \left( \sum_{a} n_{a,f}^{\rm el} E_a^{\rm el} + \sum_{\mathbf{k} \mu} n_{\mathbf{k} \mu,f}^{\rm rad} E_{\mathbf{k} \mu} \right) | f \rangle = E_f | f \rangle \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fermi golden rule} provides the ratio of transition probabilities from \(| i \rangle\) to \(| f \rangle\) as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Gamma_{i\to f}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\,|T_{fi}|^2\,\delta(E_f-E_i),\qquad
T_{fi}=\langle f|H_I|i\rangle+\sum_m\frac{\langle f|H_I|m\rangle\langle m|H_I|i\rangle}{E_i-E_m+i0}+\dots
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(m\) runs over \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} intermediate states of \(H_0\) (including states with extra photons). The sum over final photon modes is \(\sum_{\mathbf k}\to V\!\int d^3k/(2\pi)^3=V\!\int\omega^2\,d\omega\,d\Omega\big/\big((2\pi)^3c^3\big)\), using \(k=\omega/c\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Absorbption and emission are first\sphinxhyphen{}order processes and the transition probabilities are dominated by the term \(\langle f | \hat{H}^{int} | \rangle \sim \langle f | \hat{H}_{\rm 1} | i \rangle\), i.e. using the expression \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-atom-spectrum:eq:atom-spectra:H1}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Absorption, \sphinxstylestrong{assuming} an existing electron in \(| \beta \rangle\) and non existing electron in \(| \alpha \rangle\) (to avoid unnecessary complications with the notation, at least here),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     & \langle f | \hat{H}^{abs}_{\rm 1} | i \rangle = \\
     & = \langle \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_f | \otimes \langle \mathbf{n}_f^{\rm rad} | \left( \sum_{\alpha\beta}\sum_{\mathbf k \mu} M_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu}^{\rm abs} c_\alpha^\dagger c_\beta\,a_{\mathbf k\lambda}  \right)  | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_i \rangle \otimes | \mathbf{n}_i^{\rm rad} \rangle = \\
     & = \langle \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_f | \otimes \langle \mathbf{n}_f^{\rm rad} | \sum_{\alpha\beta \mathbf{k} \mu} M_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu}^{\rm abs} \sqrt{n_{\mathbf{k}\mu}} | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_{i+\alpha-\beta} \rangle \otimes | \mathbf{n}^{\rm rad}_i - \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{k}\mu} \rangle 
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus in a final state with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero transition probability
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
there’s one electron more in \(| \alpha \rangle\), and one electron less in \(| \beta \rangle\) w.r.t. the initial state, and thus \(E^{\rm el}_f = E^{\rm el}_i + E_a - E_b\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a photon with \(\mathbf{k} \mu\) is annihilated (absorbed), so that the radiation energies of the initial and final states are related by \(E_f^{\rm rad} - E_i^{\rm rad} = - \hbar \omega_{\mathbf{k}}\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As the delta condition implies \(E_f = E_i\), then \(E_a - E_b = \hbar \omega_{\mathbf{k}}\) (energy conservation), the transition probability is proportional to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|\langle f | \hat{H}^{\rm abs}_{\rm 1} | i \rangle|^2 = n_{\mathbf{k} \mu} | M^{\rm abs}_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu} |^2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Emission, \sphinxstylestrong{assuming} an existing electron in \(| \beta \rangle\) and non existing electron in \(| \alpha \rangle\) (to avoid unnecessary complications with the notation, at least here),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     & \langle f | \hat{H}^{\rm em}_{\rm 1} | i \rangle = \\
     & = \langle \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_f | \otimes \langle \mathbf{n}_f^{\rm rad} | \left( \sum_{\alpha\beta}\sum_{\mathbf k \mu} M_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu}^{\rm em} c_\alpha^\dagger c_\beta\,a^\dagger_{\mathbf k\lambda}  \right)  | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_i \rangle \otimes | \mathbf{n}_i^{\rm rad} \rangle = \\
     & = \langle \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_f | \otimes \langle \mathbf{n}_f^{\rm rad} | \sum_{\alpha\beta \mathbf{k} \mu} M_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu}^{\rm em} \sqrt{n_{\mathbf{k}\mu} + 1} | \mathbf{n}^{\rm el}_{i+\alpha-\beta} \rangle \otimes | \mathbf{n}^{\rm rad}_i - \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{k}\mu} \rangle 
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus in a final state with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero transition probability
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
there’s one electron more in \(| \alpha \rangle\), and one electron less in \(| \beta \rangle\) w.r.t. the initial state, and thus \(E^{\rm el}_f = E^{\rm el}_i + E_a - E_b\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a photon with \(\mathbf{k} \mu\) is created (emitted), so that the radiation energies of the initial and final states are related by \(E_f^{\rm rad} - E_i^{\rm rad} = \hbar \omega_{\mathbf{k}}\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As the delta condition implies \(E_f = E_i\), then \(E_a = E_b - \hbar \omega_{\mathbf{k}}\) (energy conservation), the transition probability is proportional to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|\langle f | \hat{H}^{\rm em}_{\rm 1} | i \rangle|^2 = ( n_{\mathbf{k} \mu} + 1) | M^{\rm em}_{\alpha \beta \mathbf{k} \mu} |^2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}




\paragraph{Absorption and emission of light by an atom}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-atom-spectrum:absorption-and-emission-of-light-by-an-atom}}\subsubsection*{Time dependence and energy conservation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \hat{a}_{\mathbf{k}, \mu}^\dagger & \sim e^{ i \frac{E_{\mathbf{k},\mu}}{\hbar} t} \\
 \hat{a}_{\mathbf{k}, \mu}         & \sim e^{-i \frac{E_{\mathbf{k},\mu}}{\hbar} t} \\
 \hat{c}_\alpha^\dagger            & \sim e^{ i \frac{E_\alpha}{\hbar} t} \\
 \hat{c}_\beta                     & \sim e^{-i \frac{E_\beta }{\hbar} t} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \hat{c}_\alpha^\dagger \hat{c}_\beta \hat{a}_{\mathbf{k},\mu} | n_\alpha n_\beta n_{\mathbf{k}, \mu}\rangle = | (n+1)_\alpha (n-1)_\beta (n-1)_{\mathbf{k}, \mu}\rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix elements.} Let the atom go from level \(a\) to \(b\). With \(n\) photons in the mode \((\mathbf k,\lambda)\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\text{absorption}\ (E_b>E_a):\ \langle b;n{-}1|H_1|a;n\rangle=\frac em N_k\sqrt n\,\langle b|e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|a\rangle,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\text{emission}\ (E_b<E_a):\ \langle b;n{+}1|H_1|a;n\rangle=\frac em N_k\sqrt{n+1}\,\langle b|e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|a\rangle,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
using \(a|n\rangle=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle\) and \(a^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}|n+1\rangle\). The rates are therefore proportional to \(n\) for absorption and to \((n+1)\) for emission: the part \(\propto n\) is \sphinxstylestrong{stimulated emission} (the mirror image of absorption), and the part \(\propto1\) is \sphinxstylestrong{spontaneous emission}, which survives in the vacuum (\(n=0\)) and is caused by the zero\sphinxhyphen{}point field of §3.3. A classical field acting on quantised matter gives no spontaneous emission at all (cf. Chapter 1, §2.4).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dipole approximation.} Over the size of the atom, \(\mathbf k\!\cdot\!\mathbf x\sim ka_0\). For the hydrogen Lyman\sphinxhyphen{}\(\alpha\) line, \(\omega a_0/c=\tfrac38\alpha=2.7\times10^{-3}\), so \(e^{\pm i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}=1+O(10^{-3})\) and we replace it by \(1\). The remaining matrix element is converted using \([\mathbf x,H_0]=i\hbar\mathbf p/m\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\langle b|[\mathbf x,H_0]|a\rangle=(E_a-E_b)\langle b|\mathbf x|a\rangle=\frac{i\hbar}{m}\langle b|\mathbf p|a\rangle
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\langle b|\mathbf p|a\rangle=-\,i\,m\,\omega\,\langle b|\mathbf x|a\rangle\quad\big(\hbar\omega=E_a-E_b\big),
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(for absorption \(E_a<E_b\) the same identity holds with a sign change, which drops out of \(|\cdot|^2\)). With the dipole matrix element \(\mathbf d_{ba}=-e\langle b|\mathbf x|a\rangle\) the emission matrix element has modulus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
|M|^2=\Big(\frac em\Big)^2N_k^2\,(n+1)\,m^2\omega^2|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\langle b|\mathbf x|a\rangle|^2=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2\varepsilon_0V}\,(n+1)\,|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf d_{ba}|^2 .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spontaneous emission rate} (\(n=0\)). Apply the golden rule, with \(\delta(E_a-E_b-\hbar\omega)=\delta(\omega-\omega_{ab})/\hbar\) and the sum of §5.2:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Gamma=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{1}{\hbar}\cdot\frac{V\omega^2}{(2\pi)^3c^3}\cdot\frac{\hbar\omega}{2\varepsilon_0V}\int d\Omega\sum_\lambda|\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\lambda\!\cdot\!\mathbf d_{ba}|^2
=\frac{\omega^3}{8\pi^2\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3}\int d\Omega\sum_\lambda|\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\lambda\!\cdot\!\mathbf d_{ba}|^2 .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By polarisation completeness, \(\sum_\lambda|\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\lambda\!\cdot\!\mathbf d|^2=|\mathbf d|^2-|\hat{\mathbf k}\!\cdot\!\mathbf d|^2\), and with \(\int d\Omega\,\hat k_i\hat k_j=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\delta_{ij}\) the angular integral is \(4\pi|\mathbf d|^2-\tfrac{4\pi}{3}|\mathbf d|^2=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}|\mathbf d|^2\). The result is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\boxed{\;\Gamma_{a\to b}=\frac{\omega^3\,|\mathbf d_{ba}|^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3}\;}\qquad\Big(\text{angular distribution }\propto\sin^2\theta\text{ from }\mathbf d\Big),
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the Einstein \(A\) coefficient derived from first principles (Dirac, 1927). It is the number quoted in Chapter 1, §2.4.
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-atom-spectrum:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 25.6.1 (\sphinxstylestrong{Worked example: hydrogen \protect\(2p\to1s\protect\) (Lyman\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(\alpha\protect\)).} )}



\sphinxAtStartPar
The photon energy is \(\hbar\omega=\tfrac34\,\text{Ry}=10.204\) eV, i.e. \(\lambda=121.5\) nm. With \(R_{10}=2e^{-r/a_0}a_0^{-3/2}\), \(R_{21}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt6}(r/a_0)\,e^{-r/2a_0}a_0^{-3/2}\), the radial integral is \(\int R_{10}\,r\,R_{21}\,r^2dr=1.2903\,a_0\) and the angular factor \(\langle00|\cos\theta|10\rangle=1/\sqrt3\), giving
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\langle1s|z|2p,m{=}0\rangle=\frac{2^{15/2}}{3^5}\,a_0=0.7449\,a_0 .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(The rate is the same for \(m=0,\pm1\) by rotation symmetry.) Then \(|\mathbf d_{ba}|^2=e^2(0.7449\,a_0)^2\) and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Gamma=6.27\times10^{8}\ \text{s}^{-1},\qquad\tau=1/\Gamma=1.60\ \text{ns},\qquad\Delta\nu_{\rm nat}=\Gamma/2\pi\simeq100\ \text{MHz}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The measured \(2p\) lifetime is \(1.60\) ns. By contrast, the \(2s\) level cannot decay to \(1s\) by a one\sphinxhyphen{}photon E1 transition (no parity change, \(\Delta l=0\), §2.4); in isolated hydrogen it decays by emitting \sphinxstyleemphasis{two} photons at a rate of only \(\approx8\ \text{s}^{-1}\) (lifetime \(\approx0.12\) s), about eight orders of magnitude slower than the allowed \(2p\) decay.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The classical limit of the rate.} A classical electron oscillator (Lorentz model) of angular frequency \(\omega\) radiates, by Larmor’s formula \(P=e^2\omega^4x_0^2/(12\pi\varepsilon_0c^3)\), with energy \(\tfrac12m\omega^2x_0^2\), so its energy decays at rate \(\gamma_{\rm cl}=e^2\omega^2/(6\pi\varepsilon_0mc^3)\). Define the oscillator strength \(f_{ba}=\frac{2m\omega}{3\hbar g_b}\sum_{ab}|\langle a|\mathbf r|b\rangle|^2\) (\(g\) = degeneracy; the sum runs over all sublevels). Substituting into \(\Gamma\) gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\Gamma_{a\to b}=3\,\frac{g_b}{g_a}\,f_{ba}\,\gamma_{\rm cl}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For Lyman\sphinxhyphen{}\(\alpha\), \(f=0.416\), \(g_{1s}/g_{2p}=1/3\) (orbital degeneracies) and \(\gamma_{\rm cl}=1.51\times10^{9}\ \text{s}^{-1}\), so \(\Gamma=f\gamma_{\rm cl}=6.27\times10^8\ \text{s}^{-1}\) again: \sphinxstylestrong{the quantum emission rate is the classical radiation\sphinxhyphen{}damping rate times the oscillator strength}, the dimensionless measure of “how much of a classical oscillator” the transition is. The factor \(\hbar\) has dropped out of the structure, as it must in a correspondence\sphinxhyphen{}principle statement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Thermal equilibrium and Einstein’s relations.} In blackbody radiation each mode has mean occupation \(\bar n=1/(e^{\hbar\omega/k_BT}-1)\). Summing the above over modes, the total emission rate from a level \(a\) is \(A(\bar n+1)\) and the absorption rate of an atom in \(b\) is \((g_a/g_b)A\bar n\) (because the double sum \(\sum_{ab}|\mathbf d_{ab}|^2\) is common). Balancing the populations, \(N_a\,A(\bar n+1)=N_b\,(g_a/g_b)A\bar n\), gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{N_a}{N_b}=\frac{g_a}{g_b}\frac{\bar n}{\bar n+1}=\frac{g_a}{g_b}\,e^{-\hbar\omega/k_BT},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
exactly the Boltzmann distribution. This is Einstein’s 1917 argument (Chapter 1, §2.4), where \(A\), \(B_{12}\), \(B_{21}\) were related by consistency, now obtained as a \sphinxstyleemphasis{theorem} of the quantised theory: the “+1” is spontaneous emission.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Beyond the dipole approximation.} Expanding \(e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}=1+i\mathbf k\!\cdot\!\mathbf x+\dots\) gives electric\sphinxhyphen{}quadrupole and magnetic\sphinxhyphen{}dipole transitions, suppressed by \((ka_0)^2\sim10^{-5}\) in rate: these account for “forbidden” lines.

\subsubsection{Free electrons \sphinxhyphen{} Compton scattering}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-compton:free-electrons-compton-scattering}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-compton:quantum-mechanics-qft-interactions-e-em-fields-compton-scattering}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/qft/interactions-e-em-fields-compton::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Setup.} Take \(V=0\) and an electron initially at rest with spin \(\sigma\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
|i\rangle=c^\dagger_{\mathbf 0\sigma}\,a^\dagger_{\mathbf k\lambda}|0\rangle,\qquad|f\rangle=c^\dagger_{\mathbf p'\sigma'}\,a^\dagger_{\mathbf k'\lambda'}|0\rangle,\qquad\mathbf p'=\hbar(\mathbf k-\mathbf k')\ \ \text{(momentum conservation)}.
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are three contributions at order \(e^2\), the time\sphinxhyphen{}ordered diagrams: (a) the seagull \(H_2\) acting once; (b) \(H_1\) twice, absorbing \(\mathbf k\) first then emitting \(\mathbf k'\); (c) \(H_1\) twice, emitting \(\mathbf k'\) first then absorbing \(\mathbf k\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The \(H_1H_1\) terms vanish.} In (b) the first vertex is \(\langle\hbar\mathbf k|e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|\mathbf 0\rangle\propto\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p_i=0\) because \(\mathbf p\) acts on the initial state, which has \(\mathbf p_i=0\). In (c) the first vertex is \(\propto\boldsymbol\varepsilon'\!\cdot\!\mathbf p_i=0\) for the same reason. (This is exact in Coulomb gauge: \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p\) acts \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} the intermediate momentum appears.) For a moving electron these terms are of relative order \(p/mc\), producing the Doppler broadening of the Compton line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The seagull term.} The matrix element of \(\mathbf A^2\) between \(|\mathbf k\lambda\rangle\) and \(|\mathbf k'\lambda'\rangle\) has two contributions (\(q=\mathbf k,q'=\mathbf k'\) and the swap), so
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\langle f|H_2|i\rangle=\frac{e^2}{2m}\cdot2N_kN_{k'}\,(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon')\;\underbrace{\frac1V\!\int d^3x\,e^{i(\mathbf k-\mathbf k')\cdot\mathbf x}\,e^{-i\mathbf p'\cdot\mathbf x/\hbar}}_{\delta_{\mathbf p',\hbar(\mathbf k-\mathbf k')}}
=\frac{e^2\hbar}{2m\varepsilon_0V\sqrt{\omega\omega'}}\,(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon')\,\delta_{\mathbf p',\hbar(\mathbf k-\mathbf k')},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(using \(N_kN_{k'}=\hbar/(2\varepsilon_0V\sqrt{\omega\omega'})\); the electron plane waves \(V^{-1/2}e^{i\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x/\hbar}\) supply the \(1/V\), and \(\mathbf p_i=0\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cross\sphinxhyphen{}section.} The golden rule with the final photon density of states \(V\omega'^2d\Omega/\big((2\pi)^3c^3\hbar\big)\) (we neglect the electron recoil in the Jacobian \(dE_f/d\omega'=\hbar(1+O(\hbar\omega/mc^2))\)) gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\Big(\frac{e^2\hbar}{2m\varepsilon_0V\sqrt{\omega\omega'}}\Big)^2|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'|^2\frac{V\omega'^2}{8\pi^3c^3\hbar}
=\frac{e^4}{16\pi^2m^2\varepsilon_0^2c^3V}\,\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\,|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'|^2 .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The incident flux is one photon per volume \(V\) at speed \(c\), i.e. \(c/V\). Dividing,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\boxed{\;\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}=r_e^2\,\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\,|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'|^2,\qquad r_e=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0mc^2}=2.818\ \text{fm}\;}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(using \(e^4/(16\pi^2m^2\varepsilon_0^2c^4)=r_e^2\)). This is \sphinxstylestrong{Thomson scattering}, derived here from the quantised theory, with a polarisation dependence \(|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'|^2\) (the scattered photon keeps the projected polarisation of the incident one).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unpolarised light.} Summing over the final polarisations with completeness, \(\sum_{\lambda'}|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'_{\lambda'}|^2=1-(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf k}')^2\), and averaging over the two incident polarisations, \(\tfrac12\sum_\lambda(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_\lambda\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf k}')^2=\tfrac12\sin^2\theta\) (the two polarisations transverse to \(\hat{\mathbf k}\) together project onto \(\hat{\mathbf k}'\) with weight \(1-\cos^2\theta\)). The polarisation\sphinxhyphen{}averaged factor is thus \(1-\tfrac12\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos^2\theta)\). Hence
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\Big|_{\rm unpol}=\frac{r_e^2}{2}\,\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\,(1+\cos^2\theta),\qquad
\sigma_{\rm T}=\frac{8\pi}{3}r_e^2=6.652\times10^{-29}\ \text{m}^2=0.665\ \text{b},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
using \(\int(1+\cos^2\theta)\,d\Omega=16\pi/3\) and \(\omega'/\omega\to1\). The cross\sphinxhyphen{}section is independent of the frequency and of \(\hbar\): it is the classical result of an electron driven by the wave and radiating as a Hertzian dipole, recovered as the leading term of a quantum calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two physical consequences follow from the factor \(|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'|^2\):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The component of the incident polarisation perpendicular to the scattering plane scatters with weight \(1\), the in\sphinxhyphen{}plane component with weight \(\cos^2\theta\). At \(\theta=90^\circ\) the scattered light is therefore \sphinxstylestrong{100\% linearly polarised} (perpendicular to the plane), with degree of polarisation \((1-\cos^2\theta)/(1+\cos^2\theta)\) in general. This is why scattered light, in the sky and in the cosmic microwave background, is polarised.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where electrons are free, mean free paths are set by \(\ell=1/(n_e\sigma_{\rm T})\): in the solar core (\(n_e\approx6\times10^{31}\,\text{m}^{-3}\)) this is \(\approx0.25\) mm.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Kinematics: the Compton shift from energy conservation.} The delta function enforces \(\hbar\omega=\hbar\omega'+\hbar^2|\mathbf k-\mathbf k'|^2/2m\). Write \(|\mathbf k-\mathbf k'|^2=(k-k')^2+2kk'(1-\cos\theta)\). The first term is second order in the small shift, so to leading order in \(\hbar\omega/mc^2\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
c\,(k-k')=\frac{\hbar k^2(1-\cos\theta)}{m}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac1{k'}-\frac1k=\frac{k-k'}{kk'}\simeq\frac{\hbar(1-\cos\theta)}{mc},
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and with \(\lambda=2\pi/k\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\lambda'-\lambda=\frac{h}{mc}\,(1-\cos\theta),
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the Compton formula of Chapter 1, now as the energy conservation of the Fock\sphinxhyphen{}space matrix element above. (The exact \sphinxstyleemphasis{relativistic} kinematics gives the same formula without approximation.)

(For the Mo line, the wavelength shift is \(2.4263\) pm exactly, against \(2.4277\) pm from the non\sphinxhyphen{}relativistic balance.) The relativistic theory (quoted: \sphinxstylestrong{Klein–Nishina}, 1929, requiring the Dirac field) gives for unpolarised light
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}

\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which reduces to our result when \(\omega'\to\omega\): \(\tfrac12(2-\sin^2\theta)=\tfrac12(1+\cos^2\theta)\). Integrated over angles, the total cross\sphinxhyphen{}section relative to Thomson is \(\sigma_{\rm KN}/\sigma_{\rm T}=0.937\) at 17.44 keV, \(0.741\) at 100 keV, \(0.385\) at 662 keV and \(0.125\) at 5 MeV: the forward\sphinxhyphen{}peaked, energy\sphinxhyphen{}dependent suppression that makes high\sphinxhyphen{}energy photons penetrating.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Gauge invariance and the seagull.} In the calculation above only \(H_2\) contributed. Had we dropped it as “a second\sphinxhyphen{}order nuisance”, the amplitude for a free electron at rest would vanish and scattering would be absent, which contradicts the classical (and experimental) Thomson result. The coefficient of \(H_2\) is tied to that of \(H_1\) by gauge invariance (§2.3), and the amplitude at \(\omega\to0\), \(-r_e\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'\), is fixed by the charge and mass alone (a \sphinxstyleemphasis{low\sphinxhyphen{}energy theorem}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Scattering by a bound electron (quoted).} For an atomic electron initially in \(|a\rangle\) and finally in \(|b\rangle\), with the same ingredients (the three diagrams and the dipole approximation), the amplitude is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
T_{ba}\propto\frac{e^2}{m}\Big[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\varepsilon'\,\delta_{ba}+\frac1m\sum_m\Big(\frac{\langle b|\boldsymbol\varepsilon'\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|m\rangle\langle m|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|a\rangle}{E_a+\hbar\omega-E_m}+\frac{\langle b|\boldsymbol\varepsilon\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|m\rangle\langle m|\boldsymbol\varepsilon'\!\cdot\!\mathbf p|a\rangle}{E_a-\hbar\omega'-E_m}\Big)\Big],
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{Kramers–Heisenberg formula} (1925), with the intermediate states \(m\) of the atom (including the continuum). The three regimes are all contained in it: for \(\hbar\omega\gg\) binding energies the denominators are large, the second term is negligible and one recovers free\sphinxhyphen{}electron \sphinxstylestrong{Thomson} scattering; for \(\hbar\omega\ll E_m-E_a\) the \(\omega\)\sphinxhyphen{}independent terms cancel against the seagull by the Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn sum rule \(\sum_m(E_m-E_a)|\langle m|x|a\rangle|^2=\hbar^2/2m\), leaving the \sphinxstylestrong{Rayleigh} law \(\sigma\propto\omega^4\) (blue sky); and for \(\hbar\omega\to E_m-E_a\) the denominators vanish and the amplitude has a \sphinxstylestrong{resonance} (resonance fluorescence), regulated by the natural linewidth \(\Gamma\) of §5.3.
